Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the Mims'ei of Agriculture whether any information has been given to the government with respect to the embargo against Canadian potatoes?

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for
Victoria-Carleton gave notice of this question, and in reply I believe I could not do better than to read a communication I received from the Minister of Agriculture and Fisheries of the United Kingdom. It is as follows:
Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries,
10 Whitehall Place, S.W. 1.
January 27, 1933.
Dear Mr. Weir,-
You will, of course, remember that in accordance with a promise made to you by my predecessor, Sir John Gilmour, Mr. J. C. F Fryer, director of the ministry's plant pathological Laboratory, visited Canada last October, in connection with the Colorado beetle question.
Before I come to the subject of his investigations I should like to express to you, and through you to all those with whom he came in contact during his tour, my sineerest thanks for the cordial reception accorded to him, and the ungrudging assistance in every direction which he received throughout his visit.
I have now gone into the matter with hirn with the greatest interest and care. I was greatly impressed by his account of the keenness and efficiency of the staff of your department, and of the precautions which they are prepared to take against the risk of the transmission of the Colorado beetle with potatoes consigned from the dominion. I do not doubt that the measures proposed or contemplated would be likely to reduce that danger very materially, but nevertheless I am forced to the conclusion that we cannot take the risk involved by accepting potatoes from any region where the Colorado
Deportations

beetle is known to exist. I can only ask you to believe that it is with very real regret and after the most anxious thought that I have arrived at the decision that the prohibition cannot be removed and I hope that you will appreciate that it is the only policy that I can pursue consistently with my responsibilities in connection with plant pests and diseases. It is a generally recognized policy that has been consistently followed by my predecessors in regard to all countries where the beetle exists and, much as I should like to, I cannot see my way to make an exception even in your case. '
Mr. Fryer has also reported to me the measures which you contemplate in order to prevent the export to this country of apples infested with the apple fruit fly. Much to our pleasure, it has not so far been necessary for us to place any restrictions on apples imported from the dominion. The discovery of an infested consignment last October, was, we hope, only an isolated case; and after considering Mr. Fryer's account of the steps you are taking, I have decided that it will not be necessary to impose any restrictions during the 1933 season unless the sampling of consignments on arrival in this country reveals the presence of the pest.
Yours very truly,
Walter Elliot.

Would the minister be good enough to give the committee a general statement of the progress of the Hudson Bay Railway and terminal?
Hon. R. J. MANIO'N (Minister of Railways and Canals): This vote is for the continuation of the work that has been going on for some years at Churchill and on the Hudson Bay railway. The work that has already been done consists of the railway itself which is in very excellent shape; I did not visit it last year, but I did the previous two years, and the roadbed was in splended shape though every spring, because of the heavily frozen section of the country through which the railway runs, there are a number of sink holes and that sort of thing. Consequently it still requires a good deal of money to be spent upon it. So that half of this vote is for the rehabilitation of the Hudson Bay railway itself from The Pas to Churchill as well as for maintenance and operation during construction. It is hoped that after this year or next year the railway will have been so well ballasted that these sink holes will no longer develop. At any rate, it is in good shape.
The other work that has been done is at Churchill itself. At that port we have an elevator of two and a half million bushels capacity; we have a dock eighteen hundred feet long; we have a freight shed that was more than adequate to handle the freight last year, we have coal-handling facilities, and the harbour is well dredged, except for one item that is included in this vote for dredging this year, and which it is expected will complete the dredging required at Churchill. The general work there is in excellent condition. The traffic that went through the port last year was well handled
Supply-Railways-Hudson Bay

in every way. A large portion of this item is for the completion of the water supply, the engineers having found that they had to go four or five miles from the townsite of Churchill to get fresh water. They had to connect up a number of sloughs into a fairly large lake of fresh water, which acts as a reservoir, and from which they bring water by a pipe line just above the ground. It is surrounded or is being surrounded gradually by moss to protect it from freezing. That, briefly, is a sketch of what has taken place there. I shall be glad to give any further information that is needed.

What has been the total
cost of the Hudson Bay railway, including terminals, and how much loss was incurred last year, including interest on capital expenditure?

The total investment on
the Hudson Bay railway and the port of Churchill terminals, and in respect of the deserted Nelson terminals, is, in round figures, between $53,000,000 and $54,000 000.
Including interest?

No, that represents actual expenditures that have been made. I doubt whether I can give anything like an exact estimate of the cost of traffic last year. There was not very much traffic. Two and a hall million bushels of grain was handled and a small amount of other merchandise went through. The two and a half million bushels went out in ten steamers, including the one which was sunk in Hudson straits, and a small amount, about three hundred and some odd tons, of general merchandise came in. In addition to the traffic which went out of and came into the port, there is a good deal of traffic up and down the line in between and to the port itself, and of course, in a sense, it is really at the expense of the government. The revenue and expenditures of the railway itself last year, if one leaves out maintenance, were pretty well balanced. There was an actual loss of three or four thousand on operation and it is expected that there will be about the same loss this year. Of course, there was no manienance charge, which amounted last year to about $64,000, and which snould be charged up to the operation of the road. There is interest on investment, which is not included.

It will cost the treasury
each year, a? a net loss to the railway, something between two and three million dollars. Would that be approximately correct?
I Mr. Manion.]

Yes. Of course, the
interest alone on $50,000,000 would be two and a half million dollars, roughly, so that that was a direct charge upon the exchequer or Canada. In regard to the operation of the port, there is, naturally, a loss, because so far we have not charged either elevator or port charges on any of the traffic going through. I may say frankly however-I might as well say it now as later, because I have had a number of letters from the west with regard to the matter-that the question is still under consideration as to what we shall do in that regard in the coming year. The elevator handled last year two and a half million bushels, and there were no elevator charges imposed upon that grain, no port charges by the port. It is probably only just that charges should be applied to freight going through that port, as to freight going through other ports in Canada. However, the government ;s considering the whole matter. No definite decision has been reached yet as to these charges, but I believe there will probably be some charges on a low scale this year with respect to the elevator, if not on the whole port. The government wishes as did the late government, to give every encouragement to the utilization of the facilities at that port. We believe that since we have spent so much money there it would not be wise, for the sake of a small amount, to do anything that might cripple the port. And of course the west- is fairlj' strong in its demands along these lines. Some of the eastern and probably some of the western ports are not so -enthusiastic over the rates being so low.
Does the minister anticipate any substantial improvement in the immediate years to come?
In traffic?
Yes.

Well, my hon. friend can
guess at that as well as I can.

Not quite. Is there any
traffic coming in?

Two years ago we handled two ships and last year ten. That is an increase of 500 per cent. It illustrates very well the futility of using percentages. At any rate, we did handle ten ships and I myself believe quite frankly that there will be an increase. But the whole trade of the world is in such a deplorable condition to-day that-

Hear, hear.

Supply-Railways-Hudson Bay

I do not know why my
hon. friends should cheer; I am not glad that it is so. I do not know why they should be pleased that world trade is down.
We blame you.

Anyone who does not
admit that world trade is in a deplorable condition must be more dense than some of my friends of the cooperative organization to the right.

You are
not so dense as you used to be.

I am glad that I too am
improving. I think there will be an increase in traffic; at least I hope so for the sake of the expenditures that have been made. Before elections one can prophesy, but it is not well to do so afterwards.

Can the minister
give the committee any information at all regarding the prospect of insurance rates being lowered on the route, or has the sinking of the Bright Fan knocked all this on the head?

My expectation is that
insurance rates will certainly not be higher than they were last year, even taking into consideration the sinking of the Bright Fan. I believe that the report of the commission that investigated that matter will offset any harm it might have done the route. Whether there will be much of a decrease, however, I doubt. I made inquiries and I am informed that the loss of the Bright Fan will about wipe out the premiums which the insurance companies have so far received on traffic. Naturally, the imperial shipping committee will not be enthusiastic about lowering rates. At the same time, the government, through the Marine department, which handles that branch of the work, has been impressing upon the Canadian High Commisisoner in London, and, through him, upon the imperial shipping committee, the importance of lowering insurance rates, and I can assure my hon. friend that the government will do everything it can to have the rates brought down. I do not think, even though the insurance rates are high, that they are sufficiently high to interfere with reasonable profits to such ships as go into Hudson bay, especially if they get cargoes each wray. I am informed that the ships that have already gone in have done much better in the same length of time than they would have done if plying to other ports. I should, not like to give that as absolutely authentic, but the shipping men so inform me.

The minister is
aware of the attitude of the hon. member representing The Pas and of other persons who have been up in that country, with respect to the causes of the sinking of the Bright Fan. It is generally conceded that it looked around a few days and then banged into that iceberg for some purpose or other. I do not think the idea was to do damage to the route; I think it was to collect insurance upon an old boat which had been insured very heavily. These rumours should be settled and I was wondering if the government had taken any steps, either when the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) was over in England or otherwise, to get at the bottom of these statements. I have no doubt the minister will tell us all he knows about it.

This government did every thing which I think a government was required to do; it investigated the whole matter. The result of the investigation was that the ship had not been handled very well, that the only lookout was a boy of eighteen years of age. To anyone like myself, or my hon. friend, who is not a sea-dog, that fact would seem to condemn the handling of the ship. As to looking around for an iceberg, as the hon. member for Nelson (Mr. Stitt) so picturesquely expresses it, we must realize that the ship is at the bottom of the sea, and it would be rather difficult to find out if it did really look around for an iceberg. I am afraid that is one question that will have to be left to later ministers to explain. We did everything we possibly could. We made a thorough investigation by a commission. The work of the commission, which was well done by the commissioner and the counsel appointed by the government to assist him, has, I 'think, undone any harm from an insurance standpoint which the sinking of the Bright Fan may have inflicted upon this route.
Does the minister know whether this boat was heavily insured, and if the insurance was paid? Did Lloyd's or whoever insured the boat pay this insurance?

I am sorry, but I cannot give my hon. friend that information. I did hear that the ship, although not an old one, was not in the best of condition. However, that is only hearsay, and I should not like to be quoted authoritatively in that regard. The ship was not particularly valuable, but no ship is valuable at the present time. Unfortunately this government has had to sell ships much below the cost price, and other steamship companies and governments have had to do the same thing. I imagine that if

Supply-Railways-Hudson Bay
I had a ship full of grain and it was well insured, as long as no lives were lost I would not weep very much if the ship hit an iceberg. Beyond that I should not like to go.

I cannot allow the former Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) to make the insinuations he did with regard to the sinking of the Bright Fan. The fact that a ship is old and is well insured is no reason why an hon. member should get up and say that the vessel was cast away and that the captain had committed barratry. Everyone knows there are icebergs in Hudson bay; everyone knows there are dangers in Hudson strait, and this accident should not be used as capital either in favour of or against the Hudson bay route. The statement should not be made that this ship deliberately ran into an iceberg. The minister has apologized because he did not think there was sufficient lookout upon this steamer, but I would refer him to his own youth. He could see better when he was eighteen years of age than he can to-day.

Much better politically.
Mr. MANION; I am afraid I missed that one; as it seems to be good I should like to hear it.

In order to satisfy the curiosity of the former Minister of Agriculture, the minister said that perhaps there was not sufficient lookout upon the Bright Fan when it struck the iceberg because only a boy of eighteen years of age was acting as lookout. I want to say to the minister that that boy had as good eyesight as the minister himself bad when he was eighteen years of age, before he turned Tory.
I was very young.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I hope no reflection is being cast upon the chair.

Not at all. With my slight
knowledge of marine matters I would rather trust a boy of eighteen as lookout than either the minister or myself at our ages. I would rather trust him than the former Minister of Agriculture, who, although he can see, is a little deaf in one ear; he would not be able to hear the iceberg blow its fog-horn. We should not stress the fact that because one vessel has been lost there may be danger in Hudson strait or Hudson bay. I hope that this route can be proved to be a satisfactory one, and no apologies are necessary from western members or anyone else, whether Liberal or Conservative. The Liberal government helped to build this route, it spent con-

siderable money both in Port Nelson and Churchill; the Conservative party continued that work and are trying now to complete it. There is nothing to apologize for; the fact remains that we have spent -the money and we must find out whether or not this route is a proper route.

Has the hon.
member lost any of his boats?

No. Because this boat was
lost coming out of Hudson bay, it should not be said that the captain- or his officers were to blame for the accident. I wonder if the minister could tell us the insurance rate on grain from Churchill to Liverpool, and also if the government pays any proportion of the premium either to the insurance company or to the shippers?

Although I think I could
give the approximate insurance rate, I would be only guessing. I will get the information for the hon. member before we have completed this item. I should like to quote from the report of the commission that investigated the loss of the Bright Fan. It reads?
The court thinks that a proper lookout was not kept on -the Bright Fan. There was no expressly appointed lookout and for some minutes before the collision with the iceberg apparently the only person on the ship who had any opportunity of seeing the approach of danger was the helmsman, an apprentice of eighteen years of age.
The ship was proceeding at full speed but having regard to the visibility, as to which the evidence is not very satisfactory, the court is not prepared to find that the speed was exeesr sive.
The court cannot too strongly intimate that a lookout should be maintained under all circumstances by some person or persons whose sole duty for the time being is to keep a lookout. It appears that such was not the practice o-n this ship. Under the circumstances disclosed in this case the court regrets that it is unable to exonerate the master -and first officer of the Bright Fan from default contributing to the loss of the ship in failing to see that such a lookout was maintained.
What court was that?

That was the commission
appointed to investigate -the sinking of the Bright Fan, Mr. Justice Mellish being in charge. Like my hon. friend who has just spoken, he is from Nova Scotia and knows the shipping business, having had much experience in admiralty matters. He was assisted by other officers, but unless it is necessary I would not like to give their names.

I do not wish to criticize the report of the commissioner, who is one of the outstanding judges in the maritime provinces, but I would state that in the case of a tramp steamer like the Bright Fan there

Supply-Railways-Hudson Bay
is no necessity to have two men as lookouts. The man at the helm can see through the window, whether or not it is up, practically as far as a man on the bridge. In addition to that, the first officer was on deck. I was very anxious to attend the meetings of the committee; I heard all the evidence and I was very much impressed by the captain. I have no hesitation in saying that he was a good seaman and did everything he could to get the propter directions from the N. B. McLean, so that he could avoid icebergs. There was a sufficient lookout when there was a man at the helm who could see ahead. This apprentice, this eighteen year old young man, was on the bridge and the first officer was on deck, but just at the moment the accident occurred, the latter was on deck attending to his duties, so I do not think it fair to say that the Bright Fan was lost because there was not a sufficient lookout. It is just an accident such as happens every day in the marine world. Neither the Hudson Bay railway, nor the Minister of Marine nor the Minister of Railways should be blamed for the accident.

In justice to the owners
of the ship, since I read the other clause, I should like to read a couple of remaining clauses that in fairness to them are worthy of being put on record. They say at the end of their report:
Although no specific question has been submitted in respect thereto, the evidence raised some points as to which it is perhaps proper an opinion should be expressed.
In the first place the court is of opinion that there is no evidence on which to conclude that the loss of the ship can in any degree be attributed to the improper use of intoxicating liquors-indeed the evidence would lead to a distinctly contrary conclusion.
In the next place, it cannot on the evidence be said that the loss was in any way contributed to by any defect in the equipment furnished for the safety of shipping in the locality. Indeed-such equipment has in the court's opinion, been shown to be distinctly helpful and useful.
And the other question, number five, states:
Was the vessel in all respects in ia good and seaworthy condition -when she left Churchill on the 25th September?
I may say that the answer to the question is in the affirmative. I do not wish to do any injustice to anybody in the matter. The full investigation and the report upon it are at the disposal of the committee and the members of the house. I do not think it is my duty to give my opinion on the finding of the commission.

Was not a further investigation held at London? If so, what 53719-126^
about the conclusion there? Can the minister amplify it?
I know of no investigation at London. If one had been held, I imagine the Maritime department or I would have been advised, but I do not know about it.

The British Board of Trade
held one.

I have no record and
therefore can give no information.

Could the minister get
the record of that investigation, or will he try to get it?

I shall endeavour to do
so.

No, the government had

Was the Bright Fan sunk in broad daylight?
No; if my recollection is correct, it was four o'clock in the morning, a fairly good day, with good visibility, although the judge says that the evidence as to visibility is inconclusive.
In which direction was the boat going?

It was sailing toward
England. It was going out of the port.

There came to my notice last fall the fact that the Manitoba, government is going to supervise the new townsite of Churchill. I believe this is a step in the right direction, because in northern Ontario we had an example of a great deal of speculation in the opening of new town-sites. I see the government is trying to do away with that. The question I wanted to ask is the following: Are government buildings in Churchill, including terminal elevators
Supply-Railways-Hudson Bay

and all buildings pertaining to the Canadian. National Railways as well as their terminals, to be exempt from municipal taxes?
All government buildings and property are exempt from taxation throughout Canada. I assume the situation will be the same in Churchill as elsewhere.

I believe the question is not rightly answered. In my section the Canadian National Railways constructed private houses in competition with private individuals. The question came before the board of railway commissioners, and the result was that these houses were to be taxed municipally in so far as the schools were concerned. I hope a similar condition will not exist at Churchill. I am alluding more particularly to private houses and boarding houses. In our section we carried on for at least fifteen years without receiving school taxes. This is a matter that should be taken up now so that no anomaly will exist.
I assume the hon. member is stating that houses which were built by the National Transcontinental in that section pay no taxes. That is what he stated.
Yes.

I suppose this is on the same ground that the National Transcontinental is a government railway, although, of course, it is being operated by the Canadian National, but the Canadian National Railway itself pays taxes in various places throughout Canada, the total amounting to between four and five million dollars. They are government railways in my hon. friend's section and for that reason they probably would not pay taxes, although I cannot state so definitely, but I presume my hon. friend is well informed on the matter.

In our own section, for a number of years dwelling houses for railroad officials and employees were built in competition with private owners-I might instance Cochrane-and it took us quite a long time before we received, not so much the municipal taxes as the school taxes. This anomaly was remedied a few years ago. I hope this administration and the Manitoba government will see that no such injustice occurs at Churchill.

The government has no intention of building private houses or boarding houses. Any buildings we have at Churchill will be of the kind we have at present, such as elevators, docks, sheds or buildings of that sort.
I notice in this estimate an item of $2,250 for E. B. Jost. What did he do to entitle him to this amount of money?

Mr. Jost is assistant engineer of the department, but in addition to that he is senior hydraulic engineer. This $2,250 has been paid to him now for nearly ten years, and paid in exactly the same way. If my hon. friend will look up the estimate of last year, he will find the same item. It was begun, as a matter of fact, under the late government. I am not saying that in any critical sense. Mr. Jost is our authority on the many water power leases on the canals throughout Canada, so that he is paid in two separate ways, although it is put into this item as it has to be put somewhere. Personally I imagine this $2,250 should be inserted in one of the cana.1 items, but this is of no importance as it has to be passed by the Auditor General.
What other salary, if any, has he?

He receives $4,920 in
addition to this. Of course, there would be ten per oent deducted from both amounts.

Does he reside at
Churchill?
No. he resides here.

I should like to correct a statement made by the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough (Mr. Duff), that two or three men were on deck when the Bright Fan collided with this iceberg. That is not the fact. The only man on deck or on any part of the deck where it could be seen was the boy at the wheel. The second officer was in the chart room. In connection with any remarks I have made in respect to the Bright Fan I have no apology to make and do not intend to make any. My considered opinion was that the boat was deliberately scuttled. I am still of that opinion and I shall go to the grave with it. As far as the fairy picture painted by the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough is concerned, I cannot say as much for Captain Oliver. In my opinion he is one of the biggest reprobates that ever came into my constituency, and I think any hon. member who reads the evidence carefully would come to the same conclusion about him. I know quite a lot about the actions of the crew of the Bright Fan at Churchill, and I could bring affidavits here as high as this desk to prove my statements. I am sure that some of my friends in the corner to my right will be interested in this point. One of the commissioners asked Captain Oliver if

Supply-Railways-Hudson Bay
he had a standard steel watertight bulkhead between holds Nos. 1 and 2, and he replied, "Yes." Then he was asked "Should that not have kept your ship afloat until the salvage steamer arrived?" Captain Oliver replied that the wheat had swelled in bulk and forced the steel bulkhead. Imagine wheat swelling in ice cold salt water in two hours and forty minutes sufficient to break down a steel bulkhead! Anyone who has had anything to do with wheat will know how absurd such a statement is. I have had no reason whatever to change my mind about the sinking of the Bright Fan, and as far as the Bright Fan looking for an iceberg is concerned, if hon. gentlemen will read the evidence they will see that previous to striking the iceberg the Bright Fan sailed only sixteen miles in six and a half hours, although she was a seven knot boat.
As regards the insurance, I do not know the exact figure paid on the hull or on the wheat, but I do know that there was an extra premium of $7,000 charged on each one of the ten boats that went in there, or $70,000, and the insurance carried on the Bright Fan was somewhere around that figure. So there was no loss to the insurance companies even if they had to pay the insurance on the hull, and whether they have done so or not I do not know. The whole evidence in the inquiry has been tabled, and I would ask any hon. members who still have doubts about the matter to read it very carefully before making any more funny statements. If they knew as much as I do about the matter they would have equally as strong an opinion as mine.

I do not think there is much necessity for continuing this discussion as far as the Bright Fan is concerned. I have tried to speak a good word for the Hudson bay route in spite of the fact that I was never in favour of it, but when anybody comes here and says that Captain Oliver deliberately cast his ship away, I think I have a perfect right to get up and defend Captain Oliver and his crew. My hon. friend from Nelson seemed to complain because one of the steel bulkheads in the ship did not close properly.
No, no.
He said that the wheat swelled, the bulkhead opened, and the ship sank.
Do you believe that? Do you believe that wheat would swell in two hours and forty minutes in ice cold salt water?

Whether the wheat swelled or not, or whether the bulkhead closed or not, I would remind my hon. friend of the sinking
of the Titanic when none of the bulkheads closed. It is quite possible that in stowing the cargo, the bulkhead was not closed. Perhaps the machinery would not close it. But it is not fair to say that Captain Oliver- my hon. friend did not say this in so many words-deliberately either opened the bulkhead or left it open so that the Bright Fan would sink when she struck the iceberg, which Captain Oliver, according to my hon. friend, was evidently looking for all that night. The Bright Fan, my hon. friend says, went sixteen miles in six and a half hours.
The rate of an ox team.

My hon. friend comes from
Lunenburg where they use oxen. Instead of blaming Captain Oliver for going only sixteen miles in six hours, crawling along like an ox team, as my hon. friend from Lunenburg suggests, coming from a county which has the best sailors in the world, my hon. friend ought rather to get up and compliment Captain Oliver for going at such a rate because it shows that he was a good sailor. I have read the evidence, and I heard Captain Oliver give his testimony, and the evidence shows conclusively that the visibility was not good, and after he got word from the McLean that the iceberg was in a certain position, he proceeded very slowly because he did not think it was safe to make speed. He should be commended for his caution. I say that nobody has a right to get up in this house as my hon. friend from Nelson has done and make such charges. He would not dare to make the statement outside of this house that Captain Oliver cast his ship away, because of certain things that he says he knows happened in Churchill. It is all right for my hon. friend to make these statements on the floor of this house, but I say it is not fair to Captain Oliver or any other seaman to say that he deliberately cast his ship away and went looking for an iceberg just to get the insurance.

I have said outside of this house what I have said here. Nobody has ever accused me of lacking courage in any of the statements I made. I repeat that Captain Oliver was the biggest reprobate that ever came to Churchill. I am informed he was drunk when he came in there, he was drunk all the time he was there, and he was drunk when he left there.
How do you know?

I can get affidavits to prove it. And furthermore, he sold whisky or permitted it to be sold all the time he was there. Captain Oliver knew nothing about what speed the boat was making that night because he was in bed.

My hon. friend said that he was taking extra precautions and all that kind of thing. It just shows that he does not know anything about it. He swore it was watertight. But the fact that Captain Oliver swore that the wheat swelled and burst the steel bulkhead I think should convince anybody as to the character of his evidence.

If all this

Who knows that
insurance has been paid on the boat? I do not know. As a matter of fact I understand that the board of trade in the old country is holding a further inquiry. Whether it has yet been held I do not know. Nobody has told me that the insurance has been paid.
Insurance is often paid because of other risks carried in the same company:

My hon. friend from
Antigonish-Guysborough asked about the rates. The freight rates are 3s. 9d. per quarter on grain going out of Churchill. The insurance rates are four per cent on the cargo if the ship has a gyro compass, and five per cent where there is no gyro compass, and the rate on the ships themselves is 2s. per gross ton. That is the best information I have, and I think it is correct.

A few
moments ago the minister in reply to the hon. member for North Waterloo referred to the indebtedness incurred at Churchill. What I wish to know is whether the indebtedness is included in the general indebtedness against the Canadian National Railways.

No. While in the report
of the Department of Railways and Canals it is included in the general indebtedness, it is not part of the Canadian National railway indebtedness. The Canadian National railway handles the road for the government as our agents, and we pay the losses, but the indebtedness is not included directly in the Canadian National railway accounts.

Just one
further question. What advantage has the port of Churchill over other grain shipping ports such as Saint John or Victoria?
IWr. B. M. Stitt.]
Or Vancouver?
Or Quebec?

Up to the present Churchill has had an advantage over these other ports in not having any port or elevator charges. But of course that is a temporary arrangement which obviously will have to be corrected in the very near future. It is my personal opinion that it is only fair that all Canadian ports should ultimately be on an equal basis. It was thought by the government however that in view of the fact that there were only a couple of ships coming in, and that they were test shipments, there should not be any charges imposed. Therefore up to the present there have not been any charges, even on the two and a half million bushels of grain which passed through the port last year. But in the near future it will be but fair to have the same type of charges imposed upon the port of Churchill as are imposed on other ports, but the charges should be at a rate equal to the lowest existing in any port of Canada. I think that would only be fair, in view of the large investment of the government in the development of this port, and in view of the fact that the western provinces are anxious to give it a fair trial. I believe those rates, comparable with rates obtaining in other ports, should be the lowest possible. There is no doubt that in the near future rates will have to be charged.

Assistance has been given to other ports in Canada, and I can see no reason why Churchill should not get a fair share of it. The Manitoba government, by whom the townsite is handled.

Is there any directing
effort on the part of the Department of Railways and Canals towards the opening up of the townsite?

We have nothing whatever to do with the townsite. We handle the port, but so far as the townsite is concerned, it has been handed over to the province of Manitoba, and they will have complete control of it. In consultation with them, however, we did offer a number of suggestions.

I understand the provinces of Manitoba and Saskatchewan are making all necessary efforts to build up a trade into and out of the port. Has the minister any information to give the committee concerning the success of those operations up to the moment?

The province of Saskatchewan has appointed two men, Mr. Ireland and Mr. Smith, to solicit traffic for the port of Churchill. I will be quite frank and say that some of the citizens of Saskatchewan took the stand that the Dominion government or the Canadian National Railways should appoint traffic solicitors for the port of Churchill. I took the responsibility of stating that it was no more the duty of the Canadian government to solicit traffic for the port of Churchill than to solicit for the ports of Halifax, Vancouver, Montreal or Quebec, and the further stand that since in the last few years the Dominion government had spent about $54,000,000 on the port, and since the province of Saskatchewan would be the chief contributor of any freight going into or out of the port, they might very well spend 810,000 on the appointment of traffic solicitors, thereby avoiding any criticism which would be levelled at a Dominion government for appointing such officials for one port and not

for others. In the end they adopted the same view, and as a result have appointed the two gentlemen whose names I have mentioned. Their chief duties are to solicit freight and traffic for that port.

One question more-I thank the minister for his information. I think the attitude taken by some people in wastem Canada is that the government of which the hon. minister is a member quite often has the belief and acts upon it that it is right to support infant industries by protection. As this is an infant port, perhaps a little protection would not do it any harm.

I think the government has been giving it very generous protection. I do not believe that if the government which my hon. friend followed were now in power it would think of giving it greater protection than it has had. Both in construction, maintenance and operation the Dominion government has given exceedingly generous treatment to the whole road.

May I suggest to the minister that he continue that generous support for a little while longer, until the seaport has been given a fair trial? The very fact that the loss of the Bright Fan did not injure the insurance companies to any greater extent than the premiums paid would indicate that future business should prove profitable to the extent of about one hundred per cent. Possibly after the road has been used another year or two the insurance rates will be lowered. Until that time comes I suggest that the port be given the generous assistance that the government has given in the past. May I ask the minister whether or not there will be an official opening this coming season?

I am sure the government will continue to give fair and reasonable and just treatment to the port. No government, whether of this stripe or some other, would feel that $54,000,000 should be invested and then the result of that investment be unfairly treated. I am sure that this government will see that fair treatment is given to the port in every possible way. As to an official opening, it was hoped that there would be an official opening in 1932, but there was the imperial conference, and the opening of the Welland canal which had been already delayed a year; as my hon. friend knows, there was much to be done, consequently it was put off. But the government will give every consideration, and I think favourable consideration, to the question of an official opening of the port of Churchill this coming summer.
Is it the intention of the government to transfer the Hudson Bay Railway to the Canadian National Railway so that it may become an integral part of that system?

That has not been considered by the government as yet. I think if I were one of the managers of the Canadian National Railways, until the Hudson Bay railway showed that it was going to pay its way I would object to taking it over as part of the Canadian National lines, because their deficit now would appear to be sufficient from their standpoint, without addmg to it. However, that is a matter which will ultimately have to be considered. I suppose in the course of years the Hudson Bay railway will ultimately become part of the Canadian National system.
Is it not a fact that a lot of dead horse railways in eastern Canada have been taken over as part of the Canadian National?

Yes, I certainly think there were a lot of railways of that type taken over by the Canadian National in the years that are past, roads that the Canadian National would be very much better without. That is all the more reason why they do not want to take over any more non-paying railways until they show a prospect of carrying themselves.

If one part of the country is going to benefit by the taking over of deadhead railways by the Canadian National, then to build the Hudson Bay railway and attribute its losses directly to that railway is doing it an injustice.

I had not intended to say anything in regard to the Hudson Bay railway being incorporated into the Canadian National system, but I quite agree with the minister that if I had control of the Canadian National I would not care to have the Hudson Bay railway saddled upon the Canadian National system. I will also agree that some railways have been taken into the Canadian National system that perhaps should not have been. I fear that some people might be glad to see a losing proposition like the Hudson Bay railway incorporated into the Canadian National system for the mere purpose of enabling them to point the finger of scorn at the principle of public ownership. Something has been said in regard to the desirability of giving a fair trial to the Hudson Bay road. If that means that it is desired to try out the Hudson strait route, whether ships can navigate it safely and for a

substantial part of the year, well and good. Otherwise I would say that it was not giving it a fair trial, a trial that means much, if you do not conduct that trial under the same conditions under which it will ultimately have to operate. If the government is going to pay port charges and so on, I say that is not giving it a trial upon which one can rest a fair judgment.
Do you object to it?
I am not objecting to giving it a fair trial.
Do you object to the assistance they have given?
I do not even understand what my hon. friend is driving at. Usually I do.
He asks if you object to paying the port charges.

There is one other question that I desire to ask. The minister stated that some two and a half million bushels of wheat went out during the past summer. Was that the product of the year 1932? That is, is it possible to ship grain out by this route in the same year in which it is produced?

I do not know what year's grain that was, but generally speaking I would say that it is not practicable-I do not say not possible

to ship grain out in the year in which it is grown, because the navigation season as so far determined is a little on the short side. And this will answer the question of my hon. friend the member for Kindersley; the hon. gentleman asked me about the opening and closing of the port last year. I have obtained the figures for him. The steamship Sierentz came in on August 14, 1932. That does not say that a boat could not have come in sooner, but the first arrival last year was August 14, and the last out was the Pennsilvia, which left on October 10, 1932. That would be a period of just under two months. The previous year the port was certainly open a good deal longer than that, and I think also this past year. But those are the dates of first arrival and last departure. They are all we can go by.
My hon. friend from North Waterloo (Mr. Euler) asked a question at an earlier time in regard to past years. Unfortunately I could not lay my hand on the figures at the time, but I have obtained them since. The actual revenue in 1931 amounted to S387,870.76 and the expenses to 8389,077.19, the loss being 81,206.43. That was less than the estimate for the coming year. In 1932 the revenue- in round figures-was $577,000 and operating
expenses $612,000, so that the loss was $35,000. But they estimate a little more grain this year, I think about three million bushels, and they figure that this year it will be the amount I put on Hansard a few minutes ago.

I am afraid an entirely wrong impression is being left on the eastern mind in regard to the payment for the construction of this Hudson Bay railway, and that it is being used very much to the detriment of the railway. The impression is that it has cost Canada, eastern Canada chiefly, the sum of $54,000,000. That is absolutely incorrect. What happened was that some years ago Hon. Frank Oliver, then Liberal Minister of the Interior, brought in a bill which became law setting apart certain lands in the provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta which were sold for the purpose of building the Hudson Bay railway. From this it will be seen that instead of the government of Canada being called upon to foot a bill of $54,000,000, we in the west have built the road and have been mighty little of a burden to the rest of Canada. When hon. gentlemen tell us that we are away behind, needing relief and wanting this, that and the other, while they themselves are getting millions of dollars every year for ports and marine services, although we do not get a cent, I want to tell them that they are away out. We are paying our own way and are drumming up cattle to ship over this road. I said to the people of Regina, "Get busy yourselves and secure traffic for that railway. To hang with the east; we will build

Supply-Railways-Hudson Bay
up that road ourselves anyhow." I am as good an easterner as I am a westerner, and I can tell my hon. friends that we in western Canada are prepared to assume the responsibility that is ours. We are going to do our duty. Make no mistake: that Hudson Bay railway will be a mighty big success in a short time. It is successful now, and we are going to keep it going regardless of what others say or do.
With regard to the Bright Fan, I have had conversations with people who know something about these matters, and they are very much amused at the statement that has been made that the grain swelled and broke the bulkhead. People who are conversant with these things tell me that this is absolutely silly. The grain was dumped into compartments between the bulkheads but it was all open at the top. The only thing that was on top of the grain was a lot of bags, so that if the grain did swell it would move in the direction of least resistance, which would be upwards; but the darned thing did not go up at all. A statement of that kind is absolutely absurd. The fact is that a ship went down that should not have gone down. I was not there but, from what I have heard, I am sure the ship should not have gone down. That disaster must not therefore be held against insurance rates, and if anyone tries to keep up the rates on that account, we are going to be heard from.

If I heard the question and answer correctly, there was a wrong impression in regard to the shipment of the current season's crop out of Churchill. I understood the ex-Minister of National Revenue to ask whether the crop of the current year could be shipped that year, and I understood the minister to say that it could not. That is far from being correct. It may be that a large part of the shipment via Churchill may not be the current year's crop.
I am located 126 miles west of Saskatoon, which is in the middle of the province and about 40 miles from the Alberta border. I had my grain threshed on August 30 and 31 last year. It was in the elevator and was shipped immediately afterwards, and I was not the first to have my grain threshed; they were threshing their grain ten days before that. So that grain threshed in the latter part of August, according to the minister's statement, has all of September until some time in October-October 10 last year-to get there and be loaded, and he said that the previous year the port was open much later than October 10. Generally speaking, the time until which the port is open may be 
placed between about the middle and the end of October, and that being so, with grain threshed the latter part of August or early September, I do not see why a large part of the current crop cannot move out of the port during the same year.

I do not want to be misunderstood. What I meant was this. Generally speaking, I think I am right in the answer I gave my hon. friend (Mr. Euler). I do not question the statement made by the hon. member that if the grain is harvested by the end of August some of it could be shipped out. Some would be shipped in normal times through Churchill-[DOT]
Theoretically.

No, even in practice. But even so, if one waited for the crop of that year to go out of Churchill, one would waste two months of a short season. The port opens about the middle of July and closes about the middle of October, so that a crop harvested at the end of August would probably not be shipped out of Churchill until the middle of September, two weeks after harvesting, which would be quite expeditious, and if we attempted to wait for that there would be two months from the middle of July until the middle of September which would be lost. Therefore, a large proportion of the grain that has gone or that will go through Churchill will certainly be the previous year's grain. That is not a serious matter at the present time with hangovers of 100,000,000 bushels. Some difficulty was experienced last year by people who tried to get grain shipped through that port, though fortunately for the port, the Continental Grain Company made the proposal to us of putting in at least 2,000,000 bushels and shipping out at least 1,000,000. They put in well over 2,000,000 bushels and shipped most of it, and one or two other companies shipped a small quantity.
My hon. friend from Muskoka asked a question with regard to future costs added to those I have already given. When I mentioned that figure of $54,000,000, that included this year's estimate of expenditures, and that will represent to a large extent the completion of the port so far as traffic of the present type is concerned. If the traffic became heavier, we should require more freight sheds and coaling facilities, greater elevator facilities, more docks, and so forth. I am referring to it as an up-to-date port, capable of handling fifty per cent more shipping than was handled last year. The port is in pretty good shape considered from that

angle. The elevator will handle many times the amount of wheat handled last year. In reply to the hon. member for Long Lake (Mr. Cowan) I would say that I have no quarrel to make with the statement he made;
I am quite familiar with it. I am not endeavouring in any way to differ from him or to argue that the port has been treated too generously. It must not be forgotten that the land set aside for the purpose of the Hudson Bay railway belonged to the Dominion government at the time it was set aside. I cannot even remember what government was in power at that time, but this land was set aside before the natural resources were turned over to the provinces.

That amount includes the expenditure at Port Nelson, which was something between six and seven million dollars. I think this amount is a legitimate inclusion because it was all spent in connection with the building of the road.

What proportion of
that was for the elevator?

About $1,500,000. This would seem to indicate that a particular year's crop can be handled through the port in the same year.

Could the minister
put on record the exact figures in connection with the expenditure at Port Nelson?

There was great difficulty last year in obtaining cargoes to be shipped through this port. We in western Canada asked to have this railway built and port facilities provided, but, strange to say, the grain interests have paid little heed to the request that cargoes be shipped through Churchill. If my memory serves me aright, the minister had to go out and dig up some cargoes to be shipped through this port. I think it is just about time the western cities and their boards of trade woke up and did a little digging themselves for cargoes.

The hon. member for
Dauphin (Mr. Bowman) asked the capacity
of the grain elevator. While I cannot give him the exact figures, it is something in the neighbourhood of one million bushels per day. This is a two and a half million bushel elevator with four loading belts, and it can run the grain through pretty rapidly. The hon. member for Swift Current (Mr. Both-well) asked the exact expenditure at Port Nelson; it was $6,274,217.88.
No salvage at all?

That is the net cost;
there was a certain amount of salvage, but not very much.

Replying to the hon.
member for Kindersley, the minister gave October 10 as the date upon which the last boat left the port. Was the port open for navigation longer than that date?
Yes.
Has the minister any idea how long the port was open for navigation?

We obtain information from time to time from the officials of the Department of Marine as well as of the Department of Railways and Canals. This information may be that the strait is open upon a certain day, but navigation from Churchill does not depend only upon the strait being open. Churchill bay is fed by fresh water streams and freezes up more quickly in the fall than does the salt water out in the bay and in the strait. Consequently the closing of navigation depends upon the harbour of Churchill itself. If the traffic warrants it later on, it is possible that ice breakers may be used to keep the port open for a longer period, but that has not been found necessary as yet. In the spring the reverse applies; the port is open before the strait because the ice comes down from Fox channel and interferes with the ships coming in. It is all a rather complicated picture, but the officials of both the Department of Marine and the Department of Railways and Canals, are continually making records in an endeavour to obtain accurate information over a period of years as to just how long the port can be kept open. I think at the moment it can be stated definitely that there is at least three months of safe navigation, although less than two months were used last year, and it is quite probable that the period of navigation will be lengthened in the years to come.

It is quite evident that with the elevator capacity this port can handle probably 25,000,000 to 30,000,000 bushels of grain safely in a season.

I have been waiting for an opportunity to have another say in this matter. The hon. member for Anti-gonish-Guysborough (Mr. Duff) has left the chamber, but I would like to say to him that I would be quite willing to sit at his feet to learn about the wonders and dangers of shipping. I do not pretend to know much about these matters, but one does not need to know very much to know that a "lookout" is no good on a ship unless there is an occupant in it. There was no occupant in the lookout of this ship when it struck the berg. The statement was made by Captain Oliver of the Bright Fan that the bulkhead of this boat was shoved over because the wheat swelled up after being two and a half hours in cold salt water. Whoever made that statement either did not know very much about wheat or he must have been as full as a goat himself. The captain was comfortably asleep downstairs somewhere-I know you do not call it that in a boat-and there was a boy of eighteen at the wheel. The one who should have been at the wheel was down having a cup of coffee. That seems to be a lackadaisical way to run a boat supposed to be in dangerous waters, especially when they had been told by radio that there was a roaming iceberg nearby which had not been properly parked. I think the whole thing is a disgraceful incident, and instead of protecting these men they should be exposed all over the world. This ship should not have been sent out without a gyro compass. Unless the minister does a little more to find out about these things, I am going to have something further to say later. In former years I had something to do with this port of Churchill being finally chosen and I am not going to allow this thing to stand. I congratulate the hon. member for Nelson (Mr. Stitt) for sticking to his guns and puncturing some of these cock and bull stories about the bulkhead bursting because the wheat was wet for two hours and a half. That is absolute nonsense. If the government want to protect their own hides in this matter, I would recommend that they get busy with London. I wonder if they have sent over a copy of this tabled report of the commission with regard to the Canadian investigation. It should have gone overseas. The insurance companies should know the result of the investigation. We would not have received it if it had not been for some members who were curious to know what was in it. Indeed, I do not think

we would have had it at all had it not been for the hon. member for Nelson.
That is not quite correct. The report was tabled last year.

We would not
have had the evidence had not some hon. member prodded the government a bit.

The hon. member can get off more mistaken statements than anyone else, but when he said that the government had to be prodded, the government did not have to be prodded by either the hon. member for Nelson or my hon. friend himself. If a wreck occurs and there is any question about it, the Marine department of whichever government happens to be in power investigates it. An investigation in this case followed in the usual course; the government required no prodding at all. The government does not require to "protect its hide," as the hon. gentleman so elegantly expressed it, so far as the port of Churchill and navigation through Hudson strait are concerned. The government has done everything to support the route. I have no doubt the Marine department have long ago sent the report to England.
So far as anything further to be done by this government regarding the sinking of the Bright Fan is concerned, the government has done everything a government would ordinarily be expected to do. It has made a thorough investigation. The report has been against the Bright Fan, against the operation of the vessel, as I have put enough on record to show. Certainly the British shipping people, who are the best in that line in the world, do not require any special prodding to check up insurance rates, taking into account the Bright Fan and the navigation of that ship. I just wish to correct the implication that the government has been in any way remiss in its duty in handling this matter. The government is just as anxious as any could be for the port to be a success. No government would want to see $54,000,000 spent upon any project without any return from it. I can assure my hon. friend that the government is doing everything it can to have the insurance rates lowered-I pointed that out very much earlier in the afternoon-and it will continue to do everything possible to have insurance rates lowered and to have the Churchill route given a fair and just trial.

I am glad the minister assures us that the government took the initiative on something. The information we

Supply-Railways-Hudson Bay
have is that it was the hon. member for Nelson who initiated the investigation, but whoever initiated it, I want to give him the credit.
With regard to sending the report and the evidence to London, what use was the investigation otherwise? The minister was not going to table the evidence until the hon. member for North Battleford got after it, and he had to get after it at least half a dozen times before it was tabled. I read the evidence, hurriedly, I admit, but I read enough to get a grasp of what bunk was put up by the captain in regard to the bulkhead. I was curious to know why he was talking in that way if he had a really valid excuse for the water getting into the rest of the boat. He must have known that could not be accepted as a reason for the bulkhead going over. I say again to the minister that we shall expect him to get busy and find out, first, whether that insurance was paid by the insurance companies; further, if there was another investigation on the other side of the water with respect to the matter, and if so, what was the result of it? Or was it a case of this crew being turned loose on the public to victimize them again in the next boat that wants to take a nosedive in the waters of Hudson bay; if they know they can make away with their boat by getting on a drunk at Churchill and having a little investigation at Ottawa, the cost of them is not very much if they are going to get the insurance for their vessel. Shipping, especially old junk, is quite plentiful now, and it is the duty of the government- and I shall impress it upon them-to see this matter to a finish and satisfy us as to just what happened and why, and if this boat was sunk purposely. The hon. member for Nelson stated in the house that he believed the evidence would demonstrate that the boat was sunk deliberately. The government has this from one of its own supporters, not from me; I am just making my contribution as to what I think the government should do, because I intend to hold them responsible if they do not take further action in regard to this matter. We want our insurance rates lowered and we cannot get them lowered by sinking vessels either by accident or design along the route. It was well known that an iceberg was in the vicinity. The N. B. McLean had notified that ship by radio and yet we find the captain drowsing away in his bed, the man that should have been at the helm drinking a cup of coffee and an eighteen year old boy, who might well have been on the lookout, being at the wheel. That was the situation. I am not a mariner, but I have been on salt water long enough to know when a boat is in danger, the captain never leaves the bridge. He sleeps there without undressing.
No, he does not sleep.

Well, he rests in
the chart room, or whatever you call it. I do not care who denies it, because I have seen a captain do so. I was on a boat coming from Jamaica and for two or three days in succession the captain never left those quarters nearby and had his meals brought there. There are coral reefs around there and a heavy sea was on. All I know about the matter is that men who have charge of ships, whether freight or passenger, do not loaf in bed or sip coffee away from the helm under those berg conditions of which they were warned. I do not think the crew could have been sobered up after the spree they had at Churchill.
There is another matter that should be investigated. Why should boats be permitted to leave the other side without a proper compass? I do not know what the port regulations are along this line. I know it costs a good deal to buy these gyro compasses, but if there is a proper compass, why are regulations not made to compel these boats to carry it? If the N. B. McLean had not been near the spot, these men might all have gone down or they might have got to the Labrador shore. But perhaps that is another story. Possibly they cannot be made to buy these gyro compasses; but what is the use of them if the boats do not use them? The captain gave evidence that .the compass he had was of no use to him, so that it was no better than the lookout. Just imagine going through there without a compass as well as without a lookout! The matter requires much fuller investigation. These men have to get certificates; well, they should be stripped of their certificates, demobilized and sent elsewhere, not on stormy waters or even calm waters.
Another matter. When insurance is quoted, it seems always to be quoted on a quarter basis, eight bushels, and in English money. I used to be able to reduce English money .to dollars and cents, but I have not seen enough of it lately to do any mental arithmetic in that respect. Could it not be quoted on the same basis as on our side, so much in dollars and cents per 1,000 or 100 bushels or .per bushel, whatever is required? That would be a great convenience.

My deskmate and the minister had a little dialogue on a matter that has not been made quite clear, as to sending out wheat the same year it is grown. Possibly there will be at least two months of that in an ordinary year. In a year like last year, our wheat would have been at Churchill harbour by the first of September and could be shipped from then to the first of November at least. We are not worrying about that at all. It will help to take the peak load at a time when the other ports are busy. Besides, right now there must be between fifty and sixty million bushels of wheat at the head of the lakes.
Probably more than that.

I think it is sixty million bushels, and nobody is perspiring blood over that. So why should there be so much agitation and anxiety about two or three million bushels being held over at Churchill? There are some two hundred and fifty million bushels of wheat in Canada right now awaiting export, and some of that two hundred and fifty million bushels is in porta open all the year round. So we should not get into a state of agitation because two or three million bushels are held up at Churchill in the same way. There has been no difficulty on that score, I can assure any doubting Thomases. It has not been demonstrated yet just how good the Churchill route is going to turn out, but we do not want any more Bright Fan incidents making it more difficult to get reasonable insurance rates. I consider that the insurance rates have everything to do with the success of that route. The minister told us last year that the insurance rates on the Hudson Bay route were five or six timies greater than on the St. Lawrence route. I think they have been lowered slightly since, judging by a press statement the minister made last summer, but I believe the rates on the Churchill route are still four times greater than on the St. Lawrence. The minister will correct me if I am wrong. That is a tremendous handicap. There is a great advantage in distance for the Hudson bay route, and we want to make the most of that. I would point out that the government of which I had the honour to be a member did its best to develop the Pacific route. It was not until after we came into power that the Pacific route did very much wheat business. After the Panama canal was opened it was quite a number of years before our wheat or anything else went out of Vancouver or Westminster or any otheT Pacific port in any quantity. But we had elevators built

there, established commissions in control of elevators, and had Crowsnest freight rates established, so that Alberta wheat sought out that nearest outlet to the sea, and it was not long before Vancouver was humming with wheat shipping. Sometimes there was so much .wheat going there that shipments had to be diverted elsewhere. I am not appealing for the Hudson bay route any more than I appealed for the Pacific coast route, and I hope the minister will not take umbrage at anything I have said. I think he is doing fairly well, considering the mighty little encouragement he must be getting round about him, especially in his own constituency of Fort William, when he attempts to help along a rival port. I quite appreciate that. While it is not his place to do it, I think that either the Minister of Marine or the Prime Minister should lose no time in placing this whole matter before the insurance authorities in London and getting all the information available on the subject. That is what I would suggest at this stage, and I shall expect something to be done, otherwise I shall be constrained to have another word to say later.

At this late hour I do not wish to take up much more of the time of the committee, but I can assure hon. gentlemen that this government is leaving nothing undone. What the hon. member for Melville has just suggested I am quite sure lias already been done by the Department of Marine. It was their duty, and I have no doubt whatever that the whole report has been forwarded to England long ago.
I wish to take exception to the suggestion that there was any difficulty in getting the report tabled. We had no reason in the world for keeping it back. We were in no way responsible for the sinking of the Bright Fan and in no way interested in protecting Captain Oliver or anyone else. It is our business to do everything we can to get the insurance rates down, and we have done and will do everything we can in that direction. I am sure that next year when the estimates come up again we shall have reports of any investigations that have been held in connection with this matter in Great Britain. Personally I have had no intimation of any investigation being held over there, but the hon. member for Nelson has stated that he understands that an investigation is being held, and I have no reason to doubt that his information is correct. May I say on his behalf that no constituency has a more loyal member, and

there has been no more loyal supporter of the Hudson bay route, and no harder worker for it than the hon. member for Nelson.
Hear, hear.

He has been very enthusiastic about the route at all times, as naturally he would be, because the success or otherwise of the route will probably mean the making or breaking of his section of the country. He is a hard working member and deserves the commendation not only of my hon. friend but of the whole house because of the work he has done for that route.

I was quite interested in a remark made by the hon. member for Nelson about the sinking of the Bright Fan. He said that the ship started out from Churchill looking for an iceberg to bump into, and that finally it found one, and sank in consequence. He also stated that the captain was a reprobate and a drunkard. In view of that fact possibly a lot of bootleggers may be handling grain from that port, and the bulkhead may have given way through an explosion when moonshine was being manufactured on the boat.

I understood from the minister's figures as to the cost of operation that maintenance of way was not taken into account. May I ask him if anything was taken into account for rolling stock and equipment, rentals, and whether the Hudson Bay railway, or the government on behalf of the Hudson Bay railway, owns the rolling stock and equipment or rents it from the Canadian National Railways.

The equipment is rented from the Canadian National Railways, and the cost of that equipment is taken into account. My hon. friend is quite right in saying that the maintenance charges are not taken into account. Nor have we been charging up interest to the road.

Item agreed to.
Canals-Welland ship canal-construction and betterments, $1,992,000.
May I ask the minister the total cost of the Welland canal to date, and the total interest charges on our entire canal system every year?
The total cost of the Welland ship canal, in round figures, is $128,000,000.
Has the minister the interest charges on the entire canal system of Canada?

The cost of the entire canal system, including the Welland canal, is in the neighbourhood of a quarter of a billion dollars, about $250,000,000. So far as interest is concerned, it is not charged up to the canals, but is incorporated in the general consolidated revenue accounts of the country.

My impression from some figures I received was that the total cost was somewhere around $236,000,000, and I think that last year the interest charges to the Canadian taxpayers were $12,000,000. Has the government ever considered the advisability of installing a toll system on our Canadian canals? Shipments of our grain from Vancouver to the old country pay $1.20 a bushel passing through the Panama canal, and 72 cents a ton in ballast, or a net average of nearly $1 a bushel. Last year a profit of $7,000,000 was made by the American government on the Panama canal system, of which the port of Vancouver contributed roughly $3,750,000. Of course, I know about the old treaties, but if American shipping is to use our Canadian canal system to the extent of 1,750.000 tons out of a total of 17,500,000 tons, which were the figures last year, without paying a single cent in tolls, I would suggest that the question of installing a toll system be seriously considered by the government. Here is the wheat of western Canada shipped out of the port of Vancouver paying on the average $8,000 per cargo passing through the Panama canal, including freight both ways, and I am suggesting to the minister and the administration that we might give very careful thought to the adoption of some toll system on our Canadian canals, so that we would not be losing the revenue we are losing to-day. Also there should be a policy of equalization between west and east. At the present time the western grain shippers are paying a large amount in tolls to the American government.

The matter of tolls has
not been considered by the government, because in 1903 all canal tolls were abolished by agreement between the governments of the United States and Canada. Up to that time tolls had been charged. It is true that tolls are charged on the Panama canal. Any change in the present arrangement however would have to be by arrangement between the United States and Canada and it is possible that the United States would not agree to a change.
Then, too, if tolls were charged on the Canadian canals there would be the danger of
Supply-Canals-W elland,

sending through the United States ports a much larger proportion of Canadian grain than now goes through them. Up until recently from a quarter to a third of Canadian grain had been shipped via American ports. If shipping tolls were charged on Canadian canals the shipments through American ports would certainly be increased. Then there is this further point to remember, that the best canal at the Soo is the American canal, and is used by Canadian boats. In ordinary times the Soo canal carries more traffic than any other canal in the world. It carries two or three times as much as the Panama or Suez. By far the greater proportion of the traffic goes through the American locks. I am prepared to admit that canals present a complicated question, and there are reasonable arguments on both sides. I notice that a financial paper of Canada has been waging an extensive campaign on behalf of tolls, and there is another argument from the standpoint of the railways. I should not like to commit myself however, because it is not a question which has come before the government in a definite manner, and as I said before, any arrangement which could be made there would have to be an international agreement.

The free use of our canals undoubtedly will have to be reviewed, and some other arrangement made between the United States and Canada. What are some of the facts? American coal is being transported without charge through canals which cost this country great sums of money. The eastern provinces are not in a position to send coal westward. Canada is thus practically subsidizing every ton of American coal which comes into Ontario or Quebec, by offering free passage through canals which cost us about $300,000,000.

Yes, and including free
dockage.

Yes, including free dockage. I submit that condition of affairs should not be allowed to continue indefinitely. Then, there are other factors to which I might refer, but on this occasion I will not do so. Consider this for a moment:	Outside of the
province of Ontario the canal expenditures in the Dominion of Canada are very small. For instance, in the province of Nova Scotia we have only half a mile of canal, costing originally about $600,000. If we are to allay unrest in the different provinces these matters should be considered and conditions rectified. When, on previous occasions, the vote for canals was before us, I thought of making a statement, but refrained from doing so. For years I
[Mr. Msnion.}
have been amused at the arguments made in this house by some western members about the Hudson Bay route. I made the _ statement half a dozen years ago-perhaps I am out of order, but I shall repeat it now-" that when the year came that our western friends could bring ten ships into Hudson bay and get them safely out again I would admit that the navigation of Hudson bay was feasible." As yet that has not been done. We will have to wait twenty years before it will be done. The past two seasons were exceptional. Wait and see.

I should like to support the remarks of the hon. member for Vancouver Centre, concerning tolls on canals. Ten or twelve years ago I asked in this house what logical reason could be given why a canal system should be constructed at the expense of the Canadian people, at a cost of over S300,000,000, and should be used by private interests entirely free of charge. I could see no reason for it. The only reply I received at that time came from the Minister of Finance, and was to the effect that it had always been done. That did not strike me as a very good reason. Particularly in these days, when the government is in need of revenue, unless the treaty with the United States entirely forbids, I do not see why at least there should not be a charge made for the use of canals which would pay for their maintenance. That is done in connection with the Panama canal, and in other parts of the world. I believe the average charge of sending a vessel through the Panama canal is about $4,000 or about 88,000 on a return trip. They are receiving a return of about two per cent on their investment. I would not ask for a greater return, but would suggest that surely we ought to charge sufficient to pay for maintenance.
The minister has stated that a treaty was made with the United States in 1904 providing for equality of treatment. I do not know whether the treaty goes so far as to say that there shall be equality of treatment only so far as United States vessels are concerned. I would say: Yes, let us have equality of treatment. I would say that the Canadian ship owners who use Canadian canals should pay a fair charge or toll for such use. The canals are used by private interests and for private purposes. I suppose I may expect criticism from my western friends for my attitude in this direction, and there is no doubt they will be disposed to criticize me for what I said about the Hudson Bay railway. That is quite all right; I accept their criticism. A short time ago it was hinted

Supply-Railways and Canals
to me because of my criticism of the Hudson Bay railway I might expect criticism from them concerning the Welland canal. They may criticize the Welland canal as much as they like; for my part I think it was a foolish expenditure. It will never be of any great use until it becomes a link in a complete St. Lawrence waterway system. Although I may be out of order, I must say that I hope the government will not go on with the St. Lawrence waterway scheme for a good many years to come or until we are in a better position financially than we are to-day. I suggest that the government approach the United States with a view to providing for the payment both by Canadian and United States owners of a fair sum for the use of the canals.
