What was the cost of
the official opening of the Welland canal?

The work wras done mostly by the employees who took part in construction and, as has been suggested to me by the Minister of Justice, much was done more or less as an act of charity and mercy. At any rate, nearly everyone who contributed to the opening ceremony gave his services free. For example, there was some radio broadcasting, and the companies interested charged nothing but their bare expenses. The ship which came through the canal was supplied by the Canada Steamship lines. They loaded the boat and brought it down without any cost, although they did not require it at that time. There was a little bit of decoration, because the Governor General was there, and naturally the show had to be put on in reasonably dignified form, but the cost altogether, I think-I am speaking from memory-was about a couple of thousand dollars, a small amount in consideration of the fact that the total cost of the canal was about $128,000,000.

Can the minister give
the house the percentage of Canadian tonnage that used the new Welland canal in comparison with American tonnage?

It has not been divided
that way, but there was a good deal more tonnage through the canal last year, and I think a good deal more Canadian than in previous years. I happen to know that there was a lot of tonnage to Toronto and Hamilton that previously had gone by rail: I remember the railways were protesting against it. Last year there went through the Welland canal 8,500,000 tons of freight.

Can the minister tell
how much of the 8,500,000 tons was Canadian? Could he secure the information?

I will be glad to supply
the information later, but I doubt if I will be able to supply it on this item. I do not know when I shall be able to have it.

I asked the question, in view of the remarks of my hon. friend from North Waterloo (Mr. Euler). There is a strong feeling in the minds of business people of this country that the cost of the Welland canal, a rather substantial investment for this country, will bear much heavier on the Canadian taxpayer than on the American, whereas the advantages will be in the aggregate very much more to the American shipper than the Canadian shipper. I would not like to say I would advocate the Institution of tolls on our canal system, but the fact must be borne in mind that if the whole St. Lawrence waterway system, of which the Welland canal is a part, is to be made free it is altogether probable that nine-tenths of the use of it will be by vessels of American registry and about one tenth by vessels of Canadian registry. I think before one can intelligently discuss the question whether or not we should impose tolls on tonnage going through the Welland canal we would have to have some information as to what the proportion of tonnage is between the two countries and an estimate of what it may be in future.
The other argument which the minister referred to, namely the loss to our national railways by virtue of the Welland canal diverting tonnage, is an argument probably strongly in favour of tolls on the canal system. Iron ore consigned to Hamilton and lake Ontario ports used to provide a very considerable tonnage for the national railways from the Point Edward docks near Sarnia. I think those familiar with the movement of iron ore know that there are many thousand specially built ore cars lying idle on sidings since the Welland canal was opened last year, the ore now comes through the canal without paying any toll, with a distinct saving to the shippers of the ore from the upper lakes. I think the minister would be well advised to secure all the data he can as to just what the loss is to the national railways by the diversion of tonnage through the free canals; and also what the tonnage through the canal system has been, divided between Canadian and American ships. With that information before us we will be in a much better position to deal with the question of tolls.

The rate my hon. friend speaks of, the Quebec rate plus one cent, is the only one that is out of line. I may point out that the Canadian railways have taken the attitude that even if that rate were put on the same basis as the Montreal rate, the one cent differential would not increase the amount of grain going through the Canadian ports. We hope however that the amount of grain going through the Canadian ports will be increased materially as a result of the agreements entered into. As regards the decision, the question has not been brought to my attention recently but I shall look into it. I agree with my hon. friend that appeals of that sort should be disposed of. However, he must remember that the governor general in council of the government is not a rate making body, and it is a very difficult thing to handle a subject of that kind. So far as I know, no government in the past has ever made a rate after an appeal from the railway commission to the privy council; in practically all cases the matter is referred back to the commission. It is true that in the case of the Crowsnest pass rate this was done, but otherwise parliament has not been in the habit of considering itself a rate making body. There is perhaps no question in the whole Canadian domain more complicated, more technical and more difficult to deal with than that of freight rates.

I appreciate the assurance of the minister that the matter will be disposed of. The situation was that the grain rate to Quebec was substantially reduced. Previous to that reduction there had been a one cent differential between the rate to Quebec and the rate to Saint John and Halifax, and after the reduction was made the maritime ports asked that the same differential be put into effect. This would have made a substantial reduction in the rate to those ports. So important was it regarded that the board of trade and the harbour com-

mission of Halifax united in an application to the board of railway commissioners. There was also considerable newspaper agitation about this matter. The decision was adverse and the matter went to the privy council. I have not heard it suggested that this matter be abandoned or that it is not of interest. The same situation exists to-day as existed at the time the application was launched. If the minister has any intimation of this kind, it seems to me, in justice to the government and to the country, that it ought to be made known. There should be a disposition of the matter one way or the other.

The information I have
is quite informal, but it may be entirely correct. I happen to have in my pocket a map which I have found very useful showing the rates between ports. It is worth remembering that recently a reduction was made in rates from the Canadian head of the lakes to maritime ports. This rate is now five cents lower per hundred pounds than the rate from Duluth and Minneapolis to New York, and five cents lower per hundred pounds than the rate from the Canadian head of the lakes to New York. There is certainly a differential favourable to the maritimes. The special rate given to Quebec by the board of railway commissioners was 18-34 cents per hundred pounds, and it is argued that this rate, plus a differential of one cent, should be carried through to Saint John and Halifax. This would make a 19-34 rate as against the present rate of 30 cents. It might be interesting to note that since the lower rate went into effect to Quebec the amount of grain handled through that port has not increased, and it is quite possible that if this rate plus the differential were continued to the maritimes it might not prove to be any better for those ports.

All I ask is that it be
tried.

Item agreed to.
Railway employees' provident	fund-to
supplement pension allowances payable under the provisions of the Intercolonial and Prince Edward Island Railway Employees' Provident Fund Act so as to make the minimum payments during the period January 1, 1933 to March 31, 1934, the sum of $30 per month instead of $20 as fixed by the said act, $29,000.

Will the minister give a full explanation regarding this money that is voted each year to supplement pension allowances? It seems to be hard for our railway
men in the maritimes to understand it, and it is a great deal of trouble trying to explain it to them. I cannot understand it.

In a word, it is because the minimum pension was formerly $20 and, because of the cost of living, it was raised to $30. Consequently, the cost to the government is greater than it used to be. If the hon. member so desires, I can read the statement which will explain the matter a little more fully.
Do I understand that all men who receive pensions get $30?

Yes, under the Intercolonial and Prince Edward Island Railway Employees' Provident Fund Act, they receive a minimum of $30. They may receive more. The minimum pension, as I say, used to be $20 and it was increased to $30. It was because of the difference between the $20 and $30 that the item had to be inserted. It is an item which costs the railway a good deal more than that. I do not know that I can give the exact figure. At the present time this amount of $29,000 is for the difference in the amount of pension.

Quite a number do not receive $30. Would that be because they did not have the length of service, or would it be for some other reason? Some receive $22, $24, $25 and so on. They want to know why they do not receive the $30.

My deputy, who is a railway man, says that none of them receive less than $30. If my hon. friend will give me a specific case, I shall gladly look into it. My information is that the lowest pension received by anyone who has a right to a pension, is, $30.

I shall be glad to write? my hon. friend and give him the information, I do not know whether I would be in order in referring to this matter now, but last year there was a very serious railway accident in my locality and claims for compensation are still pending. I do not know whether the

Supply-Railways and Canals
minister has any information about the matter, but I hope, if it is brought to his attention, he will give it his sympathetic consideration, because it was a very serious accident where many lives were lost. The men were called out and the blame apparently rests on the railway for carelessness in some form for the loss of those lives. I think every consideration should be given to the claims.

I may point out to my hon. friend that of course the government or the minister has nothing whatever to do with a case of that kind; it is one which is in the hands of the railway company. Anyone in an accident on the Canadian National has of course the same redress as he has were the accident on the Canadian Pacific. Generally speaking, I think both railways endeavour to be fair and just to people who have suffered in an accident. I shall gladly draw my hon. friend's remarks to the attention of the railway company, but that is all I can do, because, no matter how sympathetic I may be to the unfortunate people who were in the accident, I have no control in the matter.

Before we pass to the next item, I should like to ask the minister whether the salaries of the board of railway commissioners, as authorized by statute, are subject under the income tax, to the ten per cent reduction?
They are treated just the same as other government employees.

With reference to the board
of railway commissioners, in the session of 1931 I brought to the attention of the house the question of who was to enforce decisions given by the board. It was pointed out that in British Columbia a decision had been given and the Canadian Pacific for two years had refused to pay any atttention to it. I believe some teeth should be put into the act so that when appeals are made before the board and a decision is given, there should be some power or authority to see that the judgment is carried out.
I understand another case arose last year when an appeal was made by interests in Quebec and a decision was given whereby the rate from Quebec to Saint John was lowered. The Canadian National has complied with that, but the Canadian Pacific has not. My understanding was that the board of railway commissioners was set up to conduct matters equitably between the people of Canada and the railways, so that if an injustice arose 
either way, an appeal could be made. If an appeal is made for an increase in rates and a decision is given by the board granting the appeal, the increase simply goes into effect and the only redrees we have is an appeal to the governor general in council. But where the decision is against the railway company, the latter can simply ignore the decision. If we are to have a board of railway commissioners to act equitably between the people and the railways, teeth should be put into the act so that when a decision is made, there will be some authority to compel the railway to comply with that decision.

There is in the board of railway commissioners exactly the same authority as there is in any other court in Canada. Once they give a decision, that is a judgment of the court, and an order is given that it shall be carried out. It is true that the railways may appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada on a question of law, and that appeal might delay the carrying out of the order. If my hon. friend would visit the board, as he has a perfect right to do, and ask the secretary to explain why such an order was not carried out, I am sure he would be given the correct information. I cannot give it because I know nothing about the ctfSe. I have no more control over the board than I have over any other court in Canada. I have heard no complaints that orders of the board are not being carried out. If the hon. member will take the matter up with the board, I am sure the secretary will explain the matter as I am not in a position to do.

I took the matter up in connection with freight rates, and the information was given me that the Canadian National had carried out the order making the rate eighteen cents a bushel. The Canadian Pacific simply disobeyed the order, and their rate is thirty-five cents, with the result that twice the quantity of grain has been shipped at the cheaper rate. The point I want to bring up is that on many occasions when the board has made a ruling, the Canadian Pacific has simply ignored it. If we are to have a costly court such as the board of railway commissioner's, there should be somle authority behind it. The only recourse we have is to the governor general in council.

The governor general in council has no authority over an order of

Supply-Railways and Canals
that kind. I can hardly believe the Canadian. Pacific wouild maintain a rate double that of the Canadian National, because in that case the Canadian Pacific would get no business; the Canadian National would get it all.
There was a case in British Columbia two years ago.

If the hon. member will write me about it, I shall be glad to make inquiries, but neither the government nor I as minister have any power over the board of railway commissioners. It is a court and carries on of its own authority. Of course it is true there are appeals from that court to us after a judgment is given, but once their judgment is given, I think there are methods whereby the board can easily insist on the judgments being carried out. If my hon. friend will draw the matter to their attention,
I am sure they will see to it.
I shall endeavour to find out.

Can the minister advise us whether, in the case of an appeal against a lower rate, the board has a right to allow the existing rate to stand until the appeal is settled? Where by a decision of the board a higher rate is granted, that rate automatically goes into effect and those complaining have a right to appeal. The case pointed out by my hon. friend is that the ruling of the board was for a lower rate and the railway appealed against the rate and did not apply the lower rate to the tonnage offered pending decision on the appeal. I am asking the minister has the board of railway commissioners the right to allow the existing rate to stand while the railway companies are appealing against a lower rate order.

I presume the board has
thait right, but I should not like to express a legal opinion upon a matter of that kind. But suppose the board had ordered a lower rate, and that lower rate was sustained, I presume that the people who had paid the higher rate would be entitled to compensation.

Item agreed to.
To provide for the payment of salaries and expenses in connection with the St. Lawrence ship canal surveys and investigations, including D. W. McLachlan at $1,350 and G. W. Yates at $1,080, $38,500.
Are the gentlemen whose names are mentioned in the item members of the civil service?

Yes, both Mr. McLachlan and Mr. Yates are members of the civil service, but for many years, even under the regime of my right hon. friend, they were given this special allowance, and in order to legalize the payment it has to go through the estimates.

My point was that I think the item should include the words "notwithstanding anything in the Civil Service Act." Otherwise I imagine the Auditor General would not have the right to pay these amounts because under the Civil Service Act the members of the service are precluded from getting any additional compensation for anything unless parliament specifically states otherwise.
Without arguing that those words should be included in the item, I take it that once the item is passed by parliament the Auditor General will be justified in permitting these allowances to be paid.
I have always understood that it was necessary to include the words "notwithstanding anything in the Civil Service Act."

If that is the case, they
will probably be without the allowance for the coming year.

Is there any
possibility of the treaty with respeat to the St. Lawrence waterway coming before parliament this session?

I should not think it is
likely because it is generally understood that until the treaty has been adopted by the United States it will not be dealt with by this parliament, and it is hardly likely that the treaty will be adopted by the United States congress at its present session, although I understand that it was reported from committee to (the United States Senate within the last couple of days.

Have not representations
been made to the minister to have the operations of the car ferry steamer not charged to the Prince Edward Island division? I understand that representations have been made from year to year by boards of trade throughout the maritimes that these operations be charged to capital account.

My hon. friend is wrong
in saying that they are charged to the Prince Edward Island division. They are charged to

Mr. Speaker, the question
directed by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Heenan) was drawn to my attention, and I have had an opportunity to go into the records in connection with the cases referred to. I may say that I doubt the wisdom of spreading upon the public records the details of (these deportation cases. One reason, among others, for this feeling, is that these unfortunate people have relatives, and I do not think it is desirable to advertise their misfortunes. Nevertheless I am going to answer the question of the hon. member.
The first case, that of a man known as Tom Kirbride, whose correct name I think is Joseph Kirbride, falls within section 40 of the Immigration Act, which reads:
Whenever any person, other than a Canadian citizen or person having Canadian domicile, shall be found an inmate of or connected with the management of a house of prostitution or practising prostitution, or who shall receive, share in, or derive benefit from any part of the earnings of any prostitute or who manages or is employed by, in, or in connection with any house of prostitution or music or dance halt or other place of amusement or resort habitually frequented by prostitutes, or where prostitutes gather, or who in any "way assists any prostitute or protects or promises to protect from arrest any prostitute or who shall import or attempt to import any person for the purpose of prostitution or for any other immoral purpose, or Who has been convicted of a criminal offence in Canada or who admits the commission prior to landing or entry to Canada, of a crime involving moral turpitude, or has become a professional beggar or a public charge or practises polygamy, or has become an inmate of a penitentiary, gaol, reformatory, prison, asylum or hospital for the

Executives in Branch Plants
insane or the mentally deficient, or an inmate of a public charitable institution, or enters or remains in Canada contrary to any provision of this aot, it shall be the duty . . .
and so on. As I have said, this case falls within this section; the Man was tried in our courts and convicted of one of the offences set out in this section. A court of inquiry sat on the case under the Immigration Act; an appeal was entered and I ordered his return-I think properly-to the country of origin.
The next case is that of a man by the name of J. Waldon. A careful search of the records of the department has not disclosed that any such person is under observation.
The next case is that of John Harris and family, who were ordered deported by a board of inquiry after having become public charges. I reviewed this case. The board of inquiry was quite within its rights in ordering the return of these people to their country of origin. But after carefully going into the question, on January 13 last I decided that in this case it would be proper not to invoke the order of deportation. I think probably the family will become established here.
The other case is that of Fred Booth. This case is still under investigation by the officials of the department, and as yet I have not been called upon to pass on the question of whether or not this alien should be returned to his country of origin.
On the orders of the day:

I should like to ask the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gordon), who is also the acting Minister of Immigration, whether it is the intention of the government to allow United States industrial concerns having branches in Canada to dismiss Canadian executives and replace them with American executives brought from their plants in the United States.
I am asking this question because I have received information, which I have reason to believe is true, that General Motors of Canada and some other United States concerns have dismissed practically all their division heads who were Canadian citizens, and have replaced these men with executives from United States plants. Some time ago I spoke to the minister privately with regard to this matter, and I trust that he is in a position to answer this question to-day.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. A. GORDON (Minister of Labour):
speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
I can assure the hon. member that nothing is further from the mind of this

government than to permit such a practice as has been suggested. There are occasions when it becomes necessary in the ordinary course of business practice to permit the entry of persons skilled in particular trades or activities. Since I have been acting as Minister of Immigration I have endeavoured at all times to seek the best possible sources of information when applications come to the department with regard to the entry of persons who are said to be necessary to the carrying on of a business. On many occasions, as hon. members opposite know, I have referred to members of this house, and under my hand I have a list of persons whose entry into Canada has been recommended by members on both sides of the house. I do not know that it would serve any useful purpose to read these names, but I would be very glad to show the list to any hon. member who might desire to see it. I think I have a right to rely, as I do with confidence, on any recommendations that may be made by any member of this house with respect to matters of this kind. I have rarely found that any member has been careless in his advocacy of the admission of a very necessary skilled man in the carrying on of the industrial life of this country, and I hope it will continue so. But I can assure the hon. member that at no time would the government countenance the dismissal of the Canadian heads of industry, even in a minor capacity, to be replaced by someone from a foreign country. The subject is an intricate one. It is most difficult for one completely to encompass the complexities of all industries in this country, but I can assure the house that my officials and myself will take every possible action towards preserving to the Canadian workman and to the Canadian heads of departments in industry the position which is rightfully theirs.

I think the words I used were, not "a conference" but "the conference," referring to the Imperial conference, because there was no other conference between us. I have looked carefully into the subject and I find that my memory was correct when I said that there was no communication of any kind, official or unofficial, between the premier of Newfoundland and myself, or any member of the government, with reference to the union of that dominion and Canada. The motion will stand
Motion stands.

Whereas progress and science compel fruit and vegetable growers to use poisonous substances called "insecticides" in order to protect their products;
And whereas these chemical agents are not wholly affected by weather conditions and remain on these products, especially on fruit, and this fruit is largely consumed in its natural state;
Therefore be it resolved, that, in the opinion of this ho-use, legislation designed to protect the consumers should be enacted.
Mr. iSpeaker, the terms of one of the clauses of the Imperial economic conference agreements suggested to me the moving of this resolution. May I, however, state that I do not intend, in the course of this debate, to discuss the merit of this treaty from all angles, but simply from the standpoint of hygiene and trade.
At the outset of the session, parliament ratified a trade convention with Great Britain by which the latter grants us a preference of $1 per barrel of apples exported to her markets. To our producers and to many among us this treaty seemed advantageous. However, owing to tariff changes on chemical
fertilizers and various agents used by fruit and vegetable growers to protect their trees and plants, and because these same fruit and vegetable growers are now at the mercy of the notorious trust of chemical fertilizers, known as the Imperial Chemical Corporation, of London, whose ramifications extend throughout the world, to Holland, Baltimore and the U.S. under the name of Dupont de Nemours Ltd.; in Canada, to Hamilton,. Beloeil and Halifax, under the name Canadian Industries, I must consign to the future the care of determining whether it will be to our advantage or not; these considerations, however, are outside of my subject.
From a sanitary viewpoint, Great Britain will not permit Canadian fruit to reach its markets, unless Canada exports a strictly graded and sound fruit, in keeping with the regulations of the country, and, moreover, conforms to the international margin allowed; that is, the proportion of insecticide spray on the peels of apples should not be more than 0-01 grain per pound of fruit, therefore, the fruit should be treated, which requires further outlay for machinery, neutralizing equipment, labour and additional hands.
Being a member of the medical profession and representing a population entirely composed of consumers; moreover having some knowledge of the physiological action of toxic substances used, such as insecticides, a poison which partly adheres to fruit, notwithstanding atmospheric agencies, I am bound to recognize the soundness of England's legislation against the possible dangerous effects which the trade of untreated fruit, consumed in its natural state would give rise. I therefore, deem it my duty, wholly in the public interest, to submit, to-day, this question to Parliament.
All are aware that in the course of a season fruit growers must often spray their trees and fruit to guard against the ravages wrought by insects. The standard preparation which is universally used is a solution of lead arsenic. Sometimes a solution of copper cyanide is resorted to but only occasionally. These poisons adhere to the leaves of the trees and fruit but gradually or partially disappear under the action of wind and rain. Further spraying is resorted to and science even advises the spraying of trees and fruit sometimes previous to the picking.
We find in the 1903 reports of the Bureau of Researches, at Washington, at its Agricultural Experimental Station, that a commission of experts was appointed to investigate the quantity of poison remaining from the spraying of orchards by arsenical lead. The
Fruit Act-Mr. Deslauriers

result gave 1 gramme, 420 milligrammes of A203-of arsenical trioxyde-per kilogram after the fruit was picked. Later, in. 1914, following numerous trials, these experts stated in their reports that the quantity of toxic substance found in the residue of the fruit sprayed varied and is entirely controlled by the weather.
In 1925, under Great Britain's threat of placing an embargo on United States fruit the Department of Foods and Drugs, at Washington and the State of Indiana, amended their legislation to facilitate the fruit trade, and agreed to conform with the requirements of the international margin allowance, which restricts the deposit of arsenical trioxyde to not more than 0-01 grain per pound of fruit exported. In their reports, for the same year, these experts state that the deposit resulting from spraying is far more dangerous, if precipitation is slight, and spraying has been more frequent.
Those interested in this question will find in the Agricultural Journal, of Victoria, Australia, December number of 1931, that Great Britain made representation to the Australian government because their apples showed visible traces of arsenical lead, and owing to this, the Australian apple growers sustained considerable losses, as a result of a too imperfect cleansing of their fruit.
In the same report, the United States experts advise the producers not to use oil in their insecticide solution, because the cleansing of fruit is too difficult with this ingredient; they deny the contentions of those who state that the quantity of poison found in the spraying deposits is too small to be a danger to health, and categorically assert that arsenic is small doses, absorbed during a certain period, and especially in combination with a lead salt, is very deleterious.
The physiological action of arsenic in small doses produces no violent effect; its action on the organism is imperceptibly slow and insidious; its accumulation is easy and elimination difficult. It is with .much precaution that this drug is used' in therapeutics against certain diseases, owing to its dangerous action, because, when the symptoms of poisoning appear, the life of the patient is in danger.
The formula of this world wide insecticide, consists in 2 pounds of arsenical lead per 100 gals, of water. In the course of a season the fruit grower performs a number of sprayings and each one leaves a deposit which keeps on accumulating. The quantity of toxic substance deposited on the fruit cannot possibly be uniform because during a dry season the quantity will be greater. In the

Maritime Provinces, where rain is more frequent, the quantity would be less, while in British Columbia where rain is less frequent, the quantity would be greater. Fruit on the lower limbs of trees, subject to more spray, and less exposed to rain and wind than the upper limbs will retain more of these toxic substances, and when analysed, will be more open to criticism. There is no doubt that the public consuming fruit uncleansed and in its natural state, such as grapes from the Niagara district, runs serious dangers. Legislation enacted by those countries, which I mentioned, and their continuous researches, analyses, reports and the opinions of experts on the toxical deposits from the spraying of fruit trees, make it a question of the utmost importance.
Notwithstanding the restrictions of other countries, under our present system, each year, in summer and especially in the autumn season, millions of tons of fruit are shipped to our large centres and delivered to our homes; each day, we see on our streets, honest vendors unwittingly selling fruit bearing traces of poison; we witness children, so fond of fruit, innocently playing about with poison in their hands. When the medical profession tells us new diseases are spreading, the origin of which is unknown, such, for instance, as infantile paralysis; when they admit the greater frequency of sudden deaths, irrespective of age; when certain cases of illness develop under new forms, I state that it be1-hooves the authorities to seriously look into everything affecting human life.
There is no legislation covering our domestic trade of fruit. One wonders to what door must we knock to obtain the required reforms so as to keep pace with science. Must we address ourselves to the Department of Agriculture or that of Health? The question is unsettled. We have no research bureau as other countries have, in this respect. It is time to follow the lead of Great Britain, the United States and other countries and enact up-to-date legislation, bearing in mind that human capital is the most precious asset we possess.
From the viewpoint of trade, the cleansing of fruit, especially of our apples, is a condition, a strict regulation which must be adhered' to in our exports to Great Britain, if we wish to take advantage of the preference of $1.00 per barrel of apples.
There exists in England an act governing the trade on fruit with a view to protect the consumer; the act prohibits-subject to prosecution-the sale on British soil of fruit which by analysis indicates the presence of

Fruit Act-Mr. Weir (Meljort)
more than 0-01 grain of arsenic or toxic substance; that is what is known as the international margin allowance. Australia and Nova Scotia have had a bitter experience, in the past, of this legislation.
Apart from this, there are regulations governing the grading of apples as to uniformity and quality, this requires more labour and hands. However, the process necessitated in cleaning the fruit gives rise to a serious problem. Indeed, this process, the only one recommended, consists in washing the apples in a solution of i, 1, 2 per cent of hydrochloric acid during a few minutes, with the addition of sodium chloride either heated or not. These various operations require the use of special machinery, receptacles and neutralizing agents, this means so much more outlay, not mentioning the time and further hands required, before ever benefiting from the SI preference per barrel of apples. Moreover, the Canadian apple grower must compete with the world prices on the English market.
There exists no substitute to arsenical lead as an insecticide approved by experts. Sometimes a certain quantity of oil is added to this solution; however this is not advised as the cleansing is more difficult. The dry cleansing, although making the fruit more attractive, requires much time, is little effective, as it removes but 30 per cent of toxic substance, leaving a deposit greater than allowed by the international margin, and can only be applied to certain fruits, and, therefore, not practical owing to its limited effectiveness. The only practical method is that of washing the fruit, which is a more economic process as to time and results, and has been adopted in all countries where fruit is grown on a large scale such as in the United States, but especially, in Australia.
The outlay mentioned will naturally increase the cost of production considerably. I, therefore, cannot see how our fruit growers can compete with the world prices, when they have to face this further outlay, unless our governments cooperate generously by grants, thus helping them to hold the British market and benefit by it.
I had the opportunity of visiting many districts where fruit is grown, and nowhere did I notice the necessary installations in connection with the cleansing of fruit to meet export requirements.
It is quite clear that an extensive campaign of education among the people must be undertaken, so as to profitably carry out this system of cleansing by washing, which varies according to the peel being more or
less thick, and, so as to also teach them the proper time to pick the fruit and do their cleansing immediately before the storing of the fruit, in order to avoid the formation of wax which decreases the permeability of the deposit resulting from spraying, and, therefore, makes the cleansing more difficult.
The fruit growers absolutely require encouragement, otherwise they may be tempted to curtail their spraying, especially just previous to the picking of the fruit, as a means of economizing, saving time and dispensing with the cleansing; they will thus expose their fruit to the ravages of maggots and, in the end, they will nevertheless be forced to clean the fruit, after having sustained losses.
It is quite evident that Canadian fruit will only be sought on the English markets on condition it is uniform, of superior quality and well cleansed. Such a condition can only be realized by utilizing the process mentioned which naturally increases the cost of production, and, by a campaign of education which may be successful if the interested provinces lend their hearty cooperation by exhibitions, lectures, and publications.
At all events, I think that the question deserves the attention of parliament, and I trust that the government will find it possible to introduce the necessary legislation both in the interest of public health and Canadian trade.

Mr. Speaker, legislation dealing with the subject matter of this resolution already exists in the Agricultural Pests Control Act, 1927, under the provisions of which insecticides must be registered with the Department of Agriculture in order that these poisons may be checked for compliance with the guarantees and standards of quality, samples being taken and analyzed. The insecticides are analyzed chemically and tried out in the entomological branch for effectiveness. Doctor Macoun, Dominion horticulturist, states that there has never come to his knowledge any case of poisoning in connection with the use of these sprays and that horticulturists feel these sprays are essential if our fruit is to be harvested in the best possible form for market. In conclusion he says:
It would seem, from all past experience, that further legislation in Canada designed to protect the consumers of fruit is quite unnecessary.
In addition a great deal of investigation ha3 been done with reference to the content of arsenical poison used in sprays in British Columbia where irrigation is used. It is felt that in eastern Canada and outside the
Fruit Act-Mr. Bennett

irrigation area the precipitation itself is sufficient to remove any danger from this use of arsenic sprays. The result of the investigation carried on by Doctor Shutt, Dominion chemist, is set out in the English Analyst, volume 51, 1926. This is his summary:
Summarizing the tabulated data, it will be seen that approximately one-half the samples were entirely free from arsenic, that roughly one-sixth showed traces of arsenic in amounts less than one ten-thousandth of a grain per pound, a negligible quantity, and that one-third contained arsenic in quantities ranging from one ten-thousandth to one one-hundred and ninetieth of a grain per pound. With the heaviest amount of arsenic found, namely one one-hundred and ninetieth of a grain per pound, it would require three pounds, or one dozen apples of average size, to supply the minimum medicinal dose of arsenic, and twelve pounds, or four dozen apples of average size, to supply the maximum medicinal dose.
The results of this inquiry furnish satisfactory evidence to the effect that a very large proportion of Canadian sprayed apples is entirely free from arsenic and that in those cases in which the presence of arsenic has been detected, the quantities are negligible.

speakeroldname: Mr. MURRAY MacLAREN (Minister of Pensions and National Health):
speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
The mover of the resolution (Mr. Deslauriers) has drawn attention to the importance of close supervision of insecticides or the various substances which are used to destroy insects on vegetables and fruit, and he asks that the consuming public be protected by legislative action from the danger of poisoning or injury from such substances.
I quite agree that it is important that there should be safeguarding legislation, but I would point out that safeguarding legislation exists at the present time. If members will turn to the Food and Drugs Act, they will find that paragraph (f) of section four provides:
Any fruit or vegetable dangerously contaminated with any poisonous substance, whether added with intent or not, must be deemed to be adulterated within the meaning of the Food and Drugs Act.
Under this legislation there is in the Department of National Health a staff of chemists working, analyzing and investigating such specimens as come before them. There are something like twenty-seven health inspectors throughout the dominion, and when any such case of poisoning or even rumours of poisoning is brought to their attention the case is referred for investigation to the laboratories, existing not only in Ottawa but at four or five other points throughout the dominion. I have made inquiries in the department and I am informed that certainly within recent years no case, no report of a case, of poisoning has come within their observation. Repeated examinations have been

made during the past few years regarding celery, not so much the Canadian product, as the large amount of celery imported from the United States, and regarding which there were complaints some time ago. That has been under the observation of our chemists and the celery has been analyzed.
The same is true of apples. In the years 1925 and 1926 numerous observations were made regarding the presence of poisons on apples. At the present time, grapes and wine are being analyzed by the departmental chemists. So far as we can leam in the department, no reports have been made of poisoning within recent years or ill effects arising from these insecticides being used on vegetables and fruits. But should the occasion arise we have at present the legislative machinery and inspectors and chemists whose duty it is to analyze these products for the presence of injurious substances.
I do not gather what further protection the mover of this resolution would advocate, beyond perhaps a certain washing of fruits and vegetables, but as I understand from the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Weir), and indeed as we all know, many of these substances are, while not completely, at all events I think sufficiently removed by rain and weather conditions. I do not think that with our present knowledge there is any further step in a legislative way that can be taken for the protection of the public against these insecticides, and after hearing this explanation and what the procedure is, perhaps the mover may consent to withdraw his resolution, particularly in view of the fact that very little complaint is made regarding ill consequences from the use of these insecticides.

The proposal to protect the consumer is very commendable, but another point of view that has not been touched upon is the effect of poisonous sprays on the honey industry. Many of our citizens have gone in for keeping bees, and the honey industry has reached considerable proportions. Fruit blossoms open very early in the spring and the bee keepers are desirous that the bees should have full advantage of nectar from the blossoms. When the blossom is sprayed for protection against insects the bees, trying to obtain the nectar, are poisoned. Apiarists have had considerable losses through the apple sections of the country. This mortality in the hives should be given consideration, research should be made to find a way to obviate this loss to our bee keepers.

REDUCTION OF DOMESTIC RATES ON GRAIN AND GRAIN PRODUCTS
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, the domestic freight rate on grain, and grain products, moving from any point in the provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia, to a point in any of the said provinces, or from any point, to another point, in any of the said provinces be adjusted, or reduced, by at least fifty per cent (50%) of the differential, as now exists, between domestic and export rates.
He said:	Speaking to a similar resolution
last year, I endeavoured to point out to the house the necessity of giving some consideration to the farmers of western Canada by way of reduction in domestic rates on grain. I will not go into the whole question to the extent we did last year, but I would suggest that there is an argument that has not yet been presented with respect to interprovincial shipments. I believe the debate last session proved beyond doubt that we have reached a time when this question should be given consideration. The house was informed by the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Manion) on February first, and again on Thursday last, that he would within a few days make a statement or explanation with respect to a proposed reduction in rates that might amount to say, fifty per cent of the differential; it may be his proposal will effect the purpose of my resolution. Therefore I do not consider it necessary at this time to cover all the ground. However, I would like to refer to the appeal that was taken from the decision of the board of railway commissioners handed down in 1927,
which appeal has not yet been heard. Following the debate last year I think the western members were all of the opinion that that appeal stood in the way of any action being taken. They decided that they would, during the recess, make representations to their respective provincial governments to see that this appeal was heard. I myself interviewed the government of Saskatchewan and tried to impress upon them the importance of having such action taken. The fact that we did make representations to the provincial governments and that the argument last year was so conclusive, I think, caused this question to be brought before the interprovincial conference here last month and also the statement made by the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals last Thursday. How far they agreed on that occasion, or how far the minister will go in his statement to the house, I do not know; he may give effect to my whole resolution. That would be a splendid thing.
The second part of my resolution, which deals particularly with the shipment of grain from one point to another within a province, I think is very important. There is no doubt that in the very near future there will be a vast change in the system of agriculture in western Canada. We have from year to year a considerable carry over of grain. This has always been a problem, in its effect upon price especially during the last four or five years. Many suggestions have been put forward for the solution of the problem of how we should eliminate or decrease that surplus. One suggestion has been that the acreage sown to wheat in western Canada should be reduced. I do not favour a reduction of the gross acreage seeded to grain; rather I favour a switching from wheat to coarse grains. If in the near future the exchange difficulty, which at present somewhat hinders our trade with Great Britain, is corrected-and this may be done sooner than any of us think-then the farmers of western Canada will be only too anxious to change to a system of more diversified farming in order to develop that trade with Great Britain.
I would suggest that we advocate a reduction in wheat acreage, together with a change to the coarse grains. There are some
280.000	farmers in western Canada growing wheat. If each farmer would seed thirty acres less to wheat and put in coarse grains or fodder crops instead it is easy to see that there would be a reduction in wheat acreage of some
5.400.000	acres which, at fourteen bushels to the acre, in a normal year would mean about 76,000,000 bushels of wheat. I think this would materially assist in reducing the sur-
2034	COMMONS
Western Freight Rates-Mr. Perley
plus. This land would be seeded mainly to barley and oats, and if diversified farming were practised the farmers would require more pasture and more fodder crops for their cattle. If the farmers of the west intend to take advantage of the agreements passed by this house last November they will have to change their system of farming, and if they do that they will need these coarse grains to feed their cattle, their hogs, their dairy herds and their poultry. I should think, in addition, that the increasing demand will be found in the province of British Columbia; the farmers in the Fraser valley and other parts of that province will be only too anxious to take advantage of the trade agreements we recently adopted. So of necessity a great deal of grain will be shipped between different points in the prairie provinces in order to feed the stock, as I have outlined.
There is another point which might be developed in favour of interprovincial shipping. In the near future we may have a provincial milling industry, so to speak. I think the Department of Trade and Commerce would be well advised to endeavour to develop more trade with the orient in regard to flour. I know the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) is doing everything possible to develop trade with foreign countries, but I think the flour milled in western Canada- which is the highest grade flour in the world -should be marketed in the Orient as a product of western Canada. At present the flour milled from our wheat is distributed through the orient by the millers of Japan, who do not produce the best grade of flour, so the people in the orient have not become accustomed to the kind of flour we produce in Canada. There are great possibilities in regard to trade in flour, and I think a milling industry should be built up within the provinces. If this were to happen it would be necessary to have a lower interprovincial rate covering the shipment of the by-products, the bran and shorts, in order to make them available to farmers feeding stock.
I think it is generally agreed that interprovincial rates are too high, but I do not wish to develop that point just now. We all know the difficulties our railways find in carrying on at the present time; we know how they view any proposal with regard to the reduction of freight rates, but at the same time we must remember the difficulty with which the farmers of the west have been faced and the losses they have sustained in the last few years. They have put up a gallant fight against the greatest odds with which an agricultural people were ever faced, and they have carried on with courage and confidence. 
I believe that to-day the morale of the western farmer is just as good as, if not better than, it was a year ago, and he is prepared to go forward, showing the same initiative and feeling the same hope, confidence and courage with which the pioneers of the west laid the foundation for the agriculture of the present day. It is up to us to do everything we can to encourage our western farmers, and I think a reduction in the domestic rates would be extremely well received.
I do not wish to carry the argument further at this time, as I will have an opportunity to speak again before the debate is closed, but I do wish to suggest, that half a loaf is better than no bread. In view of the statement made by the Minister of Railways and Canals the other day I hope he may find it possible to support this resolution, so I will leave the argument at this point.

subtopic: REDUCTION OF DOMESTIC RATES ON GRAIN AND GRAIN PRODUCTS
speechtext:
In view of the remarks of the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Perley)
I will have only a few words to say at this time, and those few words will be practically a repetition of what I said a few days ago with reference to a bill introduced by an hon. gentleman opposite.
At that time I pointed out that at the interprovincial conference there had been some discussion regarding this matter, and I said we had come to a compromise agreement which I thought at the time and still think, will be satisfactory to the western provinces. When I made the statement the proposal as outlined by the railways had not gone forward to the western provinces. The proposal was to have been put in writing and submitted to myself and I was to forward it to the four western provinces which were represented at the meeting held in my office

Western Freight Rates-Mr. Manion
dealing with the matter during the interprovincial conference, at which meeting there were the Minister of Agriculture for this government and the representatives of the provinces in question. Since that time the proposal of the railways has come to hand and about a week ago I sent it on to the provinces, and only on Saturday I received from the premier of one of them his acceptance on behalf of the province which perhaps is most concerned in the matter, although I do not know that one can specify any particular province as being more concerned than another.
The compromise arrangement was something along this line. The export rate was a little less than half of the domestic rate on grain going west to Vancouver. Take for example the rates from Edmonton and Calgary to Vancouver. The domestic rate was 41^ cents and the export rate only 20 cents, and it was an actual fact that grain could be sent to China more cheaply than it could be transported to Vancouver. It was an obvious ground for complaint from the standpoint of the west that such a condition of affairs should exist. A year or so ago, when the appeal against the decision of the board of railway commissioners first came before me and the other members of the government, I discussed the matter with the railways and suggested that they make a compromise proposal. At that time I did not succeed in getting them to make such a proposal. The matter remained in abeyance until this later meeting at the interprovincial conference, and the railways finally agreed to a proposal which every representative of the west agreed would be acceptable. That proposal was that the rate from Edmonton and Calgary, instead of being 20 cents for export and 41i cents for domestic, should be reduced on feed grains, that is, grain used for poultry and, I believe, cattle feed, to about 50 per cent, or a little more than 50 per cent in fact, of the differential, and that all other rates throughout the west on feed grain going west should be reduced in about the same ratio. That was the proposal they finally put forward to me and which I sent on to the west.

The railways have pointed out continuously, and with truth, that the rates on grain in Canada are the lowest in the world for the
distance. They admit that the export rate westward is a good deal lower than the domestic rate, but that is the general attitude they took. They actually claim that the export rate does not give them an opportunity to make any money on grain exported.

I do not think that is
correct. The export rate from Vancouver is very low, and they claim that if there should be a change, instead of the domestic rate being lowered the export rate should be raised. Further, they pointed out that if one interferes with the general rate throughout the western provinces and applies their proposal throughout the whole of the western provinces to interprovincial movements of grain, it will so confuse the whole rate structure, which is already confused enough, that it will call for a complete rearrangement of that structure for the western section of Canada.
I do not know that I have anything further to say except that, as I have observed, one of the provinces has already wired me accepting the proposal and taking the attitude that it will be entirely satisfactory to that province. I have every reason to believe, from the opinions expressed by representatives of the other three provinces who were present, that these provinces will take exactly the same attitude as the one which has already replied to my communication. I would suggest to the hon. gentleman who has moved the resolution that, pending receipt of replies from the western provinces to the communication which I forwarded to them, he might withdraw his resolution after adequate discussion. I invite hon. members on both sides to continue the discussion ad libitum, but after the mover has taken advantage of his right to reply, I suggest that he might withdraw the motion, because both he and his seconder will have accomplished what they set out to do, namely, to bring before the house and the country the need of some change in the rates as they now exist. I entirely agree with their suggestions, as proven by the compromise arrangement to which I refer.
I will not take up more time but I trust that hon. members, while desiring to put on record their views in regard to the rate structure in the west, will bear in mind that the provinces of western Canada will in all likelihood accept the arrangement proposed by the railways.

The appeal which was taken to the board of railway commissioners had reference to rates on grain. This matter is quite important and I should like to hear from the Prime Minister or the Minister of Railways what is likely to become of it. Personally I should be glad to see it disposed of. If the 50 per cent reduction materializes, it will no doubt be accepted. Indeed, anything is acceptable; half a loaf is better than no bread. While we are all glad to have the 50 per cent, it does not mean that we are satisfied, but every one of us will be pleased with the reduction if it goes into effect. subtopic: PROPOSED REVISION BY BANKING AND COMMERCE COMMITTEE IN RELATION TO MONETARY REQUIREMENTS OF DOMINION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, every ten years this parliament is given the opportunity to revise and improve the Bank Act and to decide whether or not the charters of the banks shall be continued for another decade. It is safe to say that since the present Bank Act was originally drafted there never has been so much public interest centered in its revision as at the present time. During the last decade in particular the importance of credit in its relation to the economic life of the state has advanced to the very forefront of world thought. The war turned the spotlight upon the financial institutions of the world, not only because of the vast increases in debt which followed but because the nations which were financially improverished in 1914 suddenly found sufficient money to carry on the most expensive undertaking of all history. It was found that the masses of the people were much better off, economically speaking, during the four years of war despite the wholesale destruction of life and wealth than they were during the peace which followed and had preceded the war. It was noted that when the war was over and men returned to peaceful avocations even though the production of the various nations was vastly increased the economic position of the masses of the people was worse than it was during the great conflict. The inquisitive mind naturally began to ask how it was that the nations which could not find money with which to provide food and clothing for their people in January of 1914 found the money with which to engage in war in the fall of that year and to pursue that war upon a scale
more gigantic, more destructive and more costly than any war in preceding history.
May I digress for a moment at this point to emphasize the fact that some hon. members still argue that the destructive character of the great war is responsible in a large part for the present depression, and may I refer in particular to the statement of the hon. member for East Edmonton (Mr. Bury). The hon. member claimed that the war was the cause of the present depression. Those who listened to the hon. member and those who have read his speech will recall that he mentioned three causes for the present depression. The first was the great war, the second, over-production, and the third tariffs. The hon. member absolves the economic system from any culpability with regard to the present situation but he unwittingly placed a burden of the blame upon his own party. The point I wish to draw to the attention of the house is that while the hon. member tried to make out that the war was the cause of the present depression, in the same breath he stated that we were suffering from over-production. Surely, if the war had been the cause we would have had under-production, people would have been in want because goods were not being produced. But how, then, could he argue, since over-production had resulted, that the war was in any way responsible? The war did not destroy money; it destroyed goods which were made and paid for by the use of national credit during the war and therefore could not be a cause of the present depression. The interest of Canadians in financial questions was aroused by the inquiry instituted in 1923 by this parliament. The resolution which at that time marked the extent of the reference to the committee of inquiry was not taken seriously by the house; indeed, it was regarded as a joke by some, but even at that time it was not so regarded by the people of Canada.
May I summarize just as briefly as possible my argument on that occasion. It will be found on Hansard of February 22, 1923, at page 626. I argued at that time that there was insufficient financial credit to effect the distribution of goods produced in Canada; that such insufficiency of financial credit was inevitable under the financial policy so unquestionably followed by the banks and also because we were producing under a profit system; that these combined agents brought about a condition under which sufficient purchasing power was not distributed during the process of production to buy the output within a given time; that it was folly and madness to limit the issuance of financial credit to the amount of gold which we had
Bank Act-Mr. Irvine

or might obtain, since gold discovered or undiscovered bears no sensible relationship to either the producing or the consuming capacity of the nation; that the national credit, which is the nation's power to produce and deliver the goods as, when and where required, was, if properly used, adequate to distribute the national production; that the national credit was monopolized by a few individuals who operate for personal gain and who are not responsible to anyone but themselves for the financial policy which they put into effect; that the policy of private bankers is wrong because it is based on gold, because it treats money as a commodity and thus prevents money from functioning as a means of exchange and because the whole system is a debt creating one and therefore points to an inevitable collapse; that at leasrt the financial policy, if not the actual operation of banks, should be controlled by the government, instead of the government being controlled by the bankers' policy, and that the continuation of a bankers' policy would be disastrous.
All the arguments of that time, ten years ago, were ignored by the administration. Evidence of men like Major Douglas of London, England, Professor Irving Fisher of the United States, Mr. Neal East and Mr. Bevington of Alberta and others was quietly buried in the archives of parliament. The government of that day, like others since, decided to take the advice of the bankers. This, in my opinion, is like a judge, before pronouncing judgment, deciding to take the advice of the accused. What hardship, what unnecessary suffering and sacrifice the Canadian people would have been saved had the government taken the warnings and advice which were given to the committee that investigated this subject in 1923, and in particular the warning and advice of Major Douglas of England. May I refer to the evidence at page 443 and quote just one or two sentences which appear in the closing remarks of Major Douglas before the committee. This is taken from the journals of the House of Commons in 1923. He said:
My own object in coming here is to make clear that I personaly am convinced that if you go along the lines that you are following at present, and if you continue along these lines for any considerable period of time-I am not going to tie myself down to date-but for my own part, and I think my opinion is being shared bv an increasing number of people -I am perfectly certain you are heading for the most terrific disaster that the mind of man can conceive.
That was ten years ago and we are much nearer the predicted disaster than we were then. Indeed, as an hon. member has sug-

gested, we are in that position at the present moment. Major Douglas made that prophecy, if I might call it such, after he had presented to the committee elaborate data indicating the entire inadequacy of the financial system, followed by both this country and Great Britain, to meet the industrial and economic needs of the times.

speechtext:
I shall not enter into the
whimsies of my hon. friend. May I refer to the illustration given by Major Douglas and the evidence which has been mentioned. I refer to this because it will, perhaps, present clearly and succinctly what is at least one of the financial difficulties in Canada to-day. On page 464 of his evidence he likens money and its function to a railroad with the ticket system limited to the passenger capacity of the railway. He goes on to point out that if one or more people were to secure a privilege to deal in railway tickets, that is to say, to try to get four or five railway tickets in exchange for two or three, there would likely come a time when you would find passengers waiting for an opportunity to go on the train, with empty seats in it, and yet no tickets to permit those would-be passengers to go aboard the train. That is an excellent analogy of the present economic situation in Canada where we have an abundance of goods and a great consuming capacity among the people and y&t we have not the ticket system, if you like, the money system to enable the people to acquire the goods that they desire so much to use.
I do not on this occasion desire to advocate the Douglas or any other system; I am not going to put forth the merits of any particular proposal of financial reform. The time to do that will be when parliament becomes convinced that the present financial system is wrong and when it deliberately sets itself to the task of devising and inaugurating a better one. My object to-day is to have a

Bank Act-Mr. Irvine
committee of the house investigate the whole use of credit in relation to present economic conditions and to report its findings prior to the extension for another ten years of bank charters.
What if the bankers' advice should after all be wrong?
Hon. gentlemen of this house who still are convinced that the bankers' advice is right, "I beseech them," in the language quoted by the hon. member for East Edmonton, "in the bowels of Christ to conceive it as possible that they may be deceived;" and if they are deceived and the bankers' advice is wrong, we are just about to place in the hands of the bankers for another ten years a charter to carry this country on a wrong course for that period of time. Who will take the responsibility for that? Surely we ought to be absolutely certain that the policies of the bankers of Canada are right and that there be no mistake in our judgment in this regard.
I submit, sir, that it is positively dangerous for any government to follow the advice of bankers. Emerson, writing of the secret conclaves in which the Dean and Prebends of the cathedral communed with the Holy Ghost as to whom to appoint to the vacant bishoprics, said that invariably the dictates of the Holy Ghost coincided with the recommendations of the queen. Similarly the policy of sound money coincides with the wishes of the bankers of this and other countries. But the advice of bankers throughout the world has been wrong so invariably that we can no longer have confidence in it. Internationally we have as examples of misinformation and bad advice by bankers the Dawes plan, followed by the Young plan. Again, bankers journeyed all the way from Great Britain to Australia to put that country on the wrong track. Australia, however, decided to follow the advice of the British bankers just a little way, and then discovered that it would be disastrous to follow their advice completely, and so they diverged from it slightly, and to the extent only of that divergence Australia profited from the advice of the British bankers.

subtopic: PROPOSED REVISION BY BANKING AND COMMERCE COMMITTEE IN RELATION TO MONETARY REQUIREMENTS OF DOMINION
speechtext:
No, I refuse to be questioned at the present moment.
We have also the statement of the Right Hon. David Lloyd George in the House of Commons in Great Britain on February 12, 1931, when he was warning the Chancellor of the Exchequer, that- right hon. gentleman who has since been called the Iron Chancellor, but who might more appropriately have been designated by some softer material, that he
should not be afraid of the bankers. Mr. Lloyd George concluded by saying of the bankers, "They have been wrong every time."
Then we come to the tragic acceptance by the present Prime Minister of Great Britain of the advice of the bankers in that country. I believe that history will show that that was the major mistake made by that right hon. gentleman. Even before the election precipitated to secure popular sanction for the bankers' policy was over, the policies of the bankers in Great Britain were proven to be in error.
This parliament, then, should be able to advise itself on questions of credit and to dictate policies to the bankers, rather than have the bankers dictate policies to us. The investigation which I request by the resolution now before the house will tend to increase our knowledge of the subject and remove us from the necessity of having to accept the erroneous information of interested parties who are desirous of maintaining the present banking system largely for personal reasons. The resolution specifies that we should investigate the whole monetary system with a view to seeing to it that the monetary requirements of the Dominion shall be safeguarded. I want to make just one comment on that, Mr. Speaker. Between September, 1928, and September, 1932, there was a great depletion of credit in circulation in Canada. Very often we hear hon. members of this house saying that there is just as much money in Canada to-day as there ever was, and that therefore for us to argue that we are short of money bespeaks great ignorance. But let me point out to the house that in the period mentioned, from September, 1928, to September, 1932, there was a reduction of 8584,000,000 in loans by our banks and a reduction in deposits of $362,000,000, which makes a total reduction for the period of $946,000,000 in circulation in the Dominion of Canada. There is no provision in the Bank Act, so far as I can recall, by which the bankers of this country can be compelled to maintain a definite relationship between the credit in circulation and the volume of goods on the market to be purchased by the people of this country, and those are the important factors for us to keep in mind in dealing with any monetary policy.
In the next place, the resolution suggests that we ought to investigate the advisability of departing from the gold basis. Now I know that we are not on the gold basis, but we seem to have an unfortunate hankering after it, and to wish to keep as close to a theoretical gold basis as possible. In doing so I believe that we are being misled. In this
Bank Act-Mr. Irvine

connection let me quote a resolution which came before the House of Lords on December 15 last. The resolution moved by Lord Mel-chett read as follows:
That, since under modern scientific conditions productive capacity is unlimited, and since the existence of indigence and unemployment throughout a large portion of the population demonstrates the fact that the present monetary system is obsolete and a hindrance to the efficient production and distribution of goods, in the opinion of this house the government should bring forward immediate proposals for the economic reforms necessary to enable the subjects of this realm to enjoy the benefits to which their present productive capacity entitles them.
In. discussing the resolution Lord Melchett argued that the gold standard had been abandoned and would never be returned to, and further he prophesied that there was no hope of finding any way out through the proposed World Economic conference. May I also note in passing that while the resolution discussed in the House of Lords demanded that the government should immediately inaugurate a financial policy that would be calculated to distribute to the British public the advantages of the productive system which they had achieved, the resolution which is now before this parliament merely asks that we should investigate with a view to finding out whether it would be advisable to have such a policy. The resolution which was presented to the House of Lords was defeated by only four votes.

Surely any hon. gentleman has a right to refuse to answer a question. I do not want to be discourteous to my hon. friend, but I am trying to present a case which is not so easy to present as my hon.
(Mr. Irvine.]
friend may imagine, and when he interrupts in the middle of a sentence it is difficult to answer him.
The House of Lords defeated by only four votes a resolution more drastic than this. Might it not be expected, in this parliament, which no doubt imagines itself far in advance of the House of Lords in modern thought, that a resolution to investigate would be willingly accepted?
Thirty-two countries of the world, I believe, have already abandoned the gold standard. Although I am not going to argue it now, I believe that by adhering as closely as possible to the gold standard we have suffered disadvantage, at any rate the subject is a matter worthy of investigation. We are not all as convinced, as the government is, that it is wise to stay as close to the gold standard as we are. The government may be right, I am willing to admit the possibility that I may be wrong, but I do not think it is unreasonable to ask that the government give us the opportunity to investigate.
The resolution suggests also that we investigate the advisability of bringing our dollar to a par with the pound sterling. I am not blind to the tremendous difficulties which from, the beginning of its term the administration has had to face in dealing with our relationships and obligations to other countries. Again I say that I am not entirely sure that the government is right, and surely it is a question for investigation.
In this connection the Financial Times of December 30 last presents a table showing Canadian bonds falling due in 1933, federal, provincial and municipal, amounting to $603,406,000 and corporation bonds amounting to $79,994,000, making a grand total of $683,400,000. These are payable as follows: in United States funds, $266,649,000; in Canadian funds, $378,108,000, and in British funds, $38,643,000. It will be seen from these figures that an alteration in the value of our dollar would be rather to our advantage, since we would be at a disadvantage only in respect to the $266,649,000 payable in United States funds, and would be at an advantage in respect to those payable in Canadian and British funds, not to speak of other factors which would have to be taken into consideration and which might give us an advantage. For instance, I cannot see why a reduction in the value of the Canadian dollar would not give us an advantage in the British market, making possible the benefits which the government tried to secure in their trade agreement with Great Britain. Depreciation of the dollar to par with the pound would also have the effect of increasing our trade with the United States

Bank Act-Mr. Reid
or other countries which might have their currencies on or near the gold basis. It is possible, of course, that the United States would immediately raise their tariff to prevent that; they might even place an embargo against our goods. But if nothing so drastic were done, Canada would be at a great advantage in export trade and thus be in a better position to meet her obligations in the United States in United States funds without losing the exchange at all.
One other thing I desire to emphasize. It is proposed to postpone the revision of the Bank Act for a year, a course of action which I think would be very wise, provided the government afford us opportunity to study the problem in the meantime. Indeed, I had intended to include in my resolution a proposal to defer the revision if it had not been mooted by the government. The revision of the Bank Act is a tremendous task, and it would be to the advantage of this house and the country if during the remaining months of the present session we had a committee, perhaps the standing committee, investigate the whole financial system, with all possible facts and data brought before it to guide it in dealing with these debatable points, the gold basis and the reduction of our dollar to a level with the pound. Thus the government and parliament would be enabled to reach a safe conclusion for proceeding next session with the revision of the Bank Act.
