Bank Act-Mr. Reid
the 'level of the British pound, but I am firmly convinced that it would 'have been greatly to the advantage of our trade if our dollar had been so deipreciated. I believe this should have been brought about some time ago, and I think we would have obtained a great advantage if this had been the case at the time the conference met in Ottawa. To-day there are some twenty-five or thirty countries which have adopted this course of depreciated currencies while only some five or six of the prominent nations have maintained what is understood as the gold standard or basis.
Australia and New Zealand have certainly strong convictions in this regard. I do not know how it was done, but they have depreciated their currency on a line with that of the -pound sterling and, as a matter of fact, have endeavoured to keep below the level of sterling. The argument has been brought forward that Canada is in a somewhat different position from those two countries in that we have borrowed so -much money in the United States. That might be true, but the fact remains that most countries have depreciated their currencies, and instead of a world scramble for gold now we have a world scramble for depreciated currencies, which have enabled these countries to overcome almost all tariffs which have been raised against them.
Consider the case of Japan, which has learned how to get her goods over high tariff walls. That country has issued paper currency with a silver coverage, and1 it may interest the house to know that to-day Japan is shipping considerable goods to the United States, as well as to Canada. I am going to mention only four or five articles to show how this has worked out. I believe Japan is landing rubber boots in the United States at 34 cents a pair; rugs at 6 cents each; grass rugs six by twelve at 92 cents, and last year Japan exported to the United States some 54,500,000 light globes. As everyone knows, Japan has depreciated her yen; to-day the seller can get almost five yen for a dollar. That represents a premium of about 135 per cent on each dollar's worth of goods sold in the United States or Canada. In my opinion Canada is and has been at a distinct disadvantage because of the fact that her dollar has remained tied up to the gold standard, and it is generally recognized now, I believe, that the Ottawa conference agreements are of little value so long as we remain on the gold standard. Whether or not it is done deliberately I believe that ultimately our dollar will be forced much lower than it is at the present time. I believe this will be the case and the quicker the better perhaps for our trade.

Now, Mr. Speaker, the first paragraph of this resolution and the one with which I wish to deal particularly, has to do with the advisability of finally departing from the gold basis. I differ somewhat from the mover of the resolution, who believes that we do not need any metallic substance, such ,as go-id or any other precious metal, as a base for our currency. I take the view that we need gold and that we need something else as well. I realize also that one school of thought believes that neither gold nor any other precious metal is required for currency, or even as a base for currency, and I am not overlooking the fact that to-day currency is not based entirely on bullion. In my opinion, however, we must have some unit of value. The process of individual barter is too tedious and too complex. It is true that -many years ago, in the days of primitive civilization, the barter method was followed, but it was not long until that method was discarded; as civilization developed and the wants of mankind increased, it was found necessary to have some unit with which to measure not only goods but services as well, and I do not believe anyone would seriously consider going back to the days of barter. It is universally agreed, I maintain, that we must have some token- or unit of value, some standard whereby we can measure our every-day exchanges or services. I admit that we can and do use paper as money to-day, but the majority of the people have the utmost confidence that behind all that paper there is something much more tangible. It is true that the confidence of the people themselves enables us to use this paper and to conduct our business transactions with paper in the form either of dominion or of bank notes or cheques, because of the inherent and fundamental belief that the paper issued is a real unit of value and can be readily exchanged. Since the beginning of civilization the token of value has been the precious metals, either gold or silver, or both. And there can be no better tangible unit or yardstick, and certainly none in which the peoples of the world have greater faith. Silver and gold are both precious metals; they are not base metals. They have been in use for centuries not only as tokens, like cheques or dollar bills, but as tokens plus something else, as coins having a material value, a commodity, if you like.
The gold or single standard which we are on to-day, and which is the monetary basis of the remaining six prominent nations, did not come about by mere accident. Up to the year 1861 Great Britain and other countries had been using silver as the token of value.

Bank Act-Mr. Reid
In 1860 she was using gold also, but in that year she went off gold entirely and adopted silver as the unit or token of value. Although she had gone off the gold standard, she still used silver, and I believe that the word sterling itself comes from the use of silver.
In 1873 Great Britain forced the United States off the gold standard, although the United States was then using silver as its unit of value and as its currency. It is interesting to know that after the lapse of some sixty years the United States, which was forced off the gold standard in 1873, now practically controls the gold supply of the world, with the result that almost all countries with the exception of perhaps six have now abandoned gold and adopted something else, we are not sure what. It may be goods or credit; I am not quite sure. At any rate, the gold standard was not brought about by accident but in my opinion by design. The bankers and financial manipulators recognized that with a single standard such as gold they sould better manipulate and control the financial affairs of the world for their own advantage. They felt that it would be to their advantage to have a single standard such as gold, and that in my opinion was one of the main reasons why leading nations went off bimetalism. The reason, in my opinion, was that manipulation could be more easily practised. Silver was deliberately demonetized in 1925, and we heard no cry in those days about interfering with the sacred rights of the people, although sixty per cent of the people of the world were almost ruined overnight. In 1925 Great Britain forced India, with a population of 800,000,000, to accept the gold standard. I have here a report of a meeting that took place in the city of Vancouver at which this statement was made on reliable authority regarding Great Britain and India:
India, the great repository of silver, was placed upon a gold bullion standard in 1926. Adoption of the gold standard left an amount of silver rupees to be disposed of variously ' estimated from 400.000,000 to 600,000,000 ounces. The law provided that this stock be sold within a period of ten years. From then until now, India has disposed of some 80-100 million ounces.
Thus a large surplus still over-shadows the silver market. India, in daily practice, remains a silver-using country, and her people find their personal fortunes measured in terms of silver in its ratio to gold, reduced by about one-half, and this fact alone is regarded by many as a contributing factor to the prevalent unrest.
Mexico has reverted to the silver standard, the silver peso now being the only legal tender, and so we find about one-half the population of the world are silver users, and think and trade in terms of silver.
53719-129^
The surplus silver thrown into the world's market in 1925 and 1926 practically impoverished 1,200,000,000 human beings. China, with her 400,000,000, and India with 800,000,000, had their purchasing power suddenly taken from them. This surplus salver thrown suddenly into the world market brought the price of silver down from around SI .25 an ounce to something like 32 cents, and so we witnessed a world scramble for gold. The only medium of exchange, Mr. Speaker, which 1,200,000,000 people had was taken from them over night, and that by direct and deliberate manipulation of the financial and banking interests of the world.
We have reached an impasse in our trade relations to-day. Tariff barriers have been raised by almost every country and goods and produce are at a standstill, so that they cannot move from one country to another. This is due in large measure to tariffs. Only a few countries, practically speaking only two, have gold, although we are supposed to be on a gold standard. We can neither exchange our goods nor obtain this one precious metal to pay for any goods we do buy. We see to-day the spectacle of the United States and France with practically two thirds of the world's gold supply lying idle in their vaults, while tariff barriers have been raised against any goods coming from other countries. These countries which have not the gold are denied the right of purchasing goods because they have no gold to pay for them.
There is only, roughly speaking, $11,000,009,000 worth of gold bullion in the world, two-thirds of which, as I say, is held by France and the United States, and now we have the other spectacle of a wild scramble with depreciated currency. The question then arises: What shall we do? That is the question before the nation to-day. If countries will not agree to lower their high tariff walls so as to allow the free interchange of goods and if nations cannot pay with the recognized unit or yardstick, which to-day is gold, what shall we do? My answer, and the one which I put forward for the consideration of the House, is this. Stabilize silver and go back to a bimetal standard, using both silver and gold as the unit of value or measure. This is not a new formula; it is not something new but something that has been advocated by many men before. I do not know whether it has been advocated in this house but I do know that it is not a new theory. The use of silver is as old as the hills themselves and it has always worked well. Even to-day over sixty per cent of the peoples of the world use silver
Bank Act-Mr. Reid.

as the one unit of value or measure stick for services.
Others refer to a managed currency based upon paper alone. That might work all right domestically where and so long as we have confidence in one another, but paper alone would not be acceptable as between nations, the majority of which still believe in precious metals which have not only an intrinsic but a commodity value as well. The stability of prices is a very desirable thing at the present time, and I would point out to the house that over a period of years, taking the wholesale price of 550 articles, silver has varied only some fifteen per cent, while in that time gold has varied or increased one hundred per cent. There is a very close relationship between silver and commodity prices. In 1919 wheat was selling at $2.56 per bushel and silver at $1.25 per ounce. We have never had a standard to compare with the silver standard, and I ask the house to compare the stability of silver with what has happened in the case of gold. In 1928 one ounce of gold would purchase seven or eight bushels of wheat; to-day that one ounce of gold will purchase sixty or seventy bushels. In 1928 one ounce of gold would purchase one ton of potatoes, while today the same ounce will purchase five tons. In 1928 one ounce of gold would purchase one hundred gallons of milk in the Fraser valley; to-day it will purchase over two hundred and twenty gallons. Let us also consider the gold standard in relation to labour. In 1928 one ounce of gold would purchase five days of labour at $4 per day; to-day that same ounce will purchase fourteen or fifteen days of labour at $1.50 per day, which is the average price for labour being paid in British Columbia.
There is a fear in the minds of some that silver would flood the world, but I claim that this would not be the case. I have obtained the figures showing the production of silver, and they show that since 1492 the total world ' production has been only fifteen billion ounces. If silver were worth one dollar per ounce today, which it is not, we would have only fifteen or sixteen billion dollars worth of silver. I maintain, Mr. Speaker, the production of this metal has not varied, and the surplus to-day is only some 250,000,000 ounces.
Fifteen or sixteen to one was the basis or ratio used in bimetalism. This ratio was based upon the production of the two metals, and the ratio of production has not changed during the past four hundred years. The production of gold and silver for the last five years likewise shows that the ratio of fifteen or sixteen to one of gold still maintains. Again, bimetalism *s not capable of indefinite expansion; whilst the supply of silver is plentiful it is IMr. Reid.]
not unlimited. At the present time twenty-five or thirty countries are off the gold standard, while six very important ones still remain. Those countries still on the gold standard cannot trade with the countries which are not, unless they inflate or depreciate their currency. I realize unlimited paper inflation is fraught with some difficulty. Paper as money would not be accepted by other countries. It has no barter or intrinsic value; it is not a commodity like silver or gold. The precious metals are much sought after in the orient and in India with its population of 800,000000. If we had either silver coinage or paper money with silver as a coverage basis, we would have a sound money. It would not be a fiat money; it would have a real commodity value. As I said, over sixty per cent of the world's people would be very glad to have all the silver coinage or bullion we could give them. Silver has a value as a precious metal; and, what is very important, the people have confidence in it. Many of us would not be adverse to having our pockets filled with silver coins or even to having a supply of silver at home. It is the bankers and the creditors who object when we speak of any inflation, either by paper or by silver. They consider it no crime to take two dollars now for every dollar of debt created a few years ago, but their cry is of holy horror when inflation or depreciated currency is mentioned.
The stabilizing of silver upon a currency basis would add to the basic wealth of oveT half the world's population. It would help those countries which were ruined when they were forced on to the single standard of gold. Many countries are forced to sell their goods upon a silver standard and buy back in terms of gold. In other words, we refuse to use the unit of value or the yardstick of over half the world's population and then by means of tariffs we refuse to admit the goods or products of those countries.
In my opinion -the stabilizing of silver at fifteen or sixteen to one would accomplish two very important -things. First, it would check the rise in the value of gold and so stop prices from going still lower. A few moments ago I gave a comparison of what one ounce of gold would purchase in 1928 as compared with what it would purchase in 1932 or 1933; this stoppage of the lowering of prices would certainly be a very desirable thing. The stabilizing of silver would also raise the purchasing power of 1.200.000,000 people, everyone a potential buyer of our products, if we would only let them. Are we going to sit and wait until our standard of living is forced down to the level of those

Bank Act-Mr. Reid
people or are we going to do something which will raise their purchasing power so that they will be able to purchase the goods which we have to sell and which they would like to have but cannot?
It is true that bimetalism might not solve all the world's problems, but it would be a real step in the right direction. We would be giving the people sound money, we would be giving them the kind of money which has been used since the days of Christ. Silver money has always worked' well for the people but not for the manipulators and financiers.
I have no great faith in the statements of prime ministers or premiers who tell us that we cannot do this or we cannot do that in case something fearful might take place. In 1929 Ramsay MacDonald, Prime Minister of Great Britain, informed the British House of Commons that it would be disastrous for Great Britain to go off the gold standard. He said that calamity would befall the nation; that it was unthinkable Great Britain should go off the gold standard. Nevertheless she has done so; she has depreciated1 her currency 'thirty per cent and yet no calamity has resulted. As a matter of fact, Great Britain during the last year has purchased more food supplies than she did when she was on the gold standard in 1931-32, employment has increased to a considerable extent and her export trade has also increased. So when I hear prime ministers saying that we cannot do this or we cannot d'o that with our currency, I am always mindful of Ramsay MacDonald making that straight statement to the House of Commons in London.
We have plenty of silver and many silver mines, but while we have gold mines, we have not enough gold mines to supply the gold that even this country would require to pay her debts or interest outside. Japan, as I say, has issued coinage based on silver. Germany, France, China and India are all buying silver. Why not Canada? Why can we not be bold enough to take a step along those lines? Great Britain has now declared, that for many years to come she is not going to go back to the gold standard. Why cannot Canada, which has plenty of silver, use it as straight currency or as bullion to stabilize prices as was done before? Or are we going to drift and wait until our dollar is forced down as it ultimately will be? Why cannot we now take some steps that will enable us to trade with other nations, especially when one considers that less than half the world is endeavouring to do business on a small and inadequate amount of gold while the greater part of the peoples of the earth are still using silver as its basis or unit
of value? This is what the Canadian gold dollar has to fight to-day in the world's
markets:

To-day other countries are finding a way into United States markets in spite of high tariffs. Are we going to hesitate about getting into the scramble of depreciated currency, or take a step towards a system that all through the ages has been one of the best so far as exchange of values is concerned, namely, silver and gold, or bimetalism? Japan, to my mind, is a more serious competitor than is Russia in world markets. She has brought that about by depreciating her yen to one-fifth of its previous value. One way to protect ourselves is by stabilizing the price of silver. This would immediately raise the price of silver all over the world and the purchasing power of 1,200,000,000 people would also be increased. This would automatically raise the cost of goods produced in those countries and would help to counteract the dumping of cheap goods into other countries. It would also help to stabilize prices. Bimetalism would do all 1 have stated and I should like to hear hon. members who may follow voice a contrary opinion, or tell the house of any better, safer and more practical scheme.
I have not gone into every detail, but I would urge the house seriously to consider broadening the basis of our unit of value and adding silver to that of gold. Something must be done and done speedily, and I am suggesting what I believe to be a way outr or at least a very important step in that direction. We have clung too long to the single standard. As I have stated, some twenty-nine countries have taken action of their own accord and we shall very soon be forced to take similar action, because it is almost impossible for us to trade or compete with those countries which are already and are still bent on using depreciated currency
204b
Bank Act-Mr. Carmichael

and do not forget that Great Britain has depreciated her currency by some thirty per cent.
In closing I should like to quote from a message issued by Pope Pius XI in 1931, as follows:
How poor, paltry, stupid and unpardonable the voices of certain great bankers of the old and the new world crying for lower wages and lower standards of living for the hand and brain workers of the white race to enable the shipyards, mills, factories, farms and mines of the Aryan world to compete with the semislave workers of Russia and the orient!
I ask in all seriousness that the committee on banking and commerce give earnest consideration to the suggestions which I am now putting forward and that we make a move in favour of bimetalism, using silver as well as gold.

subtopic: PROPOSED REVISION BY BANKING AND COMMERCE COMMITTEE IN RELATION TO MONETARY REQUIREMENTS OF DOMINION
speechtext:
Prior to the dinner hour, debate was following along the line of consideration being given to our Bank Act when it comes up for revision either this year or next. Not being a member of the banking and commerce committee, and not finding it possible to be there when the revision takes place, I am glad of the opportunity to take some part in the discussion on this resolution. I think it would iiave been most unfortunate had the debate been ruled out of order.
In the debate this afternoon one of the speakers dealt with the possible merits of bimetalism. I was much impressed by his arguments, and possibly there is considerable force in them.
I found when I got home during the Christmas recess and held meetings among my constituents that, particularly at this time, there seems to be a general feeling in favour of reforms of some sort in our monetary system. The agriculturists of western Canada are very wide-awake and well versed in governmental matters; they feel that something should be done to help them in their present situation, and perhaps one line of thought which their minds take more than any other is reform in banking and finance, or monetary reform.
A number of criticisms may be offered against our present financial system. I do not think it helps us at all to refuse to recognize these criticisms. On the contrary, I think it is good for us to hear them, and if IMr. Reid.]
there is a remedy for any of the defects in the present system, we should be open to receive suggestions and provide a remedy.
One of the criticisms that I heard when I was home during the recess was the cost of putting into circulation last November $35,000,000 of currency. I have often been asked, why was it that it cost the government so much to put that amount of money into circulation? I think we here are all aware that that money was put into circulation in perhaps the only legal way in which it could be done, namely, through our existing banking system; but for that small operation of circulating $35,000,000 of their own money the taxpayers of Canada have to pay to the banks one per cent for a period of two years, or a total of $700,000. People find it hard to understand why it should cost so much. They also ask this question: That amount of money is put into circulation for two years, and after that time has elapsed, what is going to happen? Will the loan be extended for another year, or for two years, carrying the same charge of one per cent? If so, it will mean a further charge of $350,000 if extended for one year, or $700,000 if for two years. Or will the loan be retired? If so, it will mean that we shall have to tax ourselves to raise another $35,000,000 to retire the original loan.
I find, too, a good deal of criticism from the struggling agriculturists in regard to the profits which our banks are making at the present time. Even though our primary industries find it extremely difficult to exist, let alone make any profit, we find by the last financial statement of our banks, dated December, 1932, that their dividend rates are very substantial, one bank declaring a dividend of eight per cent, seven of them ten per cent, and one, the Bank of Nova Scotia, declaring a rate of fourteen per cent. There was just one bank in -the dominion, Barclay's, which did not declare a dividend, and it operates in only a very small way.
Another criticism is the difficulty that governmental and other organizations, as well as private individuals, experience at times in raising money for any legitimate purpose. Perhaps some of us are not aware that some of our institutions have considerable difficulty in raising money, and when they do raise it, they have to pay a rather high rate of interest. When I was home in the Christmas recess, a municipal corporation close to my own home town was taking steps to raise money by way of scrip. This practice has not become very common in Canada, but at least one small urban centre in Alberta is now on its second

Bank Act-Mr. Carmichael
year of issuing scrip. That is, they issue their own paper for services performed, and the business men carry that paper over until the taxes come in and the paper is redeemed. This municipal corporation in my constituency, comprising ten townships, is now working along that line, interviewing merchants in two of the larger towns close to the organization with a view to having them carry that scrip over until the tax money is available in the fall. They are taking this course, not because the banks will not lend them any money, but in order to get away from the substantial interest charges which the banks would make for lending the money.
We know that our banks pay a very low rate of interest on deposits, a matter of three per cent, and there have been rumours recently that the rate is to be decreased to 2J or possibly 2 per cent; yet the interest rate charged to individuals or corporations in our own west runs from seven to nine per cent. In fact, a municipal corporation generally pays 7i per cent, and a private individual 9 per cent.
Another rumour I have heard is perhaps more serious. There may not be any foundation for it, but it is that our banks are making undue profits out of the present exchange situation between Canada and the United States. I would not say that that is a fact, because I do not know, but I do know that there are rumours to that effect. Possibly the pending litigation in reference to the city of Calgary will bring out whether or not they are well founded.
The most serious criticism that may be offered in regard to banking and finance is the decrease in our note circulation, both dominion and bank notes. I have taken the trouble to compare the amount of notes in circulation in the year 1921, when the second last decennial census was taken, with the amount in circulation in 1931, when the last census was taken. I also have the figures for December, 1932, the latest I can secure. It is alarming to note the decrease in circulation of bank notes particularly during the past ten or twelve years. Without giving the aggregates I will give the per capita circulation. In 1921 it was S30.58 of dominion notes. In 1918, 1919 and 1920 there was an even higher per capita circulation than that; in 1919 it was $35.47. In 1931 it had decreased to $14.01, and in December, 1932, it had further decreased to $13.01. Of bank notes, in 1921 the per capita circulation was $22.15. In 1931 it had decreased to $13.68, and in December, 1932, there was a further decrease to $12.25. Putting those figures together we find that the total per
capita circulation in 1921 of both dominion and bank notes was $52.73. In 1931 it was $27.69, and in December, 1932, $25.26-a gradual decrease during the last ten or twelve year period.
I might point out that a large part of the dominion note circulation was composed of notes of high denominations not in the hands of the general public but rather used as a circulating medium between banks. They were of $1,000, $5,000 and S50.000 denominations. In 1931 there were over $100,000,000 of these. Taking that away it leaves a little over $40,000,000 in 1931, or $3.90 per capita circulating among the people. Add that to the circulation of bank notes, $13.68, and you have a total per capita of $17.58.
Here is something I would like to point out in regard to dominion notes: The value in circulation remained fairly steady from 1919 to 1931. In 1919, excluding the larger notes from $50 to $50,000, the dominion note circulation was a little over $35,000,000. In 1921 it was almost S34,500,000; in 1931 a little over $35,000,000. You can see that the value of dominion notes actually in the hands of the public remained fairly uniform. Of bank notes, in 1919 there were nearly $219,000,000; in 1920 nearly $229,000,000; in 1921, $194,000,000; in
1931,	$142,000,000, and in December, 1932, a little over $127,000,000-an actual dropping off of bank notes. Putting it in another way, if we take 1920 as representing 100, in December,
1932,	the bank note circulation was only 55, a drop of 45 per cent. There was also a large dropping off in bank loans; I think that was mentioned by the hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Irvine). From 1929 to 1931 there was a drop of 25 per cent in bank loans, amounting to more than $550,000,000.
This to my mind constitutes a weakness in our banking system, or perhaps a number of weaknesses, that if possible some means should be found to correct. As one holds meetings among his constituents, he finds many ideas advanced. One is that we should nationalize our banking system, some will say socialize it. Various remedies are put forward for correcting the evils that the people know to exist. May I briefly put before the house what to my mind would be a means of correcting these evils, at least to some extent? I have in mind the system of banking which is in operation in Australia. I do not purpose going into it very much in detail, because in 1928 there was a debate in this house on a resolution proposed by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) and at that time I dealt in some detail with the Australian

subtopic: PROPOSED REVISION BY BANKING AND COMMERCE COMMITTEE IN RELATION TO MONETARY REQUIREMENTS OF DOMINION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to support the resolution which has been brought before the house by the hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Irvine). In doing so I should like first of all to direct attention to the fact that the largest single
item in the estimates now before the house is the sum of $137,500,000, representing interest on our national debt.
This resolution asks for a review of the monetary requirements of the dominion. We are not going to solve the problem of deficits, which unfortunately we have had with us in the past few years, by simply adding on taxation in an effort to make both ends meet the following year. Two years ago we were unfortunate enough, owing to various circumstances, to have a shortage of $94,500,000. We tried to meet that, deficit by extra taxation, with the result that the following year we were $119,000,000 short. We are not therefore going to solve the problem this year, if we find ourselves short again, by simply adding to taxation. It costs between $365,000,000, which is the figure for this year, and something like $400,000,000, to run the business of the country, and it has often seemed to me very strange that we should do this enormous amount of business through private institutions, as we have done through the private corporations known as banks. There are various purposes for which we have to obtain money-uncontrolled expenditures), administration and public works, and so on-and the only way we have of getting the money is by taxation,, by borrowing, or in other words mortgaging the future of the country, or by issuing money. Unfortunately, and I say this advisedly, we have issued far too little, with the result that we have steadily added to the debt through unnecessary borrowing.
This year we are going to pay in interest no less than $4,800,000 more than we did a year ago on the national debt alone. At the same time we find ourselves with an extraordinary unemployment problem, in round figures 700,000 to-day. I cannot help thinking that the views expressed by the London Chamber of Commerce would, with the slight change of one word, suit our situation exactly We should aim to restore and expand the purchasing power of the people of Canada, without which unemployment must remain and defaults, national and individual, must increase. I quote:
When once a fair price level has been restored, to eliminate, so far as may be practicable, fluctuations in price level due to monetary causes.
To remove the causes which are inducing nations to strangle world trade by tariffs, quotas, exchange restrictions, et cetera.
We have heard to-night a good deal with regard to the advisability of starting a central bank. This apparently is becoming a more popular topic as time passes, and I think that the public will eventually demand a central
Bank Act-Mr. Spencer

bank, just as it demanded the government inspection of banks. Needless to say, the banks will oppose it, even as they opposed government inspection. They finally accepted the government inspection of banks after we had the disastrous failure of the Home Bank a few years ago. Public opinion then was sufficiently organized to make the government realize the necessity for that legislation. Naturally a central bank is not wanted because at the present time, without one, the banks have enormous power and can also make considerable profits. With a central bank that power would be largely taken away from them and needless to say they would not make as big profits because the government would do its own banking. We can readily understand therefore why, as private institutions, they oppose a central bank of rediscount. When we get a central bank however we do not want to have it as a bankers' bank but as a real state bank to do government business. Looking back to 1930, I notice the amount of loans the banks made at that time according to the Canada Year Book, if you allow seven per cent on the total amount of loans made, they would have made a profit in interest equal to their paid-up capital.
I want to say a few words now with regard to the departure from the gold basis. The public are beginning to realize that, as has been pointed out by Mr. McGeer, K.C., of British Columbia, supported by Professor PI umpire, gold is a myth and has been for quite a long time, and has a value only for those people who do not understand it and therefore think that some value does attach to it. They do not appreciate the fact that if all the gold in the world sank to the bottom of the Atlantic the world would go on just the same. It would be simply a matter of a few cables the day after the ship had sunk, and we should not be much worse off.
In 1932 the gold held in Canada was $143,-
500,000,	and notes and legate amounted to $315,500,000, while the deposits were equal to nearly $2,000,000,000. These figures alone show the absurdity of the belief that people can get gold if they want it, in anything but a very minor quantity.
I have often felt that the .public were misled by the fact that so much stress is placed on the working of the Dominion Notes Act, because although under that act wre allow ourselves to issue $50,000,000 of notes with a 25 per cent backing of gold, holding dollar for dollar of gold behind further issue of notes. But we undermine that act entirely when we begin to use the Finance Act, because under the Finance Act the banks are allowed to take various securities to the treasury board

and by placing that security as collateral with the treasury board to get dominion notes on a safe margin, although no gold is necessary in this case.
During the last eighteen years the banks have obtained from the treasury board no less than a little over $4,000,000,000 in this way. The rate varies. It has been down to as low as three per cent, and therefore the more we use the Finance Act in this respect the less percentage of gold have we behind Dominion notes. I mention this not because I think it necessary to have gold behind dominion notes but simply to show how foolish it is to stress the Dominion Notes Act while at the same time we bring the Finance Act into operation.
Banking to-day-and if we have the investigation this should be kept in view-is a bookkeeping system. Altogether too much emphasis is laid on coin and notes that are issued. We are all aware that money is a bookkeeping system, that new money is written into existence through loans and the buying of securities, and>
written out of existence by cancellations and the selling of securities. I have often wondered What was the value of the central gold reserve. If we have an investigation this matter should be looked into. Anyone who watches what is in the central gold reserve from time to time will find that there is often far more paper money in the way of do-minion notes than there is gold. However, that was not the case upon November 16, for which date I have the figures, when there was a little over $11,000,000 in gold and $10,300,000 in dominion notes. One who has not followed this subject might ask how the dominion notes got in there. The explanation is that when the banks take various securities to the treasury board and obtain dominion notes under the provisions of the Finance Act, they can put those notes out to the public or they can take them to the central gold reserve, leave them there in lieu of gold and issue their own notes or promises to pay against the dominion notes. As long as the bankers have the free use of the Finance Act, apparently they are not worrying about using the central gold reserve in this manner. I remember having an interesting conversation in 1923 with Mr. McLeod one time president of the Bank of Nova Scotia. Apparently he had had a good deal to do with starting the central gold reserve and it was his intention that only gold should be placed there against which the banks could issue extra notes from time to time. He was quite worried and irritated at the way the reserve was being used and he said to me:

Bank Act-Mr. Mackenzie
"It is not a central gold reserve any longer; it is nothing more or less than a gilded reserve."
In looking at the present crisis we have to recognize the fact that our problem is distinctly a money one. It is not a matter, as has been stated so many times upon the floor of this house during the past two or three weeks, of making goods or giving services. Unfortunately we have more than we can distribute of both. There are two reasons why we cannot distribute. The first is the inequality of income-some have more than they can spend and many others have not enough to spend-and, second, there is not sufficient of the medium of exchange to enable business to carry on. Our railroads are in a very unfortunate position to-day, but rather than bonus them or increase freight rates we should provide traffic. Traffic will be provided just as soon as the people have a purchasing power wherewith they can trade with each other.
As I mentioned at the beginning of my remarks, very little use has been made of the third method of making money, that of direct issue. It was used in 1914 to the extent of $26,000,000, and when the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) decided in 1930 to vote some $20,000,000 to help out the unemployment situation, it was suggested that a similar thing be done. Unfortunately it was not done. We took $20,000,000 out of the state purse; we taxed the people that amount on the one hand to give to the unemployed on the other. What we needed at that time, as we need to-day, was not a transfer of money but rather more money. A few months ago we borrowed some
S35,000,000 from the banks and issued dominion notes to them to an equal amount, losing $700,000 on the transaction in the course of two years. It is such things as these which should be looked into very carefully.
A suggestion was made behind me this afternoon with regard to bimetalism. Personally, I am not very much enamoured with bimetalism, but I am willing that the whole matter should be gone into by the banking and commerce committee. I am glad to have the opportunity of saying a few words in support of this resolution. I think it is a good one and I believe considerable benefit would be derived from a complete investigation.

subtopic: PROPOSED REVISION BY BANKING AND COMMERCE COMMITTEE IN RELATION TO MONETARY REQUIREMENTS OF DOMINION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a few observations in connection with the resolution moved by the hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Irvine). This resolution is in four parts, the first asking that the banking and commerce committee be instructed to study the Bank Act preparatory to its decennial revision. It seems to me that that portion of the resolution is far too vague and nebulous; it really means going over every single clause in the Bank Act without any special instructions being given in any particular direction. The next three parts of the resolutions are definite in their terms; they ask that the committee report on the advisability of final departure from the gold basis- the matter under discussion this evening; the issuing of dominion notes sufficient to depreciate our dollar to the level of the pound sterling-which matter, I understand has been ruled out of order-and ways and means of reducing the internal debt so greatly increased by deflation.
At the outset let me say I regret that the right hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) saw fit this afternoon to raise a point of order in regard to this resolution, referring to the amendment moved in the early part of this session by the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Coote). I submit that that amendment was entirely different from the resolution we are now discussing, which refers to a specific matter, the issuing of dominion notes sufficient to depreciate our dollar to the level of the pound sterling. The hon. member's amendment was to the motion for approval of the trade agreement between Canada and Great Britain and sought to add the following words:
-and subject also to establishment of parity of the Canadian dollar with the British pound.
This afternoon the right hon. gentleman suggested that certain observations had been made by hon. members on this side of the house during the debate in connection with the amendment moved by the hon. member for Macleod. Upon looking up Hansard of November 2, 1932, I found that the only observation made specifically in connection with the amendment was made by a member of the government, the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens). The minister went out of his way to commend not only the hon. member but the purport and nature of his amendment. I should like to quote from his remarks as follows:
On the other hand, I could cite a number of addresses that have been exceedingly helpful, exceedingly instructive, and I might say to the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat (Mr. Coote) that in the main his own address was, in my opinion, a reasonable and valuable contribution to the study of the problem.
And again in the same debate:
I think we should first dispose of this motion,-
The motion to implement an Imperial conference agreement-
-which merely gives the house the opportunity to proceed with the study of the agreements in
Bank Act-Mr. Mackenzie

detail, and then the proposal of my hon. friend could very properly be considered as a major problem in itself.
With all due respect to the right hon. gentleman I suggest that all that part (b) of this resolution asks is that this house study the question as a major problem. The minister then continued:
Speaking for myself alone, I can assure him that 1 am prepared to give this matter the most careful consideration and study. I am anxious to cooperate with any hon. member in the study and possible achievement of a solution of this problem.
Nothing was said on this side of the house until the vote was taken later on the same day. We have a somewhat anomalous situation; on the second of November, a member of the government tells the hon. member for Macleod that he welcomes a study of this major problem of placing our dollar upon a parity with the pound sterling, yet to-day when an hon. member to my left seeks to have the banking and commerce committee do the same thing, he is met with a point of order.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: PROPOSED REVISION BY BANKING AND COMMERCE COMMITTEE IN RELATION TO MONETARY REQUIREMENTS OF DOMINION
speechtext: I think the hon. gentleman has misunderstood things. We have voted already upon the matter this session and I raised the point of order in order to prevent duplication. Otherwise there would be no end to the discussion in this house.

subtopic: PROPOSED REVISION BY BANKING AND COMMERCE COMMITTEE IN RELATION TO MONETARY REQUIREMENTS OF DOMINION
speechtext: My point is that we have not. Unfortunately, this afternoon I was not allowed to give my views on the point of order. On November 2 the hon. member for Macleod moved an amendment to the motion of the Prime Minister that the Imperial conference agreements be implemented. The words, as I recall them, were ''subject to the establishment of a parity with the pound." This clause (b) of this resolution is something quite different.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: PROPOSED REVISION BY BANKING AND COMMERCE COMMITTEE IN RELATION TO MONETARY REQUIREMENTS OF DOMINION
speechtext: I do not know whether the hon. member is quite in order in discussing the ruling of the Chair.

subtopic: PROPOSED REVISION BY BANKING AND COMMERCE COMMITTEE IN RELATION TO MONETARY REQUIREMENTS OF DOMINION
speechtext:
I am not quarrelling with the ruling. I am just explaining why I was not allowed to establish my point of order. Clause (b) reads:
The issuing dominion notes sufficient to depreciate our dollar to the level of the pound sterling.
In other words, clause (b) is specific. The other was only generic in the conclusion which the hon. member for Macleod sought to establish-parity with the pound. I maintain that clause (b) of the present resolution and the amendment of November 2 are entirely different.

Might I deal for just two or three minutes with the resolution before the house? It asks the banking and commerce committee practically to deal with the financial structure of the Dominion of Canada. As far as I have been able to analyze modem economic thought in this and other countries, there are at the present time two main schools-and we have them possibly in every party in the house- dealing with the fundamental causes of the present crisis. There is the school which was termed by Edie in his great book Banking and Prosperity, the school of the industrial equilibrists; that is the school which thinks tariffs are at the root of everything with regard to trade. There is, on the other hand, the monetary school of thought, which is very prevalent at the present time and gaining in strength, that believes the present economic crisis is primarily a monetary one. My opinion, for all it may be worth, is that these two schools are not irreconcilable; you can dovetail the economic thought of the school of industrial equilibrium into the economic thought of the school of monetary reform. It is an economic axiom that the value of your dollar must in the final analysis depend on trade, but when your trade is locked and stifled and is not allowed, on account of the economic policies and narrow nationalism pursued by the various nations, to ride free, you can do much by way of monetary solution to override the difficulty inherent in the trade policies at present being pursued.
In this evening's paper I saw an announcement made by the Prime Minister of Great Britain, wherein he suggested the program for the pending conference in Washington between the government of the United States and the government of Great Britain, and dealt with six major problems. Four of the six, as I recall them, dealt with the monetary structure of the empire and of the United States, so that when the Prime Minister of Great Britain outlines the problems that are to be studied-and I think the agenda is the same as that which is to be studied at the world economic conference-we should have very soon a pronouncement of policy from the administration in regard to what submissions the Prime Minister is going to make on behalf of Canada before the world economic conference in May.
What happened at the imperial conference? We had great hope of what Canada might do and say but-and I do not think I am saying anything radically wrong in suggesting this-the monetary' policy of this dominion was made subservient to the British Chancellor of the Exchequer, because the final report of the committee is practically

Bank Act-Mr. Mackenzie
an acceptance of the main submissions of the chancellor. Let me suggest this to my right hon. friend: Although the main economic doctrine of the mother country may, so far as the main economic principles are concerned, apply to Canada, the economy of Great Britain is in radical ways different from that of Canada, because Great Britain for years and years has been in control of the international market. What is the situation in this country? I am not blaming any government particularly for this, but we are to-day financially economic vassals of the great republic to the south of us. The tragedy of the situation, as I see it, is that various governments, according to their own well considered policies and doctrines, have been trying to orient the trade of Canada-and I am not criticizing them for that-to the empire and to Great Britain. Yet, when they try to tie our financial policy to that of England and the empire, our greatest critic is the Prime Minister who would like to be termed the foremost champion of imperial preference and trade. For one, I am convinced that you cannot separate financial policy from trade policy; that is, the policy in regard to our external trade from that in regard to our international obligations. Recently we have been considering the crushing debt which we owe to the republic to the south of us. The Prime Minister has throughout the country been making speeches-and I am not criticizing him for that; I am only stating facts-in which he has been saying to the people of Canada: "We have honoured all our maturing obligations in gold." Is that exactly true?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: PROPOSED REVISION BY BANKING AND COMMERCE COMMITTEE IN RELATION TO MONETARY REQUIREMENTS OF DOMINION
speechtext:
I said, in terms of the
contract.

subtopic: PROPOSED REVISION BY BANKING AND COMMERCE COMMITTEE IN RELATION TO MONETARY REQUIREMENTS OF DOMINION
speechtext:
In terms of the contract. That must be nearer the truth, because the terms of the contract actually call upon the nation which is to honour the contract to meet its payments in gold or pay them in services or go through a process of refunding, so that Canada has not and cannot meet her maturing obligations in gold. How could we do so with our gold production last year amounting to only
S73.000.000, and with our tremendous debts payable in gold by our federal government, our provincial governments, the Canadian National Railways and public corporations? I find that our gold coverage last Thursday was 39-3 per cent, or roughly $70,000,000 for a note issue of $180,000,000. Where is your sound money? This reminds me of the Latin phrase, Vox et praeterea nil, or "sound and nothing more." Where is the sound money when I produce my dollar bill for which I
am entitled to get payment in gold? Where was ouf sound money when Calgary, the right hon. gentleman's constituency, asked for gold for her good Canadian notes? Could Calgary obtain Canadian gold? We have no sound money according to the tenets of the right hon. gentleman.
Last year he made a very fine statement. He said that we have roughly S50,000,000 guaranteed by a partial coverage of 25 per cent in gold, $49,000,000 protected dollar for dollar in gold and the rest, $71,000,000, I think it was then-I am not sure of the exact figures now-covered, as he said, by the security, character and integrity, of what? Of the Canadian people. I refer my right hon. friend to the finest economic report ever made in any country, the famous Macmillan report of two years ago. The right hon. gentleman has the pleasure of being very well acquainted with the brilliant and distinguished chairman of that committee. Sir Josiah Stamp said in regard to it that a committee of such brilliance, ability and distinction never before functioned in any land. What was the finding of that committee in regard to this great question of gold coverage? One of the specific findings of the Macmillan committee, implementing the findings of the gold committee of the League of Nations, was that a gold basis was no longer required for internal currency. That is not the fly-bynight theory of my hon. friends to my left or the radical opinion of some of us who sit on this side; it is the well-founded opinion of my right hon. friend's own brilliant economic friends in Great Britain, that you must dissociate once and for all your domestic currency from your external obligations. What does that mean? If the right hon. gentleman told us here, as he did in April of last year, that outside that $99,000,000 the consideration was the security of the Canadian nation, and if the Macmillan committee said that you can have a safe note issue amounting to one-fifth of your total bank deposits, what does that mean? If your economic policy in Canada is sound, it means, according to the scientifically economic analysis at which that committee arrived, we could have on the same basis of the security and integrity of the Canadian people, a note issue in this country of one-fifth of our total bank deposits, or one-fifth of $2,000,000,000, as of last year, or $400,000,000. It would mean $200,000,000 more than the $180,000,000 which you had according to the return which I got from the Minister of Finance yesterday. That is not printing money. That is simply arriving at a careful policy of a managed currency, on a scientific basis, as promulgated
Bank Act-Mr. Mackenzie

by the ablest economic committee that ever sat in modern history. We cannot be blamed if we see some merits in a careful policy such as that.
I do not like the word inflation. I think it is a dangerous word, and inflation a dangerous policy. But what have we had in Canada during the last few years? Under the craziest financial structure in modern history, through the Finance Act, we have had inflation in this country under the Conservatives from 1914 onwards, and during the Liberal regime from 1921 to 1929. We have had a modified policy of inflation during the last three years, under the terms of the Finance Act, and at the same time, strange to say, we had the biggest deflation in the history of Canada, caused by what has been mentioned by some of the speakers here to-day-the contraction of credits by the banks of this dominion.
That brings me to the point I wish particularly to emphasize to-night. Any policy in regard to currency, any policy in regard to credit control, must be built around a new central organization which is going to regulate the whole policy of banking in this dominion.
1 do not think any party should go unduly to the left or be unduly Conservative in financial policy. I believe there is as much ianger in uncontrolled inflation as in adhering to this fictitious policy of sound money which the Prime Minister and his government consistently advocate. The safe and sound and sensible policy is to take the middle way, ;o establish a central organization of experts snjoying the confidence of the government and of the Canadian people; because the day has gone by in Canada when the people will tolerate a condition under which the ordinary mercantile functions of Canadian banks shall be associated with the policy of banking credit and financial control which the banks now possess. The control of credit must be taken away from the banking institutions of Canada. When I say that, although I have the greatest admiration for the record of our Canadian banks, I would ask, why should they not have a wonderful record and be marvellously secure? There are only nine or ten of them now where formerly there were twenty-five, and they enjoy the biggest financial monopoly in the history of modern civilization, with the entire- credit of the dominion treasury behind their every move. So why should they not have done well?
My right hon. friend, dealing in Toronto with this question of bringing the dollar on a parity with the pound, asked how it could be done? He knows quite well how it could

be done. It has not been difficult for other nations to do-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: PROPOSED REVISION BY BANKING AND COMMERCE COMMITTEE IN RELATION TO MONETARY REQUIREMENTS OF DOMINION
speechtext: Unless they were insolvent or short of currency.

subtopic: PROPOSED REVISION BY BANKING AND COMMERCE COMMITTEE IN RELATION TO MONETARY REQUIREMENTS OF DOMINION
speechtext:
The
Prime Minister said that there was no need to go on a parity with the pound unless you were insolvent or short of currency. Neither one nor the other obtains in Canada, he said. I am not so sure. I fear much, and I hesitate to say this, that within -the next few months the right hon. gentleman will hear from some of the western provinces which may have to ask for very generous terms in order to meet their obligations, or else be faced with defaulting on their bonds. We cannot afford to pay, and we cannot pay, our present debt and our present interest charges in the Dominion of Canada, and the sooner we wake up to the facts of the situation the better for us. Our interest on the national debt was $12,000,000 before the war. It was $135,000,000 last year, and this year it is $137,500,000. There are two and a half billions of national loans, including funded debt, railways and other operations, $7,582,000,000 of, obligations, of bonds payable in gold, and the entire amount of gold in the different countries of the world amounts to between $11,000,000,000 and $12,000,000,000.

subtopic: PROPOSED REVISION BY BANKING AND COMMERCE COMMITTEE IN RELATION TO MONETARY REQUIREMENTS OF DOMINION
speechtext: We owe over eight, billion dollars in bonds.

subtopic: PROPOSED REVISION BY BANKING AND COMMERCE COMMITTEE IN RELATION TO MONETARY REQUIREMENTS OF DOMINION
speechtext:
I accept
the correction of my hon. friend. Perhaps the other figure included private corporations. The total gold supply in the world is between eleven and twelve billion dollars, and how can *we possibly meet our maturing obligations in gold? It cannot be done. The greatest necessity before parliament is to meet the situation of our public debt and our private debt with courage and vision. The Australian people met the situation last year, and we must do it. We must write down our debt.
I advocate a big conversion loan in this dominion. We must summon up the courage and the patriotism of the Canadian people, and I would also advocate that earnest consideration be given to modifying our financial policy by the issue of dominion currency. It was done during the war. Why not do it now in the war against poverty, misery and unemployment which we are waging to-day? The security of this dominion is as good as ever it was.
I also suggest that we commence a wholesale cut in interest rates, commencing with savings bank deposits, and have a cut right

Bank Act-Mr. Mackenzie
across in the interest rates charged by mortgage, trust and loan companies. Let us have a debt and interest readjustment upon the principle of equalization of sacrifice throughout the dominion. The farmers have already practically sacrificed their all. Almost all the lumber companies in my province are on the verge of bankruptcy. The producer has paid his price. Why not let the moneyholder now come under the principle of equalization of sacrifice in this great crisis?
So I appeal to my right hon. friend to be good enough some day in the near future to enunciate to this house the policy he intends to present to the world economic conference on behalf of Canada. I suggest to him that he give most careful consideration to the advisability of a great national conversion loan, a voluntary loan by preference, but compulsory, if that is necessary. It was compulsory in Australia to the extent of seventeen and a half million pounds. The remarkable thing about the situation in Australia was this. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) told us the other evening that the financial situation in Australia was much worse than in Canada, but here is the record of Australia. Out of a total of 556 million pounds, there was converted immediately by application 490 million pounds; by effluxion of time 48) mi'llioin pounds, leaving only 17i million pounds to be converted compulsorily. The compulsory element is to be regretted if it can be done voluntarily. The point I am trying to impress upon the house as forcibly as I can is that in my humble judgment we cannot meet our present indebtedness, federal, provincial and municipal, unless we summon up the entire strength and resources of the Canadian people. It is no use talking of a policy of sound money so long as I cannot get gold for my dollar when I present it to the bank. Suspend, if you like, the redemption of dominion notes in gold.
The question has been asked, how can we establish parity with the pound? It can be done in two ways. It can be done by giving up the policy of unnecessarily buttressing the Canadian dollar to keep it as close to the American dollar as possible, which has been followed by this administration for the last two and a half years.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: PROPOSED REVISION BY BANKING AND COMMERCE COMMITTEE IN RELATION TO MONETARY REQUIREMENTS OF DOMINION
speechtext:
We have not done any
such thing.

subtopic: PROPOSED REVISION BY BANKING AND COMMERCE COMMITTEE IN RELATION TO MONETARY REQUIREMENTS OF DOMINION
speechtext:
It has
been done either deliberately or as a result of the financial policy of this government. That has been the result in any event. If that is not successful, follow out the scientific analysis of the Macmillan committee in England, and go in for a policy of a managed currency, which is the distinct and deliberate policy recommended by that committee to the British government. Have the British people suffered from abandoning the gold standard? They may be asked as the price of an international debt settlement to consider returning to the gold standard, but I venture to suggest that such a return will not be considered by the British nation for many, many years to come because, after all the juggling by international financiers, as is so well described by Einzig in his various books, and which continued from 1922 to 1931, Britain has on acute and painful knowledge of what happened in the realms of international finance. She has survived the shock and is to-day on the upgrade, and I believe she will be the first country to emerge from the present depression. Why? Because her economic advisers have told her that the present economic crisis is primarily a monetary crisis. I tell my friends who believe that tariffs are the only panacea for all the woes of the present economic upheaval, you must have the two factors working hand in hand; you must readjust your financial structure and recast the powers of the banks, give them full scope in ordinary mercantile pursuits to follow in security and integrity the banking practices they have so well developed, but take from them, once and for all, the control of credit and currency in the Dominion of Canada and the power over the note issue. We are living in changing times. I am sure if my right hon. friend would give up his attachment to the fallacy and fiction of "sound money" and deal immediately and fearlessly with the tremendous problem of meeting our debt and interest obligations, he would have the grateful regard of the Canadian people.

If when the motion is again called he is not in his seat I shall take his place and make a statement. In the meantime, in order to preserve that situation, I move the adjournment of the debate.

maintopic: PROPOSED TJSE OF SURPLUS WHEAT FOR RELIEF- SALE ON LONG TERM CREDITS TO DISTRESSED COUNTRIES
PROPOSED TJSE OF SURPLUS WHEAT FOR RELIEF- SALE ON LONG TERM CREDITS TO DISTRESSED COUNTRIES
speechtext:
Whereas unemployment, scanty clothing and hunger throughout the land continue to be all too prevalent; and

Farm Relief-Mr. Motherwell
Whereas, this persistent economic depression not only adds to the growing relief requirements in many centres, but also subtracts from the number of voluntary contributors, many of whom are now feeling these social efforts growing more and more beyond their capacity to carry;
Therefore, be it resolved, that, in the opinion of this parliament the government of Canada should place a sufficient quantity of our surplus wheat stocks, at the disposal of the Red Cross, welfare bureaus and other similar organizations, to supplement and more fully take care of the food requirements of the unemployed, the poor and the hungry throughout Canada.
And be it further resolved, that the government of Canada take such steps as are necessary and expedient to explore the possibility and practicability of selling on long term credits a substantial quantity of our embarassing wheat carry-over to China, or any other available country where poverty, hunger and misery prevail.
He said: I think this motion is quite capable of being understood, and there is nothing original about it. It has the advantage of having been tried in our neighbouring republic and found quite satisfactory, and no reason occurs to me why it may not prove equally satisfactory in Canada, with such variations as may be found necessary to suit our peculiar requirements. I suppose there is not an hon. member in this house who during the last two or three years has not been confronted with this question:	How do you
account for it that in this land of plenty people are in want and going to bed hungry? I used to be somewhat provoked at that question myself. Last summer when I was in the elevator in our town I found a farmer expatiating very vigorously on this situation, taking the ground that someone was to bLame for it, though he did not mention who that somebody was. He enunciated the doctrine we hear so frequently, that the difficulty is not in production but in distribution. I made a proposal to my brother farmer: How would it be if you and I should start out on this new method of distribution? The next load of wheat we bring to town suppose we start distributing it among the villagers, some of whom are bound to be hard up this coming winter. About twenty-five bushels would feed a family of five; one load of seventy-five bushels would take care of three families. You try that out with your next load, and I will do the same with mine, and see how it works. "Oh," he said, "I cannot afford to do that." "Well," I said, "that is about the way with me; the cheaper wheat is the more I have to sell to get a bit of money."
That is true of the individual, but it seems to me there are certain further duties that devolve upon the' national government. I know its burdens are heavy; our provinces 
and some of our municipalities are also near the end of their tether. The Dominion government has done remarkable work in the way of relief, first in one form, then another, and now in direct relief. So have the provinces and the municipalities.
In the United States they had accumulated a large surplus of wheat through the federal farm board and the stabilization committee. They carried that load openly, everyone knew about it, and finally it became such a tremendous burden that they gave a lot of it away to get rid of it, distributed a large quantity through the Red Cross and similar organizations and sold some on long term credits to Germany, China and other countries. I think it is practically all gone now, so one of the great burdens on the market has been removed, although without appreciable effect as yet upon the price. However, if we follow suit and some other country does the same, eventually we shall get this great burden of carry-over wheat removed, without which we cannot have a restoration of prices. What better purpose can we put it to than to help out people less fortunate than ourselves? The burden is weighing very heavily on the voluntary givers. In this city, in which surely you will not find a larger percentage of out-of-works than elsewhere, over $130,000 was contributed last fall to take care of the poor and himgry, and so all over the country. Wherever I have been I find there are getting to be more and more to feed and clothe and less and less people able to provide for them; therefore the burden is getting heavier on both individuals and governments. Well, it occurred to me, why could not we follow the example of the United States in the distribution of this surplus wheat?-seeing we have followed their example in acquiring it, in a laudable desire to hold up the market. Possibly that object was attained to some extent, but the fact is that wheat was grown in such volume that it has become an embarrassment to every country that carries it; it hangs like a millstone around our market's neck.
However, the amount distributed to organizations such as the Red Gross and welfare bureaus and relief organizations would be comparatively small. We have ten million people in Canada ; say there are one million on relief-there are not now, but possibly there will be in a year-it would only take about five million bushels to provide them with all the bread they require. It would relieve the local authorities, however, to that extent. That has been done in the United

Farm Relief-Mr. Motherwell
States and found satisfactory and I see no reason why it should not prove satisfactory in Canada.
Then a further proposition is to sell or barter to countries that are less fortunate than ourselves substantial quantities. That will appreciably reduce our cany-over and tend to bring the price back to normal. I mentioned China in the resolution, but it need not be confined to China; why not India-they sometimes have famines. I understand that in northeast China 25,000 people were flooded out over a year ago and are largely on relief.
The objection has been taken that farmers in other countries where we sell this wheat would complain that we are flooding them with cheap wheat. I think that should be avoided as much as possible; it might be sold in such parts of China as are on relief as a result of that great flood. The same applies to India. And what would be the objection to selling some to Russia? We have been selling some through the regular channels of trade. A year ago there were substantial shipments from the Pacific coast to Russia. No objection was made to that, and I do not think there would be to this. Russia is reported to be short of wheat not only for bread purposes but for seed. I do not think it would be good policy to sell wheat on long terms to Russia for seed to compete against ourselves; that might seem too much like turning the other cheek, nevertheless, if they are short of wheat for flour or flour itself to feed the people why should we not supply it either on barter or on long term credits? Do you not think we would be more likely to make a friend of Russia? I take the ground, Mr. Speaker, that we cannot solve this problem of wheat without the cooperation of that country. We cannot do very much in the way of reducing acreage or following any other systematic plan designed to reduce production to something like the consumption requirements of the world unless Russia is a party to the arrangement. Without raising that controversial question of putting an embargo on some of the products of that country, do you not think Russia would pull better with Canada if we in a friendly way cooperated with her for a change, instead of continuing our present policy?

I never knew Russia to break it as much as we did ourselves or to sell wheat as cheaply as we did. Let me answer further my right hon. friend: Every country in the world making a sale of wheat to-day has to do a measure of dumping; it 53719-130
has to beat out the other fellow in regard to both price and quality. You have to make a market by selling quality at a price the buyer cannot resist; in other words it is a buyers' market to-day with all that that implies. Russia may have done that at one time; I do not doubt but what she did, but we have done it since. That is the unfortunate part of the whole situation.
Let me enumerate some of the advantages of compliance with this motion. At least it will be a humanitarian way of disposing of our surplus. We should not destroy our wheat, as some countries are said to have destroyed their overages; I would utterly oppose anything of that kind. If it is axiomatic that this surplus must be substantially reduced before there can be any restoration of prices to anything like normal, surely there must be some way by which we can get rid of our wheat. For the sake of argument, Mr. Speaker, I will admit that if present prospects materialize there is a chance that we may reduce this overage somewhat by next, fall. The United States crop seems to be very indifferent, and Russia is in the same position. The Argentine and Australia probably will get rid of their carryovers by next fall, or hope to, but I do not think that will apply to us. Probably we will have the largest surplus we have ever had, though some people estimate otherwise. Perhaps I am not sufficiently optimistic; competent men have stated during the last two or three years that soon we would see a better day with regard to wheat prices. Well, they have been getting better the wrong way; they have been getting no better fast. We have reached the point now where we are giving away five bushels of No. 1 wheat for a dollar, and it is time we thought- seriously about this huge carry-over. The whole trouble with our calculations in this regard is that just when we think Russia will cease to export wheat because of her home requirements, she stalls to export; she becomes an exporter of wheat when it is well known that later in the same year she will have to import wheat.
