Yes, that is right, but she is forced to adopt that course. That puts all our figuring astray, and I have no doubt that some other unexpected contingencies would appear in other countries as well, as they so often do.
The first advantage of this method, then, is that this will be a humane way of disposing of our surplus, and incidentally we may make

Farm Relief-Mr. Motherwell

a friend of such country upon whom we may be glad to call some day for a market. These countries needing wheat ait intervals are the countries with immense populations and an immense capacity for consumption. When they get stable governments, a-s I hope they will some day soon, they will become great consumers of our products. In the meantime let us cast our bread upon the waiters, and in a few years it may return unto us in the form of valuable markets.
In the second place, this method will remove the reproach-which I feel quite as much as though I were a member of the government-that all the public men in the country cannot find some way to answer this everlasting question of why distribution is not more perfect when production is so wonderful. If this house will adopt this proposal we can remove in some measure at least that reproach. I am not wedded to this particular method; anything better will suit me, but let us do something that will reduce our carryover and at the same time help meet our increasing requirements with respect to relief all over this dominion This plan will create a market for several million bushels of wheat; it will lessen the embarrassing carry-over; it will supply the railways with additional business. That is perhaps a small item, but it is of importance. In addition, this will lessen the demand on voluntary contributions.
Those are the advantages I see in this method, Mr. Speaker. Now let us look at some of the disadvantages. In the first place, it will be abused, but unfortunately that is always the case; Every good thing like this is more or less abused. It does not matter whether it is relief or seed grain; I have never seen any government capable of carrying on anything of this kind so perfectly that some little abuse has not crept in. When you analyze those abuses, however, and compare them with the volume of business done, you see that they do not amount to very much after all. Recently we all have read in the press what has been going on in a certain town in this province. That sort of thing will happen, but are we to withhold help from the people in need because two or three localities may abuse that help? My experience, which covers many years, has been that you will always find abuses when anything is being given out by the government, and I suppose that always will be the case until we attain that high degree of civilization to which my friends to my left refer so often. We hope and believe that day will yet come, but it is not here yet.
Another objection is that whole wheat cannot be disposed of by some relief bureaus, nor

flour either, as many relief applicants insist on ready baked bread. We are not committed to the distribution of whole wheat; it may be distributed in the form of flour, but whole wheat has certain advantages not possessed by flour. It is a healthful food and can be converted into a larger variety of cooked foods. Again, I was met with the argument that in many districts the people buy their bread and do not know how to bake it, so that neither whole wheat nor ordinary flour would be of use to them. I am afraid that is true, but I think it is about time people learned how to bake bread and many other household requirements all over again. To-day I inquired at the old Knox church, which is now used as the administrative centre of the relief bureau in this city, and which was thronged with people applying for their orders for supplies. I found that the National Council of Women and other similar organizations have started instruction classes designed to help those who wanted to learn how to bake bread and do other kinds of cooking. The practice of buying bread and of purchasing other foods in small cartons and cans became general because people could afford to do so, and many of the old practices of home cooking have almost disappeared. 1 think this is a time to revive many home duties similar to what we did during the war. We should start as many of these old practices as possible, giving the people a new zest in life and affording them some employment as well. Let them make their own bread. If the women have so many children that they have no time to bake, then let the old man learn how to do it. He has so much time on his hands now that he can tell the government and everyone else how to run things. Well, let him get busy and learn how to make bread. Many of us in our bachelor days made bread out in the west, and what man has done man can do.
Another objection made is that people are not familiar with the uses to which whole wheat can be put. During the war the government distributed many leaflets and publications showing the various uses to which certain foodstuffs could be put; they pointed out a variety of dishes that could be made from rhubarb, for instance, and fish. The same could be done with respect to this commodity. You can make muffins or porridge or coffee and many other commodities that would be very healthful.
Another objection sometimes heard is that it would interfere with the volume of business done by local bakers. That is a real objection, because the bakers are doing this business now; but it seems to me that the interests

Farm Relief-Mr. Motherwell
of the many will have to be regarded as paramount and will have to take precedence over interests of the few. I do not think the bakers would object very much. They have a pretty good business, I fancy, and if they lost this business knowing that it was for the benefit of the many I do not think they would object strenuously. I am trying to discover all the objections that can be advanced and to weigh the advantages against the disadvantages.
A gentleman in the west who held the position of trade representative in China drew my attention to the fact that the Chinese papers within the last six months or year have been complaining on behalf of the farmers of China that that country was being made a dumping ground for American and Canadian wheat at such low prices that their own farmers were being injured.

speechtext: And Australia principally.

maintopic: PROPOSED TJSE OF SURPLUS WHEAT FOR RELIEF- SALE ON LONG TERM CREDITS TO DISTRESSED COUNTRIES
speechtext:
Yes. I suppose
there is something in it, but it is one of those things we seldom think about. We look on China as a far distant country in which half the people, as I am informed, scarcely know where the next meal is coming from. Nevertheless they have enough farmers to grow more wheat annually than Canada does, and they are wondering just how far the wheat growing world will go in its effort to make a dumping ground of China. As I have indicated, however, there is no reason why this wheat could not be directed into those areas which are flooded out, and if China does not want it perhaps India could take it, or Russia might want it. So that that difficulty could be got over. You can always find difficulties if you look for them, but we should consider the advantages that accrue to any proposal such as this. We cannot disabuse our minds entirely of some selfish ideas, and naturally we want to help our own people first. The whole movement as I see it is primarily to get rid of this ghastly carry-over and to bring about normal conditions and favourable opportunities in regard to price and at the same time help others. After you have done that it will not be long before the farmers will be making a little money and the banks will again feel like making loans, because the people will be able to pay them back. Certainly you cannot pay a loan to the bank with wheat at 20 cents, which is the figure that prevailed in western Saskatchewan. I believe it is about 25 cents now. As soon as you pay a loan to the bank it creates a feeling of confidence, so that the banks will begin lending and the mortgage companies will not worry you until at least you are more on your feet.

Business will start to move, credit will be restored and you will give the railways profitable business. Some of our wheat will not move under our present freight rates. We are not asking for any increased freight rate for export wheat but if it gets lower they will have to, because the wheat simply will not move into consumption.
As regards the destination of the wheat, I do not care where it goes to. I would not consign it to the place we speak of when in anger, but I object to its being wasted when there are hungry people at home or abroad.
A certain amount of propaganda has been indulged in, and properly so, on behalf of reduced acreage. Under the export quota basis, which will involve another system of oversight on the part of the three provinces that grow so much wheat, it will not be an easy matter to carry out. It depends on the cooperation of four or five other countries with ourselves. That always takes time, but this other matter of salesmanship is one between ourselves at home and the individual country with which we transact business. I hesitate at reducing acreage by deliberate arrangement until we first adopt the two methods I have mentioned, of feeding our own people bountifully, thus relieving the local people of some of their contributions, and also relieving the government of some of their embarrassing carryovers. That should be done first, I think, before there is any systematic attempt to reduce acreage. As a matter of fact acreage will be reduced to some extent anyway this spring under the ruthleas principle of the survival of the fittest. We have come to that stage where many farmers in the regional areas find that it just pays in a good year to grow grain but does not pay in a bad year. These areas are being closed to cultivation. They are left to grow grass and weeds and many farmers are unable under their own steam to put a crop in. Acreage reduction would have happened sooner had it not been for the large areas of newly settled land in northern Alberta and northern Saskatchewan and to a lesser extent in northern Manitoba, coming into development to take the place of the southern areas going out of cultivation.
The point I want to make is this, that until we do get rid of the overage by these or other means there will not be a very forceful argument for a systematic cooperative policy with other countries for reduction of acreage. I suppose we all have a little superstition in our make-up; I know I have. There is a superstition among farmers that if you go out and kill a litter of young pigs, on the ground that it does not pay to raise them, if you kill them
20G0

Farm Relief-Mr. Motherwell
at birth, you will not have 'luck with your next litter. I do not know whether there is anything in that, but certainly I should not like to try the experiment of destroying the wheat overage. I would rather sell it on generous terms to anyone who would enable us to get it out of here so that it might do some good instead of a lot of harm to ourselves where it is now.
I hope I have couched my remarks in such language that neither the Prime Minister nor any other member will be offended. I could not help referring to Russia because it is I think the key to the whole situation, and I referred to it as mildly as I knew how. I have no doubt the government realizes, as we all do, that we are facing a serious situation in Canada, as well as the world over, and if I can contribute the smallest quota to help matters in the way I propose or otherwise I am satisfied. But even if you blot this out and give me something that looks better, I will put up both my hands for it. We are continually being faced with the odium-we get it in the press, from the pulpits and on the streets-that as legislators we do not know how to get this abundance of goods to those who need it most.
If the house were in committee of the whole I should be very glad to answer any questions, but I invite a full discussion on this matter. This stigma should be removed. Notwithstanding a'll the assistance which has been given, this great pyramid of carry-over wheat has grown until it is at the point of drowning us. Did you ever see, Mr. Speaker, a bunch of cats thrown into a stream with stones around their necks? Those stones were meant to act as sinkers, and they generally succeeded in sinking the cats. We have a buyers' market millstone around our necks just as effective, and it is dragging us as sellers down to the very depths.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister) :
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: PROPOSED TJSE OF SURPLUS WHEAT FOR RELIEF- SALE ON LONG TERM CREDITS TO DISTRESSED COUNTRIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I desire to congratulate
the hon. gentleman (Mr. Motherwell) upon the very excellent address he has made, an address which reflects credit not only upon his humanity but upon his discernment. Nothing is more encouraging to those who at this time have to carry an unduly heavy load than to have those normally politically opposed offer suggestions as to how best the difficulties can be met. The fine spirit manifested by the hon. gentleman in his address is, I think, very satisfying and pleasing to all of us. He has had much experience; he has seen the growth and development of our country; he has seen a great territory which once produced an abundance of wealth become almost as desolate as the desert; he has
IMr. Motherwell.]
seen people who had excellent homes-notwithstanding the statements made, not many of them according to the census returns were covered by mortgages; things were not as the advocates of blue ruin would have us understand-find those homes rendered almost valueless.
Last year when the federal government found that a very large part of the population of the province of Saskatchewan, a population which had been well-to-do, had had three successive years without a crop, we treated the matter as a national disaster, just as in times gone by we had voted money to assist in caring for those who suffered from disasters in the islands of the sea and in far distant foreign parts. We regarded it as a national disaster; and it may strike some hon. members as amazing that there was less said about this than would have been expected. The government has been very sparing with propaganda in dealing with this matter. It has not advertised what it has been endeavouring to do; it has been doing it without advertising. Over 300,000 people in the province of Saskatchewan were being cared for by the federal government during a part of last year. We were not desirous of publishing that to the world, but we were desirous of having this house know that in conformity with its unanimous opinion, its view so strongly expressed that a national disaster should be treated as such, we had set in motion the machinery which gave, shall I say, at least comfort, clothing, food and fuel to that population. It was a great achievement which reflected credit upon those responsible for the administration, and I am glad to know that the hon, gentleman has seen what has been done.
Assistance has been given in other provinces. One of the forms of assistance suggested last year was that we should purchase a quantity of wheat which would be milled to ensure plenty of flour being available for those who were in want. The hon. gentleman knows better than I do that a diet of boiled wheat is not one upon which humanity long lives; it brings about physical diseases and disasters which are apparent very quickly. The small mills in the communities in Saskatchewan felt that they could take care of the situation by grinding the wheat in a manner which would be satisfactory to the population that lived nearby. A large quantity of flour was purchased and distributed under conditions which I think have not been subject to criticism. This was distributed to the needy population of the western provinces, of Saskatchewan in particular.
The answer, therefore, to the first portion of the hon. gentleman's resolution is this:

Farm Relief-Mr. Bennett
All the wheat that was necessary, nay, more than could be used by the needy population and others in western Canada, has been supplied by the Canadian producer.

speechtext:
I think the right
hon. gentleman is right.

maintopic: PROPOSED TJSE OF SURPLUS WHEAT FOR RELIEF- SALE ON LONG TERM CREDITS TO DISTRESSED COUNTRIES
speechtext:
It follows therefore that
it would not be possible to sell more wheat; the Red Cross or any other organization would not make a further distribution of wheat possible because wheat in the form of flour has been distributed so that every person has had plenty. It is quite true that in the United States the federal board did distribute, I think. 85,000,000 bushels of wheat through the Red Cross to be used for milling purposes and for distribution, but unfortunately, according to the last report, the farm board lost the huge sum of half a billion dollars. No person has received more than he could consume and no person here has received less. I submit that nothing that could be done in that direction would in any sense lessen the overages or the carry-over of wheat in this country at this time.
In so far as it is possible to give effect to the suggestions made by the hon. gentleman, I assure him that they had been given effect to before he made them; they had been acted upon by those charged with responsibility for relief. To a large extent the wheat has been milled at the local mills scattered throughout the province. My memory does not serve me as to the exact number of mills engaged in this work, but it is quite substantial. In the first place a contract was given to the large mills upon the ground that they would be able to discharge the obligation of distribution perhaps a little more readily than it otherwise could be done, but in other cases the local mills are taking care of the situation.
I fear that nothing that could be done in this direction would sell an additional bushel of wheat, would bring comfort where there is any lack of it, supply food where it is required; in other words, these things could not be done to a larger extent than is being done already. I say that because I desire again to pay tribute to the fine spirit which the hon. gentleman has manifested and the earnest effort which he has made to find some solution of what he regards as a pressing and difficult problem. But I assure him that the action which has been taken is such as to give effect to the very views which he has expressed.
Upon the second point I am bound to say that last year there came to me personally an offer-whether it was a bona fide offer or not,
I cannot say-that we should arrange for the purchase of large quantities of wheat to be shipped to China, and the price proposed was twenty-nine cents at Vancouver. We did not seriously entertain the proposal; for, if long credits are to be granted, obviously they would be better granted to those who are not engaged in war. That, at least, is the thought we had in our minds. In addition to that, if long credits are to be granted, they should not be granted on terms fixing the price of the commodity at the figure I have indicated. Therefore, so far as China is concerned, we did not make any sale, for the government of Canada has no wheat bo sell. It has no farm board that is the owner of wheat to be disposed of in any part of the world. All it could do would be to provide the means whereby the wheat could be purchased from the Canadian cooperative wheat fellers; for they and they only have any large quantities of wheat representing the carry-over to which the hon. gentleman referred.
Other communities made proposals to those who had wheat to sell. In some cases, at least so I am informed, they proposed to purchase wheat on long term credits and in some instances reasonable credits were given. But I w'as very glad to hear the hon. gentleman say that in the name of humanity it was not to be expected that we would supply seed grain to Russia on long term credits to enable her to destroy the price of wheat in the future as she had done in the past. That would probably be agreed upon by everyone. The hon. gentleman, who perhaps has followed this matter with much greater interest than any other hon. member, .said at once that necessity compelled the offering of wheat by Russia at a price which constituted dumping. I have already told the house of my own knowledge of what took place some years ago in connection with the price of wheat. Whatever else may be alleged by those who desire to support a position, this must be admitted, that the attitude taken by the .soviets in the disposition of wheat was responsible for the primary break in price. From that there can be no escape; it is a matter of common knowledge. It can be ascertained as accurately as one can ascertain anything the correctness of which he desires to demonstrate. It is true, as the hon. gentleman has said, that as a result of that action Canadian wheat prices .suffered, because Canadians offered wheat at similar or lower prices. Necessity, the law of supply and demand, fixed again the price, but when you have a commodity offered for sale without regard to
Farm Relief-Mr. Bennett

the cost of production and competitors endeavouring to sell the same article, they must accept the market price that is established by those who, as I have stated, tsell without regard to the cost of production. That, unfortunately, is true throughout.
Just let me mention three commodities in regard to which - that has happened in this country-wheat, timber, fish. When I heard the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Mackenzie) this evening in his admirable address, make reference to the bankrupt condition of the timber operators of British Columbia, my mind at once reverted to that contract which was offered a few weeks ago in Great Britain, whereby it was provided that, whatever fall in price may come about, Russia will go still further and thereby, regardless of competition as such, regardless of the cost of production as such, destroy the possibility of a market being made in Great Britain for British Columbia timber.
As regards fish, there are within sound of my voice hon. gentlemen who are thoroughly familiar with the -situation. When the hon. gentleman added a rider to his suggestion with respect to the sale of Russian wheat, I thought he was taking a correct course, if he would pardon me for saying so and not understand me as commending his remarks to the attention of the house. The position is this: There has been overproduction of wheat in the world. If I were inclined to do so I think I could explain to the house the reason for this. Wheat was a commodity that during the war was capable of being converted into now wealth on perhaps the easiest terms of any commodity in the world. The grower ploughed, harrowed, sowed, reaped and sold, and in one season new wealth was produced on a very large scale, because the prices paid for wheat during the war were, as the hon. gentleman said, very high. For some reason it was thought after the war that conditions that prevailed during the war would be continued and wheat would be supplied by Canada, Australia and the Argentine in increasing quantities to the former warring nations that were then at peace. But, alas, the fact is that in practically every country in Europe that had been engaged in the war, they began to devise methods, by the use of chemical fertilizers and otherwise, whereby they might increase their production of wheat, and at the same time they imposed high tariffs against importations of wheat from other producing countries. The result was that in one year France, as hon. gentlemen know, exported 15,000 tons of wheat to Great Britain, thus breaking the Canadian market there. The

Danubian provinces sold large quantities of wheat to nearby territory; Hungary was an exporting country and even Germany produced more than she required. The consequence was that markets that had heretofore been available for Canadian wheat were no longer available. Then came the situation to which I have just referred, so far as Russia was concerned. Regardless of the wants of her people, regardless of the necessity of the preservation of them from hunger and starvation, wheat which could be easily converted into money on the English market was rushed there and sold at a price that bore no relation to the cost of production, the result being that all the rest of the world suffered. As regards Australia, where wheat is sold in an entirely different manner from Canadian wheat, where it is all bagged, and is somewhat softer in quality than much of our wheat, a market was found in China and other parts of the orient. With the depreciation in currency, an increasing market is being found in Japan, because the wheat that has thus far gone to that country has been bagged wheat and not wheat in bulk such as we ship out of our elevators.
The problem that confronts the Canadian people is that propounded by the hon. gentleman, namely, the disposition of the surplus production of wheat in Canada. Last year, when the season ended, the producing countries had on hand, without any new crop, sufficient wheat to meet the entire requirements of the importing countries. It was in furtherance of the very thought which the hon. gentleman has expressed tonight that a wheat conference was held in London at which informally the Russian government was represented, and certain conclusions were reached. The hon. gentleman knows better than I that the same disposition on the part of the wheat producing countries has been expressed unofficially, as to the necessity for lessening the production and acreage. In this country the acreage could not be lessened by the action of this parliament except by resorting to export licences or methods of that kind, because it is solely a matter of property and civil rights within the purview of the provincial power. The matter has engaged the attention of the wheat producing countries of the world, the Argentine, Australia and European countries, and they have expressed the view that some action might be taken; but obviously that aotion, in which selfishness must play a very considerable part, is difficult to make effective because the extent to which there shall be curtailment of production is a question thni

Farm Relief-Mr. Bennett
is looked upon from a different angle by each, of the wheat producing countries. I suppose the house is familiar with the fact that a bill recently introduced in the congress of the United States contemplates the possibility of making curtailment of acreage the test or standard by which a certain bonus is to be paid to those who restrict production. The bill has no.t yet passed. I suppose it is difficult to say what its fate will be, in view of the fact that the present congress will end its labours at the end of this month.
I can assure the ihon. gentleman, first, that every step that can be taken to increase the consumption of Canada wheat by Canadians has been taken. It has been taken in various ways. The use of wheat in larger quantities has been impressed upon the Canadian, people, and in the matter of relief it may well be said that perhaps we have been over generous in so far as the distribution of flour and wheat and agricultural products is concerned. That complaint has been made, but I assure the hon. gentleman that one of the reasons why there has been a generous disposition of agricultural products, including wheat and flour-I should say flour rather than wheat-is that it lessened the quantity of wheat which was left in the country for sale and which found and oould find no market here.
Secondly, no action that could be taken through the Red Cross or any other voluntary organization could in any sense increase the quantity of wheat that could be consumed, or could in any sense lessen the quantity available for export. Lastly, every effort that could be made consistently with the maintenance of any price level at all for wheat has been made. I know of no case in which there has been the slightest hesitancy, shall I say, on the part of those who control the supplies of wheat to sell if the opportunity offered at the current market price. The only case of which I have any personal knowledge was when a suggestion was made for the sale of substantial quantities of wheat on a long credit basis but at a price several cents below the market price, and of course it would be impossible for the Canadian government to assist in the consummation of such a transaction.
I trust without going into the question of relief at this time, which I know the hon. gentleman does not expect me to do, and without amplifying the remarks I have ventured to make regarding the general principles which have governed us in the utilization of Canadian products, that the hon. gentleman will realize that no good purpose would be served by pressing the resolution beyond the purpose that has been served) already of having enabled him to make clear his desire to assist in every possible way, by suggestion or otherwise, in the solution of the difficult problem that confronts the Canadian people through their overproduction of a great world necessity. I think that every purpose that oan be served has been served by the address which the hon. gentleman has made. I thank him for affording the opportunity of bringing this matter to the attention of the house, and I trust that he will agree that the motion may now very properly be withdrawn.

speechtext:
I have been astonished, Mr. Speaker, by the statements of the hon. member for Melville (Mr. Motherwell). Before this house adjourned for Christmas some statements were made in the house by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) with regard to certain relief camps in the west. The hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid) also made reference to the same matter. Being interested in the camp in the
Farm Relief-Mr. Mullins

Riding Mountain national park I felt it my duty to go out and see what the actual conditions were. I found the men in that camp employed, well fed and well taken care of, and with not a complaint of any kind whatsoever. So the statement as made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre before the Christmas adjournment was not correct.
In my trip west I went through to Victoria, and accompanied by the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. Plunkett) I motored forty miles to look at the Outer Point camp. I sat down and ate a meal with the men, as good a meal as you could eat any place in Canada. Those men are well cared for, well fed with food of the very best quality. I looked at the supplies in camp and found that they were of the very best. I came to Victoria island and motored out some thirty or forty miles to Langley. I went into the camp there and I can say that the statement as made in this house by the hon. member for New Westminster, when he referred to the purchase of some wheelbarrows and to certain conditions said to exist in that camp, was entirely wrong. It was also unfair in view of the conditions as I found them. I also visited with Mr. Rogers of Jasper Park, who has a large number of men in a large camp there. These men are also well taken care of and well fed. I asked the men openly if they had any complaints to make, and they said, "No, none whatever." I felt satisfied that the men were being well fed and well taken care of.
I visited the city of Winnipeg and found conditions there the same. Then I went to Toronto and went into the little mission on Yonge street, where I saw four hundred men being fed food of the very best. I asked if they had any complaints of any kind to make and they said, " None whatever." They were being well taken care of. The only thing they wanted was work, but they realized the conditions.
So, Mr. Speaker, I say that this country is doing its very best for the unemployed. It is feeding them well and taking care of them, and surely there is no reason whatever for any such motion as is now before the house. I have stated the conditions as I found them in the various camps from Ottawa to Victoria. I am sure that Canada is doing her duty on behalf of these men, and if only hon. gentlemen would visit these camps I am sure they would not make the statements they do on the floor of this house. I heard the hon. member for New Westminster speak of a machine that was in use where these men

were on relief, and he said that you had to go seven or eight miles to turn it around. Mr. Speaker, you can turn that machine around on a quarter of an acre of land. I saw the machine myself, just to check up on the statement made by the hon. member for New Westminster. These rash statements that are being made are all erroneous. They must be made for some purpose, and I cannot understand what the purpose is unless it is to capitalize on the present day conditions. It must be that; it cannot be anything else. I cannot understand why the hon. member for Melville would put a resolution such as this on the order paper. If he would visit the different camps as I did, I am sure that he would change his views entirely.

I am, however, glad the hon. member visited there, because he did actually find the steel wheelbarrows there and they are still there.
When he says no complaints were made I would like to read one complaint that was published just after he was supposed to have visited this camp. This is from the Vancouver Province of January 29. It says that "in January two men drove up in a big car; one of them, very well dressed and with a big ring on his left hand, came into the shack to change his socks. He was covered with mud. After the man in the relief camp had helped to scrape the mud off the well dressed man, the latter handed him a big nickel." I can think of no one that could be but our hon. friend, and I am surprised that he would come back and make statements like that in the house. I would like further time to debate this, because I am not taking back any statement I made on the floor of this house regarding the misspending of money for relief purposes during that time. I have no com-

plaints about the camps now; the men, I believe, are well looked after and, I believe, well fed. In my criticisms I never made any complaint regarding the treatment of the men in the camps.

The hon. gentleman has spoken already.
Mr. J, L. BROWN (Lisgar): I was not aware that this resolution was to come up tonight or I might have been provided with fuller details than I have with me at the moment. The hon. member for Melville (Mr. Motherwell) has discussed the measure chiefly from the standpoint of disposing of the accumulated surplus of wheat. It is not my purpose to discuss it from that standpoint but rather to indicate what might be done in view of the experience of relief committees in the United States in making use of a product we have in such abundance. It has been my good fortune and pleasure to come somewhat in contact with the system followed over there, True, as the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) has pointed out, we in Canada are not in quite the same position as they were. The movement for the use of whole wheat was begun in a very small way in the town of Oberlin by one who had had some experience in its use in the early days in Manitoba. It began with wheat cracked in ordinary small hand mills. The movement grew larger and larger, and quantities of wheat were sent in from the surrounding country. Instead of using hand mills I saw them using two old cast off coffee mills and a farm grinder driven by electric power. This was in the town of Lorain, Ohio. At this time the movement had gained considerable momentum. The Prime Minister has said that boiled wheat will not keep people in good condition for very long. It may be that boiled wheat is not a very attractive diet, but it was clearly demonstrated that wheat ground in this primitive way could be used for the making of different products that were very attractive. I myself ate cookies and pancakes and muffins made from wheat ground in this manner. After the movement had been under way for some time application was made to congress to pass a bill granting, in the first place, forty million bushels, and I happened to be in Loraine when the first car of that wheat arrived from Chicago. I think the last word I got was that nine or ten cars had been used in that
one town alone. The movement spread all over the United States, until now I understand they have absorbed all the wheat that was held by the farm board.
I can agree pretty largely with the statement made by the Prime Minister that this particular movement would not relieve the farm surplus in any great degree, but I wish that relief committees in the various parts of Canada who are carrying on voluntary relief would investigate what has been done along this line in the United States. They would find that the sometimes meagre funds at their disposal could be used to very great advantage. I know the statement was made by the relief committee of the city of Cleveland that they had reached the end of their voluntary offerings, and then they received the wheat from the farm board. If my memory is correct they made the statement that this wheat would save them about $50,000 in that one year.
I believe this movement for the use of our wheat by relief committees already has begun in Canada. Shortly before I left home the announcement was made that if farmers would contribute quantities of wheat it would be ground and sent to the relief committee in Winnipeg. I do not advance this suggestion in the hope that it will take care of any great quantity of our surplus wheat, but I am quite satisfied that if the relief committees throughout Canada would investigate what has been done, see the various ways in which whole wheat flour may be used and the attractive dishes that can be made from it, they might find themselves able to carry on their relief work more satisfactorily than at present. I have not the slightest doubt, in spite of what the right hon. Prime Minister has said with regard to all cases of need being cared for adequately, that there are still many people in our cities who would be glad to get larger supples than they are receiving at present. While I was in the town of Lorain I saw the people come to the place where the wheat was being ground; they received supplies of the flour, and they expressed great satisfaction with what was given them. So it must not be supposed that this proposition simply involves giving wheat to people to be boiled, as might be taken from the words of the Prime Minister. That wheat was ground and the flour baked in such a way that no one, no matter what might be his tastes, need object to making use of what was furnished. If my words could be brought to the attention of relief committees in various cities of Canada I should be very glad to put them in communication with those who initiated the move-
20i56
Farm Relief-Mr. Stevens

ment in the United States, and who have followed its course during the last two or three years. I may say that from time to time I am in communication with those who began the movement, and I am quite satisfied that it has been eminently successful. As I said before, our government has not on hand a large store of wheat such as that held by the farm board in the United States; the circumstances are quite different, but I believe it is quite possible that relief committees in our cities might take advantage of what has been done in the United States in order to use their funds, which in many cases are all too inadequate, to greater advantage.

In the first place I would say that no matter how complete might be the adaptation of his suggestion in Canada, it could not very seriously affect the quantity of wheat which we have for sale. At the same tame, I agree that it would be desirable to stimulate the consumption of wheat and wheat products in Canada, which is such a prolific producer of wheat.
May I make just this further suggestion to my hon. friend and to others who may be interested in bis suggestion: Would it not be very fair to suggest that the relief organizations right in the heart of the wheat producing area, such as Regina, Winnipeg or other western cities, might try the plan which has been put forward so admirably by the hon. member for Melville (Mr. Motherwell) and the hon. member for Lisgar? Perhaps it would interest the house to know that a large corporation in this city, about as far removed from interest in or the production of wheat as any organization could be-I refer to the Canadian Bank Note Company-issued a most admirable brochure on the very subject which my hon. friend has mentioned. They had a dietitian work out a number of very excellent recipes using wheat, and I am sure they would be glad to place that brochure at the disposal of any organization interested. I do suggest very earnestly, however, that this plan might be tried in one of the great centres of the wheat growing area, and then probably it would spread rapidly to other centres.
In his resolution the hon. member for Melville refers to two matters, to the first of which I have just made reference, and which

I think was very well covered by the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett). The second suggestion is:
. . . selling on long term credits a substantial quantity of our embarrassing wheat carry-over to China. . . .
I wish to refer to this suggestion for a few moments. My hon. friend from Melville said:	"Let us sell the wheat on any terms;
get rid of it at any price". I submit to my hon. friend, though perhaps he was indulging in a superlative, really for the purpose of impressing the point-

Seriously, Mr. Speaker,
I want to draw to the attention of my hon. friend the possible danger in such a suggestion. As a matter of fact I rather deplore any suggestion of the kind going forth from this house, because I am afraid it will have a depressing effect upon an altogether oversensitive world market. Canada ought not- and I hope to demonstrate this in a moment -do anything that will give the impression abroad that we are in the position of having to sell wheat at any price. If we did that in connection with only five million bushels, which would not help a great deal when we are handling three hundred mitlldon or four hundred million bushels, it would inevitably depress the price for another forty million, fifty million or perhaps seventy-five million bushels. This market is an exceedingly sensitive organism, and the one thing we have been trying to do in Canada is to hold the marketing of wheat on a stabilized and what we might call an orderly basis. I can say this, I think, with confidence: I am sure that those who have followed the market with care, as I do daily, will agree that the Canadian marketing system has not beared the market unreasonably during the past year, but they have never refused to sell wheat when at was asked for by any market in the world. It would be deplorable were we to adopt in any sense the suggestion that we should sell wheat and sell it at any price.
To bear out what I have said, I wish to give to the house some rather interesting data. maintopic: PROPOSED TJSE OF SURPLUS WHEAT FOR RELIEF- SALE ON LONG TERM CREDITS TO DISTRESSED COUNTRIES
speechtext:
If the hon. gentleman will follow me for the next ten minutes I will endeavour to disabuse his mind of that depth of pessimism into which he has floundered. We are not being borne down or overwhelmed with an unreasonable surplus of wheat at this time. I venture to say that even with the large crop we have garnered this year the carry-over will not be more than it was last year. It may vary a little up or down but I do not think it will be much over; in fact I think it will be a little under. But circumstances outside of Canada are entirely different this year from what they were a year ago, so that even if we do have such a surplus at the end of the crop year it will be under conditions distinctly advantageous to Canada and not as they were in the previous year.
Let us look for a moment at the world situation as it is to-day. I have given it a great deal of very careful study and I base these observations upon the fullest possible information available. The world situation is this. Europe is bare of wheat, and that does not apply merely to the large centres where wheat is normally gathered, such as Hamburg, Antwerp, Rotterdam, Liverpool, and so on. I mean the country supplies of Europe. It has been the practice for centuries over there to carry in the stack considerable quantities of wheat on these small fawns. It has been a common practice for many years, but owing to two factors, first the bonuses in the way of high tariffs that have been given to the producers in Europe, and secondly to economic pressure, the farmers of Europe have sold off this supply.
Now it should be borne in mind that this supply hitherto held upon the farms in Europe has never entered into the statistics of the various countries When (figuring on wheat. This first came to my attention some months ago when I was making a careful anallytical
study of the figures of production and consumption of wheat, and I found the discrepancy. It was very difficult to understand it, but after we had given it a great deal of study we found that this invisible surplus in Europe, which has been -there normally for centuries and consists of a quantity estimated as between possibly 200,000,000 and 500,000,000 bushels-I think it is impossible to estimate it exactly-we found, I say, that this invisible unaccounted surplus -has been fed- on the market during the last three years particularly and accounts for the discrepancy in the figures we have had before us from time to time.
Bearing out my suggestion in that regard, there was a report issued -the other day by Broomha'lls, and although I am speaking from memory, not having it before me, I think I am safe in saying that in that report he pointed out that the stocks in Europe, visible and invisible, were largely exhausted; and he intimated, I think, that they were at their lowest point in the -history of buying countries. He -made the further observation that now was a good time to replenish these stocks because of the low price of wheat throughout the world. That is to say, in the buying countries the stocks of wheat normally visible and those that were invisible have been substantially if not almost wholly exhausted.
Turning to the other side of the question, we find that the winter Wheat area of Russia is below what it has been in recent years; that is, the acreage that has been sown and the condition of the wheat during the fall months of November -and December have fallen off. The land is not in good condition and the acreage is not as large as it has been, by a considerable number

I saw a figure the other day showing a diminution of 4,000,000 acres. Many of these figures one must not take too seriously, but it is a certainty that there has been a substantial diminution of acreage in Russia. Now the spring wheat area in Russia is known among agriculturists as in foul -condition, owing to new methods of farming and the rather disturbed conditions of the lasfc four or five years. There has been a growth of weeds which is familiar to many of our western farmers, who know how difficult it is to produce a good crop under such conditions. It can therefore be reasonably asserted that Russia will not be a serious competitor, certainly not if she feeds her own people in the next year or two.
We come next to the Balkan area, in part an exporting country although upon occasions it is an importing country. It is a heavy producer of wheat and the winter wheat area, although not seriously injured, is reported to be in a subnormal condition.
Farm Relief-Mr. Stevens

We turn from that to the Argentine. The present Argentine crop is a fair crop as far as quantity is concerned, but it is below normal in quality. Argentine wheat is one of the chief competitors of Canadian wheat, and I venture the assertion that it will not be on the markets in its higher grades to the degree expected a few months ago.

The point is that that grade is not up to normal.
We come next to Australia. This year they have a crop of good quality, but it is their third or fourth successive good crop, which is an abnormal number of successive good crops for that country. There has been a substantial increase of acreage in Australia, the present crop having been taken off an acreage some 2,500,000 acres above what it was in previous years.
The United States has been one of the depressing factors in the world markets for the last three years because of their veTy large surplus. I neglected to point out that in 1928-29 all the producing countries of the world had phenomenally large crops, and in addition Russia entered the market in the manner referred to by the Prime Minister a moment ago. All the countries were left with large surpluses, the total amounting from 350,000,000 to 400,000,000 bushels above what they were able to get rid of in the world market. I think the United States have been quite reasonable in their methods of marketing during the last two or three years; they have certainly not been unreasonable. The present crop of winter wheat in the United States is in a subnormal condition. A reduction in acreage has been referred to, but in the case of the United States there has been a greater reduction by nature than could be achieved by any constituted authority.

maintopic: PROPOSED TJSE OF SURPLUS WHEAT FOR RELIEF- SALE ON LONG TERM CREDITS TO DISTRESSED COUNTRIES
speechtext: What does the minister mean?

maintopic: PROPOSED TJSE OF SURPLUS WHEAT FOR RELIEF- SALE ON LONG TERM CREDITS TO DISTRESSED COUNTRIES
speechtext:
I am referring to the winter kill. The effects of this blight have been tantamount to a very substantial reduction in acreage. It is unlikely that the United States, even with a good spring crop, will have any more wheat than is necessary to supply their own needs. At the most there will be only a small surplus.
Canada has had a very good average crop. In some sections it was poor, but on the whole

it was of good average. As I indicated a moment ago, if I had expected this matter to come up I would have had the precise figures before me. Our wheat has been got out to the markets of the world in an excellent manner. Prices have been 'low and depressed but there has been a fair demand and our wheat has moved out better than in recent years. I think we are justified in saying that the marketing or the disposal of Canada's crop has been very satisfactory, other than in price.
We come now to the situation which may be faced next year. I say without much hesitancy that there is no likelihood of a depressing surplus this coming crop year, that is, after the midsummer period. Undoubtedly there is enough wheat in visible supply to take care of the world's needs, but, taking it by and large, there is not a surplus beyond what has in the past been looked upon as a reasonably safe margin. With one exception all the factors are present for an advance in the price of wheat, and that exception is the depressed and dislocated economic position of the buying countries. The buying power of the people in the purchasing countries undoubtedly is dislocated and subnormal, again using that term. All this is keeping down the price of wheat. I think the price of wheat is held down more by the inability to buy or the fact that people do not wish to buy than by the actual surplus of wheat visible on the world market. The outlook is not too blue and our people should face the present situation with a degree of reasonable confidence. I do not think it would be a good thing to have a sudden rise in the price of wheat or other commodities, but certainly an accretion in the price of wheat and other commodities is desired by all.
If we launch upon a policy of definite curtailment of acreage, I think there is a danger of stimulating still further the production in the buying countries. It must be borne in mind that the buying countries such as France, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands and other small European countries have in recent years, by means of quotas and high tariffs against foreign wheat, tremendously stimulated the production of wheat within their own boundaries. I do not think it would be wise for the producing countries artificially to advance the price of wheat by a curtailment of acreage. If this matter is to be discussed, to my mind it ought to be discussed with the purchasing countries sitting in. We must bear in mind that wheat oan be grown anywhere between the Arctic and Antarctic circles; it can be grown quickly; it can be produced in such countries as Persia and

Farm Relief-Mr. Stevens
northern Africa. A very considerable quantity is produced now in northern Africa to supply France with a portion of its requirements. If the big producing countries were to adopt a policy of unduly and artificially advancing the price of wheat, there would be that reaction.
My hon. friend suggested the marketing of some of our wheat in China, but there are one or two things that ought to be said in regard to that. Some months ago a group of clergymen waited upon mie to advocate this very thing. Their views were based entirely upon humanitarian grounds; their suggestion was motivated, I think, purely by a desire to have some cheap food given to those whom they conceived to be starving in China. We went into this matter with considerable care; we did not lightly dismiss it. I took the trouble to have our officers who are on the ground give it close attention and study. But in China certain conditions now obtain which make it physically impossible to get the wheat to the desired objective. For instance, let us take last year's flood area of which we are aware. I was told by men of repute, whose word could not be questioned, that it would be impossible to get in there, because lying between the seaboard and those areas were numbers of substantial army organizations with ambitious generals who were exercising jurisdiction over large provinces and who would intercept anything passing through. So that really had we done this the wheat we sent into China ostensibly for the relief of private persons suffering in some interior point would have been sequestrated by ambitious war lords who would use it for the purpose of supporting their armies. Of that I do not think there can be any doubt.
Another point in regard to the placing of wheat in China is this:	It is not, I think,
generally understood in this country that most of the wheat and flour that enters China goes through the Shanghai area. That is perhaps one of the largest milling centres and also one of the best organized business centres in the world. They think of these things purely and simply from a business standpoint. They are at present buying large quantities of wheat. They are jealously guarding the trade within, shall I say, the ambit of the area in which they are able to trade, and there is little possibility of passing flour or wheat through that area and distributing it, in any satisfactory way known to us, in sections either served by them or beyond the circle of their influence.
So I want to assure the hon. member for Melville that we have not failed to study the
question, but we feel the suggestion is impracticable. At the same time I should like to point out that very substantial quantities are now being sold to China, although Australia is selling much larger quantities than we are, the reason being the use to which the Chinese desire to place wheat or wheat flour, namely, for what is known as noodles or for the pastry type. They do not use light yeast bread to the same degree as we do. What we are trying to do, through the influence of trade commissioners, and so forth, is to stimulate the use of bread wheat and bread flour there; but the chief purpose for which they use wheat is to make soft wheat products such as noodles and confections. The consequence is that they prefer Australian wheat to ours, but there is this comfort for us in the fact that the larger the quantity of Australian wheat that finds a market in the orient, the less the pressure upon the Liverpool and European markets, so that whether it is sold one place or the other makes comparatively little difference. Nevertheless we are sending very substantial quantities of wheat and flour to Japan and northern China. We have recently opened a new market in the Dutch East Indies, and in many other places we are extending the market for Canadian products and doing everything we can to enlarge their sale.
It has been suggested by the Prime Minister that possibly the hon. member, seeing that we have had this prolonged discussion on his resolution, might withdraw it.
